maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the discussion that is now before the House I might be permitted to pause for an instant to place on Hansard a verbal wreath from the electoral district of South Renfrew to the memory of our - distinguished leader, the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose empty chair is a daily reminder to the members of the House that this great, this grand old veteran statesman, is -with us no more. His Canadianism was in a class altogether by itself. It was of the purest type, moulded on the world's best standards of patriotism. He ranked while living with the world's greatest statesmen and now that he is no longer with us in the flesh we unconsciously associate his name with those most prominent in world history-with Macdonald in our Own land, with Gladstone arid Disraeli, as well as with a host of other great and shining lights who have graced

Mr. Pedlow's speech was interrupted by the entry to the Chamber of Col. C. W. Peck, V.C., D.S.O., member for Skeena, B.C., who had just returned from active service. The House paid a tribute to Col. Peck's distinguished war record by hon. members rising in their places and cheering as he took his seat.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
As a parenthesis in the remarks that I was proceeding to make when the distinguished officer,

the hon. member for Skeena, B.C., entered the Chamber, I pause to express our sense of the great honour that he has conferred not only on Canada but also on this House. He has, like many another soldier:
" Trod deadly road to deadly toil Thickly strewn with dead,
Where noon-day sun and midnight oil Light the soldiers' tread.
I am delighted to have the privilege of welcoming him to this House to-day, and I trust that his distinguished career will be continued, to the benefit of this country, for many years to come.
When the distinguished hon. member (Mr. Peck) entered the House, I was about to call attention to some of the qualities of our late lamented leader who has passed beyond that bourne from which no traveller returns, and I was associating his name with those of some of the men most prominent in the world's history-with Macdonald in our own land, with Gladstone, and Disraeli, as well -as a host of other great and shining lights who have graced the brightest pages of history, in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe, as well as of Lincoln and others in the great nation to the south of us, all stars of the first magnitude, as Laurier undoubtedly was. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier's wonderful and many outstanding graces endeared him to all who had the pleasure of coming into his presence. To know him intimately was to love and admire our old chief beyond my power to express in words. Alas! this striking, unique personality will grace these halls no more in the flesh, that great masterly intellect is stilled for all time to come, but the work he was permitted, during his fifty odd years of political activities to do for his own beloved country will live forever more as an everlasting monument to his life and memory:
Short davs ago
He lived, felt dawn, saw sunsets glow,
Loved and was loved, but now he lies
In yonder fields.
To you from falling hands he threw The Torch-be yours to hold it high.
If you break faith with him who died He shall not sleep though roses grow
In yonder fields.
My next duty, Mr. Speaker, is to refer to the leader of our party who has been selected to occupy the place of our late lamented chief. While performing our duty to the memory of our late chief, we, on this side of the House at least, are not forgetful of our duty to his successor, and the loyalty we owe to him. It is with the very greatest of pleasure I assure him today publicly, as I have already assured 	I
him privately, of my loyalty in the very important position, both in the party and in the country, to which he has been elected, with so much unanimity by his fellow members in the House. His Majesty's loyal Opposition has at all times a very important part to play in the affairs of our nation-never greater than at the present moment, and the person filling the trying position of leader of the Opposition deserves, and will have, in order to induce good government, the united, wholehearted assistance of every one of his followers in this Parliament.
The entrance a moment ago to this deliberative assembly of the distinguished officer (Mr. Peck), to whom I made reference, reminds one forcibly of the fact that the war is over, and we thank God for it. After four long weary years of incessant appeal to the god of battles he has heard and answered our cry, and the prayer for peace is no longer heard in the land. In its place we have songs of praise out of grateful hearts, instead of the spirit of heaviness, for national salvation, and the greatest victory in freedom's cause ever fought and won, bringing in its train the dawn of a new era with such startling suddenness that we hardly knew how to give the thanks that we actually felt the occasion demanded of us. It is not with the slightest desire to dim the sword of Foch and his gallant fighting men, or to take from it the slightest touch of its power and glory, but I would say with him, and all the great commanders associated with him on both sea and land, in the words of Richelieu :
Let us own it; There is "one" above	

Sways the harmonious mystery of the world Even better than prime ministers.
Napoleon once claimed that the Lord was on the side of the cause with the greatest number of battalions, yet he, too, although almost a world conqueror, met his Waterloo. But with us the eternal question today is, how was the invader of Belgium held in check at Liege and in Northern France at Mons, and from' Mons to the Marne, until the cause of right was able to secure the greater weight of arms and men? Was the ability to struggle on against tremendously overwhelming odds simply and solely based on the dogged human pluck of men, -or was it not that there was something greater than mere material will power, something inspired? Was there not that something behind the arm speaking through the souls to the minds and muscles of the men? kitchener's little army of

contemptibles, in order -to stem the tide and onrush of the German hordes, fought every inch of the way from Mons to the Marne and buried themselves in everlasting glory by the thousand in France and Flanders' fields. And so, Mr. Speaker, let us to-day with a new vision repeat, once more, and with an added meaning, the prayer of Kipling's Recessional:
Lord God of Hosts be with us yet,
Lest we forget, lest we forget.
Now, Mr. Speaker, turning more particularly to the matter that is immediately before us on this occasion, the speech from the Throne, I have much pleasure, in common with all who have preceded me on both sides of the House, in tendering my hearty congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address. The hon. member from Calgary East (Mr, Redman) certainly acquitted himself most excellently in the effort that he put forth on the occasion of his address, and as to the effort of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), nothing else was to be expected than the able and eloquent speech which we had the pleasure of listening to from him. I was Tather interested though in some of the remarks of these hon. gentlemen, and I feel satisfied, notwithstanding the fact that they acquitted themselves well, that there was something held back, something ,that they did not care to lay before the House as coming from them, notwithstanding the fact that they claim to be the representatives of the returning men, and all honour to them because they themselves are returned men, but a fellow-feeling should make them wondrous kind. And for some unknown reason these hon. gentlemen seemed to hold back the information that they possessed, and failed to name the conditions that they wished to present to the House. For instance, the hon. member for- Calgary East stated'that the returned soldiers should not be hampered and irritated by red tape and unnecessary rules. .That, Sir, indicated to my mind that the hon. gentleman from Calgary East knew more than he cared to put on the pages of Hansard. I have evidence here to prove that there is considerable red tape in connection with the return of our soldiers from overseas. There is much uneasiness in the minds of returned soldiers; they are not at all satisfied with their treatment on coming back to Canada, having in view the fact that before they left Canada for the front they were assured that nothing would be too good for them when they came back. We find that the conditions on some of the
transports which brought soldiers home were not any too good. We find also that when the men return here they do not receive at the hands of the Government the consideration that they deserve. I have in mind one case of a young man who a( the age of sixteen volunteered as of an older age to serve the British Empire in the South African war. Immediately on the outbreak of the war on August 4, 1914, that same boy, who was then an employee of the Government in Ottawa, volunteered for service overseas and spent three years of his life in the fighting line in France and Flanders. He returned to Canada and again took up a position in the department from which he had retired to go overseas.
I would expect' the member for Calgary East (Mr. Redman) and the member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Man-ion) to champion the cause of such men, but they did not rise to the occasion, although I feel sure that they had the evidence at hand. After spending three years overseas on military service, this young man finds himself out-distanced and outclassed by men who failed to volunteer for service and who have been holding down positions in the Civil Service of Canada during the war. This returned soldier is in receipt of a salary of $1,500, while those who were his juniors when he left for- overseas are receiving $1,900 and $2,000 for similar services. From the evidence which is placed in my hands from day to day, it seems to me that the returned soldier and the returning soldiers are not receiving at the hands of this Government the treatment that they were assured they would receive, not even the treatment that they deserve.
I have here a letter of another character.' Two boys of the same family volunteered for military service immediately on the outbreak of war in 1914, and both are still overseas. In the early months of the fighting one of them was taken prisoner and was in captivity in Germany for over three years. When the armistice was signed he was a prisoner in Holland. On November 22 he was returned to England, and since, that date he has been so moved about from pillar to post that he has become lost in the " machine " over there and we cannot find any trace of him. I will read a letter which he wrote to his mother, dated at London, February 3, in which he states:
I am back in London; it is not that I want to be here, but that X got frozen out ^ of the camps. I have been down at Witley since December 5th, trying to get sent home, without any success. They sent us from Witley to Sea-

speechtext:
I bow to your ruling, Sir, but at some later date I shall certainly discuss this matter.
I should now like to place before the House the Liberal platform as enunciated at the Liberal convention held in the city of Ottawa on January 14th last'. It includes : Fair treatment for returned soldiers; generous care of the dependents of the fallen; restoration of the British preference to its pre-war status; reciprocity in food stuffs; gradual progress towards freer trade; the democratization of labour; the abolition of government by Order in Council; the repeal of the War-time Elections Act and support for a league of nations.
The achievements of the Liberal party when in power from 1896 to 1911 will be within the memory of some of the members of this House. They were briefly as follow's :
In 1897 there were 48 articles added to the free list and duties were reduced on 147-including farm implements.

In 1904 there were 14 more articles added to the free list and duties were reduced on 14
others.
In 1907 the duty on harvesters, mowers, reapers, and self-binders and binding attachments were reduced from 20 per cent to 17J per cent.
To Great Britain there was given a preference by way of deduction from the general tariff amounting to 33 4 per cent.	*
With the United States an agreement was effected in 1910 whereby the minimum tariff under the Payne-Aldrich Bill was applied to Canada while the maximum tariff under the same Bill was applied to other countries by the United States.
In 1911 the Liberal Government of the day negotiated a Reciprocal Tariff Agreement with the Government of the United States, under which when effective certain natural products were to be admitted free into both countries, and the duties on a limited number of other articles were to be reduced.	-
On submitting its policy to the people, the Liberal Government was defeated and was re' placed by a Conservative-Nationalist Administration under Sir Robert Borden.
After the Borden Administration attained office, the duties were increased on certain specified articles, and a further general increase of 71 per cent was placed in the Tariff on all commodities coming into Canada {rom outside Great Britain, and an increase of 5 per cent was placed on the .goods coming in from Great Britain.
Besides opposing the said Tariff increases of 71 per cent and 5 per cent respectively, the Liberal Opposition on different occasions since 1911, and more particularly on January 28th, 1914; on February 10th, 1914 ; on March 11th, 1914 ; on April 23rd, 1914; on April 28th, 1914; oit March 16th, 1915, and on February 23rd, 1916, moved in the House of Commons for reductions in the tariff on specified articles, and on each of the occasions mentioned their motions were defeated by the majority supporting Sir Robert Borden.
On May 23rd, 1917, the Liberal Opposition in the House of Commons moved an omnibus resolution embodying practically all the proposals for tariff reduction previously made by them in Parliament and defeated as in the next preceding paragraph mentioned.
The said omnibus resolution of May 23rd, 1917, was also opposed and defeated' by the Borden Administration.
The election manifesto issued in November, 1917 by Sir Wilfrid Laurier as the Leader of the Liberal Party, contained a declaration as Tariff Reform in these words:-
" In further mitigation of disadvantages to Agricultural production, I would immediately remove the duties on Agricultural Implements and' other essentials, as demanded hy the western farmers. A general well-considered reform of the Tariff for the purpose of helping Canadian production and relieving the Canadian consumer would also he an object of my administration."
Therefore he it resolved that in the opinion of this Association, not only should the said Tariff increases of 7 1-2 p.c. and 5 p.c. be immediately repealed, but that there should also be an immediate downward revision of the Tariff in accordance with the above mentioned omnibus resolution moved by the Liberal Opposition in the House of Commons on May 23rd, 1917, in these terms:-
"1. That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
" 2. That farm Implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
" 3. That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and foods therefor be admitted Into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
" 4. That substantial reductions be made in the general Tariff on all articles Imported into Canada, excepting luxuries.
"5. That the British Preference be increased to fifty per cent of the general tariff."
That is the platform on which the Liberal party stands four square at the present time. L make mention of it in order to show that it is in line with the demand of the community in general and especially of that portion of the community but feebly represented in this House at the present time-ll refer to the united farmers of this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having dealt at so great length with many questions, let me deal as briefly as possible with another- matter, one with which I am more familiar, perhaps, than with any other subject in the list; I refer to the matter of finance. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. iCarvell), on Wednesday evening last, sang a most doleful dirge over our federal finances, or at least his words certainly were not such as to make one very enthusiastic over the situation. He led us through an intricate maze of figures on into the slough of despond and left us there, without indicating how we were to make our way out-he left us to work out our own salvation in fear and trembling. His main query on the subject of Dominion finance was not exactly that made famous at one time in Ontario provincial politics, " Where " did " the money come from?"- but his query was;	" Where " will " the
money come from?" The position in which he landed this House on this question was enough to make pessimists of us all. To use an illustration that has been made famous, the hon. gentleman considered the doughnut and saw nothing but the hole-not a glimpse did he catch of the ring around the hole. He told us, among other things, that the public debt of this country in 1914 was $336,000,000, whereas it is now about $2,000,000,000. Rive years ago our interest charge on public debt was about $10,000,000 or $12,000,000, but now that charge has increased to the enormous sum of $110,000,000. This charge upon our resources, he tells us, will remain, if not forever, at least during our lifetime. Turning to the other side of the ledger he pointed out that our customs receipts would amount to $140,000,000; ex-



18, amounted to $2,054,915,245, and that manufacturers' exports, which included war material, during the same five-year period, amounted to only $1,499,020,143, showing a difference in favour of agriculture of $555,895,102, and proves conclusively that the agricultural community is the bone and sinew of this country, the foundation stone on which this country must build its future.
I find, also, from the Official Record- and, by the way, this is a paper that was established by Order in Council during the past year, I do not know for what purpose, the hon. member for Brorne ('Mr. McMas-ter) and myself hunted the library and reading room of this building a few days ago without succeeding in finding a copy of that publication; it was supposed to be established for the purpose of informing the public generally, but there was not a copy of it in either place mentioned, at least not then. However, I succeeded in obtaining a copy eventually, and from that publication I have taken these figures: Table I, National Wealth of Canada, $19,002,788,125. Of this total $5,216,117,000 is derived from agriculture, or over twenty-five per cent. I commend this fact to the notice of the House to establish further my contention that the agricultural section of our community is the foundation rock on which we must build the future progress of this country. We cannot, we must not, depend entirely on manufacturing concerns for our progress in the days to come, because these industries do not produce quite fifty per cent of as much of the wealth of the country as does the agricultural class. Now, the manufacturers claim that it is impossible to continue in business in this country and succeed, unless they are doing business behind the high tariff wall. If you continue building up this tariff wall you certainly will protect the manufacturers, but at the same time- you shut off the Customs revenue of the country. But let me give a case in point to explain my contention that it is not absolutely necessary that the manufacturers should receive the attention and consideration they demand. I have in mind an institution organized in the town of Renfrew for the manufacture of cream separators in the year 1910. I might just state that cream separators were placed on the free list in 1897. There were none made in Canada prior to 1897. A few only were assembled prior to that year, but not made in this country. The concern I refer to was established in 1900, that is the Renfrew Machinery Company. It has gone on successfully doing business in this country until its output covered the 
market from end to end of this Dominion. Not only that, Sir, but it has entered the United States, and is competing successfully for business with the best producers of cream separators in the United States and in the markets of the world.
There is another matter I would like to call attention to while I am on this subject, and that is the duty levied on motor cars.
A car costing $500 in the United States, costs, laid down here $712.50. A car costing $1,000 in the United States, costs laid down here $1,421. A car costing $1,500 in the United States, costs laid down here $2,137.50. To the Canadian price must Ipe added a duty of thirty-five per cent, plus seven and a half per cent, or forty-two and a half per cent in all.
Now, Sir, if you want to make the farmers satisfied with their lot in life, if you want to improve their surroundings, one of the best methods would be to supply them with motor cars at the lowest possible price. If you continue to collect the revenue that I have referred to on these necessary items for their service and use then, Sir, you will delay and retard the farmers in their operations and make them dissatisfied with their surroundings and life. Now what are we to have in Canada? Are we to have stable industries based on sound business principles, or are we to continue the maintenance of industries that require twenty-five, thirty-five or forty-two and a half per cent protection for ever more? I claim, Sir, that the time has arrived- nay, it is past due-for a revision of the tariff, and that it is not in the best interest of Canada that this House should pass over that important subject to a more convenient season. The country is up in arms against delay in the matter.
The Minister of Immigration the other night seemed to think that there was no need for alarm, but he certainly has not been studying the press of the country, especially the western press, or he would have a different opinion. I have heard of alarming conditions obtaining in the Western Provinces, on this subject-tariff reform-and I have read of extensive demands being made on representatives from western constituencies who are members of the Union Government. Such being the case I think the Government should address itself to the subject of tariff revision at the earliest possible moment.
Mr. Speaker I have transgressed at great length upon your patience, and the patience of the House, and I now beg to thank you for your kindness and your attention.

Lieut.-General Sir SAM HUGHES (Victoria) :	Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) on succeeding to the seat so ably and so long occupied by the distinguished and worthy statesman who has recently departed this life. I think possibly the leader of the Opposition will be frank to admit that in years gone by your humble servant contributed a good deal towards placing him in the position he now occupies. We used to have great delight in the olden days in annoying the hon. member, getting him to display his talents and his ability, and in that way he became skilled and polished and has risen to the high position which he now holds. (May we promise him that we will endeavour to test his temper occasionally again? <1 am sure that discharging the high and distinguished duties which he is now called upon to discharge, he will not hesitate to respond as he used to in the olden days.
The mover and seconder of the Address have distinguished themselves, not only on the floor of the House but elsewhere. The mover of the Address (Mr. Redman) in his dogged, determined, fearless manner, gives the key to why the Canadian position stood at St. Julien, and held back twenty times their number of the enemy. He was one of the lads who won distinction there. He got knocked to pieces a bit, but he is still able to hold his seat in Parliament and to do nearly as well as those of the community who did not go to the front. As for the eloquent seconder of the Address, (Mr. Manion) I was thinking while he was speaking, Sir, that if he had not kissed the blarney stone himself, he had either followed in the footsteps of some person who had, ox-had been conveniently near to some pretty girl who had performed this picturesque feat.
His address was a model in many ways. But, Sir, lest the public should think that these are the only two members of the House who have been to the front, permit me to draw your attention to the fact that a distinguished soldier has taken his seat in the House to-day. I refer to Colonel Cyrus W. Peck, the member for Skeena, who has won the Distinguished Service Order, with a bar, and also the Victoria Cross, the coveted highest honour of the Empire.
I wish to take the liberty of giving the names of other distinguished soldiers who occupy seats in this House, as well as of members of the House who are the fathers of distinguished soldiers. The list which I am about to furnish may not be complete, and I shall be very glad to receive any
13i
additions that may be offered. I trust that there will be no opposition to adding to the Hansard record any odd name that may be left out, because I think it is important that the complete list should go down on the record.
First, I find the name of a gallant lad who went over to the front, young Andrews, of Winnipeg. His father is Major George William Andrews, member, for Winnipeg Centre. I remember one morning in the year 1915 when I was passing down the trenches-the German trenches were about 80 yards away-I came across the familiar face of my dear old friend Andrews. He had a rifle, over his arm and he looked just as he used to look in the old days at the Dominion of Canada Rifle matches when he and thousands of other Canadian boys learned the art of rifle shooting, which they so aptly applied on the Germans when it came to facing them at the front. I asked Major Andrews what he was doing and he said that he was instructing snipers. As I passed, however, one fellow whispered to me saying that Andrews himself had "picked out" five that morning. I think that five a day was about Andrews' average. Father and son did their duty at the front fearlessly and well.
Then, there is the name of Colonel James Arthurs, of Parry Sound, whose son also was at the front. Colonel Arthurs went over in command of his battalion, reverted, went to the front and fought in the trenches in a subordinate position.
Colonel C. C. Ballantyne, -a member of the Government, took his battalion over and did his duty fearlessly and well.
Another name on the list is that of Willis Keith Baldwin, member for Stanstead.
Robert James Ball, of Grey, has a son at the front.
I need not say that Hon. Dr. Beland spent long, weary months in prison in Germany. Two others, step-sons, fought in the Belgian service.
Dr. Matthew Robert Blake, of Winnipeg North, was in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but he did not get across, through no fault of his; the fault was mine.
A case of distinguished service comes next. Mr. Ferris Bolton, member for Lisgar, had three sons who went overseas, and all three are to-day buried in Belgium,
Dr. Samuel Bonnell, of Kootenay, served at the front. Dr. John Wesley Brien, of South Essex, who had the distinguished honour of being born in the riding which I represent, also served faithfully and well at the front.

Our good friend, Mr. John Hampden Burnham, of West Peterborough, threw off his mufti, donned the uniform, took his training and went over to the front and did fearlessly and well his duty as he was called upon to do it.
Colonel Chabot was also in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but owing to the condition of his health I did not feel that I should let him go to the front.
Dr. Michael Clark, of Red Deer, sent three sons to the front, one of whom fell. One of those boys went away with the Princess Pats. When I was over there in 1915, I called the regiment out and inspected it. I asked how many of the original regiment were there, and I found that there were only nineteen. Talking to the boys, [DOT]one after the other, of the original Pats, I .-came across a lad by the name of Clark. I looked at him and knew in a moiment that he came from Red Deer. I asked him what he was doing there, and he said that they were going over the top every time they were called on. The Officer Commanding told me that Clark was the only man in the entire battalion who had never missed once going over the top-a chip off the old block.
Hon. Frank Cochrane had two sons at the front, one of whom has since died.
Mr. William Foster Cockshutt of Brantford had three sons at the front. I think that two were wounded, and I believe that one of them was wounded twice.
Major Richard Clive Cooper, member for Vancouver South, served at the front and was severely wounded.
Mr. Walter Davy Cowan, of Regina, has a son at the front, and was himself on duty with the Canadian Expeditionary Force at Regina.	'
Major Hume Cronyn, of London, had two sons at the front.
Hon. Thomas Wilson Crothers had one son at the front.
Robert Cruise of Dauphin, has two sons at the front, one of whom, I believe, has fallen.
Colonel John A. Currie, member for North Simcoe, served at the front with distinction at the Battle of St. Julien. I want to point again that the name of Colonel John A. Currie has been confounded with that of another, and deeds have been attributed to him that have not been creditable and that have absolutely no connection whatever with Colonel John A. Currie.
Mr. Arthur L. Desaulniers, member for Champlain, has a son at the front.

speechtext:
This is the list as far as I have been able to get it, and I

think it is proper that it should be placed on record. If there are any omissions, they are unintentional, and I am sure the House will permit me, if necessary, to amend it at any future time. I am very pleased to correct some omissions already.
Mr. E. W. Nesbitt, member for North Oxford, has his son at the front.
I am also told that Mr. W. D. Euler, member for North Waterloo, has a son at the front. I do not know whether Mr. Euler has German blood in his veins, but I am prepared to pay the very highest tribute to Canadians of German origin who went over with the first contingent and who fought as fearlessly and well as any of our men for Canada.
To these let me add the name of Col. Sam. Sharpe, who commanded the 116th Battalion at the front and rendered gallant service.
I had the honour, the same as many others, of being elected a member of this Parliament at the last general election. Long before Union Government was ever heard of, long before there was an election, I was pledged to. do my duty as in me lay for the upbuilding of the cause of human liberty and the over-throwing of autocracy in Germany, Austria or any other part of the world where it might raise its hydra head.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has overlooked the Postmaster General (Mr. Blondin).

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I am dealing only with the Commons. I would be delighted to add his name. We have from the Cabinet the distinguished names of General Mewburn and Mr. Ballantyne, both of whom I regard as my boys. I am sorry, however, that the Cabinet is not better represented, however few of the ministers have sons of military age to send.
I was elected a member of Parliament to help win the war, and I pledged myself on the platform as well as in this House to support this Government or any other Government in power, in every effort that might be made towards the successful prosecution of the war. In the session previous to the last general election, the Military Service Act was passed. I did not publicly criticise the Act, but I did speak to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and other members of the Cabinet about it. I pointed out the rocks that were ahead of them. That man certainly had very little political sagacity who did not see in the Military Service Act a first-class opportunity

for every man who wanted to stay at home to do so. That is what I pointed out to the Minister of Justice at the time, and 1 have never seen any reason to change my opinion of that Act since. I repeat, I was elected to support every measure for winning the war. I shall not here discuss whether the Government since the election has taken the action it should have taken towards winning the war, but I shall simply point out that I am not satisfied that they have done their best.
There are various forms of government, but to my mind there is only one form that should be encouraged in any country, aDd that is responsible government-government by the people, through the people, for the people. Under this form of government the leader of the party winning the election is chosen Prime Minister and selects his Cabinet, not from those pledged to oppose him, but from among those who travel along the same political lines as himself, and he stands or falls by his responsibility. In 1878 we had a Union Government in this country. It was not a machine-made affair, but went to the polls as a Union Government. The platforms of the opposing parties were laid before the people, and the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald was returned to power with a following thirty-five per cent of which was composed of former Liberals. That was a constitutional coalition. It was not a coalition of labels, but a coalition of ideas. In 1896 the Liberal party was returned to power by a large majority and twenty-five per cent of its following was composed of men from the Tory party, a great many of them being Orange-Tories who had been humbugged on the Manitoba school question. But whatever may have been the cause of that union, it was a legitimate coalition on constitutional lines. Then, in 1911, it is claimed there was a coalition between the Liberal-Conservative party and certain gentlemen in the province of Quebec who did not label themselves Liberal-Conservatives, to defeat the Liberal party in that election.

speechtext:
I shall deal with the coalition of 1917 at another time. There is no doubt whatever that in 1917 the great bulk of the Liberal party in many of the provinces would have cast in their lot with the great Liberal-Conservative party coalition or no coalition. I believe that every one of the former Liberal members of this House who have joined us on this side would have supported in any case the great Liberal-Conservative party at the last election. There would have been a natural coalition, instead of this patent machine-made affairs of Sir Joseph Flavelle, of the city of Toronto.
I have observed all the Orders in Council passed by the Government under the War Measures Act and I have yet ito see any necessity why the Government should have clothed themselves with these powers, except to guard themselves from the members of the House of Commons and from the people at large. I have yet to see any solitary Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act which has advanced the interests of the country in the slightest degree; I have said that before, and I now go further. I have yet to see where Ithe Pood Control Board was of any use to Canada, instead of being, as it was, a confounded nuisance to all the country. I have yet to see what good the Fuel Controller has done, except to add from two to five dollars per ton to the cost of coal. I have yet to see the necessity for any of these repressive commissions that have been set up under the War Measures Act. They were not necesisary in the administration of the affairs of this country and have done no good. I have not yet seen any justification for departing from the usual form of responsible government in war time. Any argument that can be used in support of all this repressive work in war time, to my mind, can be used with double force in peace time, 'and if we are going 'to have autocracy in time of war, let us have it in time of peace, too, and send for the Kaiser to run the country. I challenge any man in the Dominion of Canada to show me he necessity for one solitary act done under the War Measures Act.

There are a great many people who go around saying "I am not a politician. I take no stock in politics," and so on. I have never seen such a man who did not require careful watching. I can well remember the time when Sir Joseph Flavelle, the owner of this Government, delighted in pointing out that men in politics were quite unworthy of recognition, that one engaged in politics was to be loathed, or at least avoided, side-stepped. I have been a careful student of human nature all my life, and I say that I have never seen one of these gentlemen, whether preacher or citizen-well, I will not say preacher-who was not worth watching with both eyes open.
I am delighted to see such an independent House. There is a spirit of independence on this side, and I believe on the other side as well. I do not think for a moment that the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) can lead that array of talent, beauty and ability just ih the way he chooses or just in. the way that a caucus may decide. He will find a spirit of independence abroad in his following such as he has never found on that side before. And I know that I can speak for the leader of the Government when I say that the Government realize that they will have their hands full if they try to cajole, butter down, or side-track the gentlemen on this side of the House who have just causes of complaint to bring forward. This is not going to be the old-time patronage game. Those in authority are going to move, or the boys will know the reason why. I happened to be looking over an old magazine the other night and came across a picture of sturdy, staunch old John Bull, typical of British manhood. There was no camouflage about old John Bull, no particular attempt at courtesy, no preaching of "moderation" and all that sort of thing. Unfortunately the attempt is made to set up another type in place of the staunch old man, something of the Oscar Wilde type, the smooth, oily, pussy-footing type of statesman. But, thank God, the war has driven him out and reestablished plain, staunch John Bull as typical of British manhood. And Canada has been represented by the type of Jack Canuck, a stalwart young fellow-hat on, sleeves rolled up, collar open. I hope there will be no attempt made to replace him with the frock-coated, silk-hatted Jack Canuck as there seems to be some reason to dread in connection with Canadian public life today. I recall very clearly an expression I heard "years ago. A gentleman called at

our home, and when he had gone, my mother said, "Watch him; he is too smooth to be wholesome." Now, I do 5 p.m. not want any of the present Cabinet to take that to themselves-not necessarily.	Of course, if the
cap fits any of them they can put it on. I see two or three of them blushing. My good friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) is partly hidden behind the Minister of Militia (Major General Mewburn), but I can see the mantling blush steal over his features; while the acting leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) is bland as ever, but his cheeks show slightly heightening colour. I do not wish these gentlemen to think that I mean them; but, as I say, if they think the cap fits them, they can put it on.
Now, let us pass along. The acting leader of the Government commends moderation. I am delighted at his change of manner. In 1914 I had the honour, as Minister of Militia to be raising the forces, at a time when consternation bordering almost on paralysis pervaded the land. A government and people inexperienced in the art of war were brought face to face with the gigantic struggle of the ages. There was wide-spread lack of confidence on the part of the people in their own powers. And let me say, Sir, that that was one of the great things I had to do-to get our boys to feel that they could measure up with these machine-trained Germans. I knew what our boys could do. I had marched for years beside the Germans in manoeuvres, and had studied them; and I felt that, old and awkward as I was, I could handle any dozen of them. And I knew what our stalwart young fellows at home, the free-born sons of Canada, could do, even though they lacked training. I knew that they could do just what they have done-trim the Germans to a finish every time they got the opportunity. That is the great thing I found necessary-to work up the confidence of the people in their own power to fight. You all remember that. There was dread of the very name of German-like the dread inspired in France in the old days by the name of "Malbrouk." The clank of the German sword sent a shiver through our people. But, thank God, there were hundreds of thousands of our boys for whom the clank and jangle of the German sword was a challenge that roused them to instant ac tion.
There was prejudice, and envy, and jealously, on the part of one or two of my colleagues and of some others. There were some few attempts at favouritism. There

was criticism and fault finding galore, but in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred when traced up it was found to come from interested sources. Then I had to contend with the general reverence for the British model. I had the honour of telling one of the most distinguished soldiers in the British army-and communicated the information to the Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden) a few minutes afterwards- that the halo had gone off the British officer as a model many a long day ago, so far as I was concerned, and that the boys from Canada were going to be trained and managed according to modern ideas-my ideas. Then there was the other tradition that we must have men three years in training before they would be of any use in fighting. It was the old question:	Regular versus
irregular. But I realized what the French citizens had done in the revolution, when they defeated on many a hard-fought field the best professional soldiers of Europe- -machine trained soldiers. I had been an athlete and on many occasions I had met with my companions trained professional athletes, and I never knew an occasion when our amateurs could not work them off their feet without much trouble. I felt that the same' could be carried out in war. It was carried out in South Africa, and I took part in it. And in this war it has been carried out by soldiers not only from Canada but from New Zealand, from Australia, from South Africa, from Britain-these irregulars are able to hold their heads high in the company of the best British regulars. I do not wish to say a word to depreciate the British soldiers, the regulars. For next to the second battle of Ypres, which we call the battle of St. Julien, where our boys won a victory never to be forgotten, the first battle at that point, where Rawlinson's splendid corps held the position with only one man to the yard against twenty-five Germans to the yard and succeeded in defeating their foe, stands out in history as one of the great battles of ages.
Then, I had to maintain Canada's rights. Nearly every one thought our soldiers were merely British regulars. I had to fight that out single-handed. I am sorry to say, for the Canadian High Commissioner seemed to consider it his duty to thwart every move I made for the advancement of that cause. We had bad financial conditions in Canada -but of these I do not speak now. At that time, I regret to say, certain distinguished members of the Government were not moderate in their views or in their actions. Why, I have had ministers of the Crown
bombard me on behalf of different interests and in order to keep this business, that business and the other business from failing, from going to pieces, I was asked to buy a few hundred yards of cloth here, and a few hundred there. The Dominion of Canada was down to such a state in financial matters that we had to practically dole the contracts out, to give some business here, some there, and some elsewhere and this became a very serious drawback. But this matter will come up at some future time and I shall not go into details farther than to say that in 1914 the German propaganda was being put forward, peace was being talked all over the country and all of these matters were being raised in order to stop action on the part of the Government.
I found myself from the outset handicapped by the attacks of certain newspapers, the Montreal Daily Mail and Evening News, the Toronto Telegram, and another serious infamy was the course pursued by the London correspondent of the Toronto Telegram.. I was persistently maligned without the facts of the case being given and this course was pursued to the detriment of the Canadian service. The same gentleman who edited the Montreal Daily Mail and Evening News has been promoted and is now, I understand, head of the Canadian Official Record, I presume, as a reward for the attacks which he so persistently made upon me in the columns of the Daily Mail and Evening News. He has the honour of being a brother of the Minister of Finance.
I was in Toronto one evening away back in 1916 and I found that a number of the leading citizens-of course they were Tories -had been meeting at the hotel. They had been at the meeting, and they said there was a discussion as to the candidate in a certain division in Toronto and that some politicians not of their number would have to go to Ottawa to get a man with a special brand of politics to run in the constituency. There was a certain distinguished statesman rwhom it was desirable that they should get. But no one could be found to endorse the proposition. I was amazed. Next day I had the honour of speaking at the Empire Club. My staff officer, Col. Williams, came to me and said:	There is some mistake about
this because the distinguished statesman who was being reported last night as being unable to get a nomination in Toronto is in everybody's mouth here today as the man who should succeed Sir Robert Borden. They say that the Prime

Minister is a fishworm,-no backbone, not a strong enough man,-and that he must make way for this great statesman. I said: " That is very strange." I could not understand it. But I asked who was So-and-so, and I found that there were eight canvassers in the audience representing the various insurance companies, financial organizations and other business interests carried on under the auspices of Sir Joseph Flavelle who were busy passing through that audience, canvassing as far as they could against Sir Robert Borden as Prime Minister and demanding that he make way for another man. That opened my eyes.
I remember the conspiracy of 1915 to get rid of dear old General Bertram and Colonel David Carnegie, to whom the British Government and humanity owe much, who did such splendid work in connection with the production of munitions in this country. I remember that in 1915, in every restaurant, in every smoking compartment in a car, wherever one went, all over Canada, there was an agent of one kind or another, and when we came to trace that up we found that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred they were agents of this organization to which I am referring and they were canvassing against General Bertram and demanding that the Shell Committee should be reorganized. I remember that as part of the conspiracy.
Sir Joseph Flavelle became head of the Munitions Board, this work having been-transferred from the War Department in England to the Munitions Department. Then, following that, we find a certain distinguished citizen obtaining large contracts both in Canada and the United States for the supply of meats and meat products. We have had some evidence in Canada about meat profits, but we have only touched the fringe of it yet, and we have not got anything about what was going on in the United States. I am informed on very reliable authority that upwards of $5,000,000 monthly was handed over in the last three or four years in the United States under contracts with the British Government and other governments to this gentleman, apparently by reason of the position which he held as head of the Munitions Board, which gave him the prestige that enabled him to get all these things into his own hands, little by little, until the whole affair was brought in as an appendage to the business interests run by this Toronto organization. Its estimated profits will be upwards of $100,000,000 in the last four years on these commodities alone.

Then, having obtained control of the Munitions Board and having obtained large contracts, these gentlemen turned their attention to politics. Their political ambitions were as yet unsatisfied. I remember one Sunday morning entering a hotel and seeing seated at a table Sir Joseph Flavelle who had always tabooed politics, Mr. A. E. Ames of Toronto, who had never been a party man of any great standing, Mr. Bundle-I am not saying a word against these gentlemen; they are all very good fellows in their own way- Mr. Rundle of the National Trust, who succeeded the hon. the Finance Minister, Mr. Gundy, a nice little fellow who has evidently an eye to business whether it be in connection with the handling of munition contracts or the Victory Loan, at least these are the names given me-I found these gentlemen and some others'seated at a table. Probably Sir Joseph had obtained a respite from Gabriel during this short time on Sunday morning to talk matters over with these gentlemen. I do not know whether they had any other unction or not. But at all events it would not make any difference whether they had or not.
These gentlemen then proceeded to carry on their work of saving Canada. They went to the residence of Sir Wilfrid Laurier by arrangement at 12 o'clock and I understand that the luncheon was very fine. They stayed there until four and they tried to induce this worthy old statesman to join in a Union Government with them. They were going to be content with Sir Wilfrid Laurier remaining Prime Minister for six or nine months, or a year, then he was to make way and was to be succeeded by one of their friends not a thousand miles away from the seat occupied by the Finance Minister to-day. The wily old statesman sent them away and they returned to the hotel to consult some of the lesser lights of the Liberal party. An arrangement was made, I understand, that a meeting of the warriors of the Liberal party should be held the next afternoon. The Premier of Quebec happened in and I do not know whether it was a patriotic reason or not that brought the hon. gentleman who is now the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) but he also blew into the city on that day. I do not know whether he figured as the second lieutenant or as the first lieutenant. I could not say what part he played, but he was in town. Nothing came of it. At all events the result was that the

wily old statesman declined to have anything to do with it.
Let me recall the circumstanct s to you. Let me recall to your minds what had happened. There was a speech made in Ottawa some time before that in which the statement was made by Sir Joseph Flavelle that whatever government was formed the French element must be dominant in it, must have a voice in it-in fact, all the peculiar elements in Canada must be represented in that great Cabinet. The following Monday, I understand, there was to be a speech delivered in Toronto by the hon. the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White). It had been placarded, and thousands- some say tens of thousands-of cards of invitation had been sent out by friends in the city of Toronto to come and hear this address, that there was to be a very important message delivered. But the awful correspondent of the Toronto Globe in Ottawa happened to send a despatch that night showing what the game was-that Borden was to be thrown out, or disposed of in some way. He and Bennett were away on a junketing trip in the West at this time, but Borden was to be thrown out, and the mantle was to fall on the shoulders of the young gallant and handsome Finance Minister. Whatever happened, the important message was never delivered. A wet blanket fell on the meeting, and it was said that it was one of the deadest shows that ever took place in the city of Toronto, excepting the meeting addressed by the Prime Minister and Mr. Bennett later on, the following month, when they had to hustle down three battalions of soldiers from the Fort in order to make an audience at all for them. Well, Sir, a change of scene occurred a little later, when, failing to wheedle Sir Wilfrid Laurier into the leadership of this new party, they turned around and the cry became very vociferous to condemn Quebec. She must be ostracised, and all the enemies of Canada and of the Empire must be disfranchised in the coming election.
We were asked sometimes by people in our ridings what this Government had done. Well, to make as nice a story as I could, I always told them: "They have appointed, the Knights of Columbus have appointed, somebody to some job in the riding, and things are going on very nicely; I am relieved of patronage, and I have no more to say in matters of government, but they are getting on very nicely." One of the questioners came to me one night, and said: "They are adopting high-handed methods
by the suppression of free speech, they are shutting out all criticism. Knowing a young gentleman who was to speak in the city of Winnipeg, but was held up as if he had been worse than a German, I can speak in the interests of Canada. They are trying to build up an oligarchy in Canada, and the Government is being run by orders in council." He said further: " The Acting Prime Minister may as well take a packet of poker chips in his pocket and let the rest of you all go home."
Now let me deal with certain measures that have been enacted. The Dominion Registration Act, one of the most infamous laws ever enforced, has been borne by the people with more than patience. In other words, we are in thorough training for Kaiserism. The Military Service Act, and the Registration Act, I shall not discuss here, nor the provost marshal and military police work. All this, and the detective work in connection with this class of thing, is contrary to the dictates and wishes of a free people. The press, by means of sweetening, and also by censors, has been worked with conspicuous zeal. In the shape of sweetening we find that $50,000 was given the Canadian press for wiring intelligence from coast to coast, although I do not object to that at all. But there was the fixing of the price of news print at $50 a ton on November 19, 1918. That was extended to January 14, until after the elections had taken place, when the price was placed at $69. Then there is the cost of advertising the Victory Loan, and the advertising connected with registration and repatriation. The Government has been very good in buying 250,000 copies of The Veteran, the organ of the veterans, to send to the boys. Again there is the cost connected with maintaining the Director of Public Information and the Canadian Official Record to be added to the expenditures which I have enumerated-in other words, the sweetening of the press. That is very nice and I suppose the press is supposed to be paid for all this propaganda and camouflage work, and so on, of the various ministers. Let me refer in this connection to certain very interesting procedure which took place. It seems that one of the ministers was getting too much prominence on the front page of this Canadian Official Record every week. A solemn protest was accordingly entered on behalf of the other ministers by a certain gentleman, and it seems to have been heeded, because if you look at the Canadian Official Record now you will see that f ormerly the Minister of Finance was given front page recognition for weeks

in succession, and it was too much for the other ministers. Now one week attention is paid to the Acting Minister of Justice and the Minister of the Interior. Another week it is the President of the Privy Council, and so on. They are distributing the moneys, these gentlemen who are running neck and neck, for publication purposes, and that gets them notoriety before the public. If you watch it, you will see the official organ going out along these lines regularly now. I do not know whether it does any good or not, but that is neither here nor there.
Now, Sir, the Dominion of Canada trained an army of free men. That army has distinguished itself, and it needs no commendation here or elsewhere. I challenge the world to show where any soldiers in the world have conducted themselves better as soldiers than the men who composed this army. They spent months and months training in Canada, they went to the front absolutely under control, absolutely well trained, absolutely the best shots that could be found, and in no solitary instance, barring one or two affairs of liquor, has there been a solitary case that would be worthy of police court record in the whole Dominion of Canada. The force sent overseas by Canada is something that any country might be proud of. I therefore feel more or less out of touch with the ordinary feeling that is expressed in this House and the country about these soldiers, as to what we must do for them when they return, and how we must coddle them up. I do not think, Sir, that that is the right attitude to take at all. What should be done I will deal with in a few minutes when I come to the question of demobilization and re-establishment. What I want to point out is this: I recommended, while in office, to the British Government and to the Canadian authorities, certain suggestions with regard to the composition of our forces. After building up one division, we had two divisions formed. After creating two divisions, we had four divisions formed, and that made a corps. I wanted to have three divisions in a corps, and three brigades in a division, with an extra battalion in each brigade, besides the divisional corps. The plan was adopted in Germany, it was adopted by the British, but it was not adopted by the Canadians at the front. The obstacles to the adoption of that policy I shall not discuss here further than to say that the two Ministers of Militia-the gentleman here and the gentleman in London-ran foul of each other.

There was no co-ordination between the two departments, there was no co-ordination between the Militia Department in the Old Country and the High Commissioner's Office-one seemed to be thwarting the other. They tried to thwart them then as they tried to thwart matters in my time. There was a vendetta practically between the boys in England and the boys at 'the front, there was Government favouritism, and interference, and unworthy ambition on each side of the Atlantic. This handicapped the thousands and thousands of gallant fellows who were anxious to do their duty. However, this little intrigue went on until 1919. My information, which has been borne out by every man who has returned from the front, was such that I wrote to Sir Robeift Borden on January 14, 1918, as follows:
Ottawa, Ontario, January 14, 1918.
Dear Sir Robert,-There are a number of important matters1-now that the elections are over-which I think should be laid before you for consideration and action, and it has occurred to me that it would he advisable to talk these matters over first before they would be placed in concrete form in detail, or brought up in the House.
They concern such matters as,
1-Six divisions and two corps instead of four divisions and one corps.
2.	Little intrigue regarding the supplanting of
Haig by Byng, and the action of certain Canadians therein.
3.	Appointment of senior officers.
4.	Potent influences affecting senior promotions and appointments in the Canadian army.
5.	Lens, and somewhat similar massacresand the object in each.
6.	Condition of AFFAIRS IN BRITAIN, and
the causes thereof.	[DOT]
Will you please address your reply to Lindsay as I am leaving for home to-night.
Faithfully,
(Signed) SAM HUGHES. The Right Honourable,
Sir Robert L. Borden, G.C.M.G.,
Prime Minister of Canada, Ottawa.
In reply he told me that he hoped to meet me towards the end of the month, and I came back on three different occasions. On two of them I could not see him; the third time he was away. Following that came the great disaster at St. Quentin. On March 25, 1918, the Prime Minister said in the House of Commons-page 116 of Hansard-after reading the reports from the front:
So far as one can judge, the Germans are undoubtedly throwing absolutely their full force into this attack. It seems to have been met with great success as was anticipated from the first. It is beyond question that very much depends

upon the issue; and I know the heart of the people of the whole country will be lifted up in intercession that the right may prevail.
I then said:
Intercession is very proper, but with the view in a slight degree possibly of helping on the cause I desire to ask the Prime Minister the following questions :
1.	Inasmuch as Canadians are engaged in the titanic struggle now going on for the preservation of human liberty, is the Government taking necessary steps to maintain to the highest degree the pride, the courage, the resolution, the steadfastness and the confidence of the splendid and gallant soldiers of Canada, as well as of the Empire at large in this struggle?
2.	Have the Government taken precautions in the management of the forces, the appointment and the promotion of officers therein and the granting of honour, awards and decorations thereto, that favour from female society, creed or other undue influences, shall not prevail, but that all shall be awarded on the one basis of merit and fitness alone?
3.	Does the Government purpose doing anything to prevent panicky and sensational despatches which merely cause nervous excitement among soldiers and population in Canada and overseas, from being issued by a few mentally epileptic newspaper reporters from overseas?
4.	Has the Government any explanation of why the allied forces, splendidly armed and equipped, and in chosen positions of their own, made up of the best men in the world, and numbering from seven to ten men per yard of front-/
It is estimated that I was considerably [DOT]under the proper number. (Reading):
-recently gave way before an enemy not their equal in manhood nor superior in armament, even though they numbered thirty men to a yard of front in attack?
Then came the secret session. Without divulging anything that happened at that marvellous, blue-ruin session, I may (joint out that my attitude was this: Although we occupied the lowlands, there was nothing to prevent our defeating the enemy with the greatest of ease provided we had the heart, the resolution, the courage, and the organization. We had better men, we had better armament, and our cause was just. I pointed out on that occasion what Rawlinson had done and what the Canadians had done at St. Julien, and contended that with the necessary degree of resolution restored to the British forces, before many months they would be doing exactly what they did do-driving the Germans back over the same ground from which our forces had retired a few days previously.
A short time after this the Prime Minister suggested that I talk over with him some of the matters that I had referred to. I pointed out, however, that the blow which I had sought to avert had fallen, and that it was therefore useless to discuss the matter. On the last clay of the session the Prime Minister sent for me and asked me
to communicate to him any suggestions that I had to make as he was leaving for England. I pointed out to him that I was not any longer his adviser, and he repeated the question, but I declined to comply with his suggestion. I gave as my reason the fact that the gentlemen with whom he was associated in the Old Country would undo whatever he might of himself be willing to do; that the officer in command of the Canadian forces in the field and the Canadian High Commissioner, who has exercised a malign influence on the Prime Minister ever since the formation of this Government, and others in the old land would exercise this malign influence over him and that it would be useless for me to do what he suggested. He then asked me to give him the names of any Canadian officers whom he might consult. I asked him what his object was; whether it was to have certain gentlemen still further hunted, driven from the forces and ruined, as had happened to every man who was known to be a friend of mine in connection with the service. So I declined. I did speak to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Hon. J. A. Calder) who, 1 was confident, would keep his mouth shut unless it -was advisable to give out the facts. I did give him a few pointers, hut I did not feel that I was called upon to give them anywhere else. Every pointer that I gave turned out to be absolutely correct.
However, on February 25,	1919, Sir
Thomas White said-p. 33 of Hansard:
It will be an eternal source of pride to the people of this country that the first troops to enter Cambrai, which was the 'great bastion of German defence on the West, wore the uniform of Canada. It will also he a source of noble pride to the people of this country that on the last day of the war Canadian troops entered Mons, from which the British forces at the beginning of the war had been driven by overwhelming enemy forces.
Well, Sir, from the outset of this war I am on record as standing for the saving of tiie lives of our boys unless it was absolutely necessary that they should be sacrificed. This wasting of gallant lives went so far that on one occasion I notified the 'British Government through' Field-Marshal Sir John French that this petty nibbling, these foolish attacks-"stunts," they called them-should cease, and that if these movements were to be carried on, the Canadian forces would lose hundreds of men with no possible advantage as a result. They fought the battle of St. Julien without having gone through any of these stunts for training purposes, and they had smashed the German forces to a finish.

I am not blaming the Government, as this may be due to some sub-agent or heeler, but the Government must assume the responsibility. I have no use for Civil Service Commissions for the purpose of filling jobs. I have every faith in the Civil Service Commission for the duty for which it was constituted. But, in years of service in this House, I stand now next to my good old friend the hon. member for Grenville (Hon. J. D. Reid), I have never dodged my responsibility. I have always held that the member or the defeated candidate should be responsible for the patronage of his riding, because some one must be the responsible head in every riding to look after the patronage. I have never evaded my responsibility, and in my county I have never made an appointment with which any fault was found. Under this Government, we cannot assume the responsibility and this dodging, pussyfooting and side-stepping must cease. This is a democratic Government, a responsible Government; and as a member for a constituency, occupying a seat in this House, I shall insist on the responsibility being exercised by some one other than irregular organizations such as the Knights of Columbus and associations of that kind in the riding that I have the honour to represent.

Oh, no, I treat all just as they come. In regard to demobilization, the first thing is to get population. I like to look back on the development of the Great Northwest. I see gentlemen occupying seats in this House who will remember the days long ago when one would travel hundreds of miles throughout the Northwest without coming across a house. In 1895 I had the honour of drawing Sir Clifford Sifton's attention to the fact that those places were fit for settlement. Sir Clifford Sifton pushed the roads through, and great credit is due to him for developing that part of Canada. He may not have done it to suit everybody, but he has done it well. The men from the Northwest have been a credit to the British Empire and a credit to Canada.
First of all, get population; get people with money. Develop the country. Build railways and get people to settle on the land and produce, and then you will have banks and churches and schools and lawyers' offices and every other kind of activity. There are hon. members of this House from
[Sir Sam Hughes.!
the Northwest who remember when they went in there ten or fifteen years ago the country was unsettled; but to-day it is all settled, and thirty years from now the portions of the great Northwest that are unsettled to-day will be dotted with cities and towns that are now never dreamt of. I would build railways to new sections opening up. I would give the people drainage facilities. The hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) said the other evening that upwards of a million people could be settled in a certain district out west if they had proper railway facilities. I would build wagon roads alongside new railways. 1 would also build river bridges. I would build coal roads from the Rocky Mountains to the city of Winnipeg, and on to Ontario, Quebec and from Nova Scotia. I would use four roads for this purpose from the Rocky Mountains to Winnipeg so that every section could be served, and I would have the tracks so arranged and the cars so constructed that one engine could haul as big a trainload as the ordinary steamer. I would develop the fish industry, by providing trawlers, ocean cold storage for fish, refrigerator cars, cold storage houses, and utilize fish offal. The fish industry has great possibilities. I would also develop our timber, both hard and soft, and develop water-powers. I would have central municipal coal yards with control over distribution and prices. I would develop the minerals from the Mackenzie river to Ungava, and would have harbours on the new coast. I would build a railway to the Klondyke. and buy a sea coast strip from the United States. I would have a study made of the chemistry of natural and other products. I would settle the soldiers on the land as far as possible, and afterwards sell land to settlers other than soldiers. We shall need millions of men, instead of a few hundred thousand. These soldiers returning to Canada will not be content with second-rate Civil Service jobs. It has been my privilege to look in the faces of thousands of our boys. I saw in Detroit not long ago a man with a cork leg walk five miles without a whimper. These men do not want coddling. They will tell you themselves "For God's sake, get them to let up on this coddling business." What we want is an opportunity to earn a living. Give us that opportunity, and we will not pester you for elevator and post office jobs." Give the boys a chance to open up new country, and you gentlemen sitting around me who went to the Northwest ten or fifteen years ago not so wealthy as you are to-day will find your success duplicated by our

soldier boys in the years to come. The soldiers are the best men we can get. Physically, some of the poor fellows are not what they should be, but mentally they are better than they ever were. They are more stern, more serious than they were. The war has added twenty years to their lives. As an illustration, I would point to the Mowat family. Sir Oliver Mowat's father was an old soldier. Sir David Mac-Pherson was also an old soldier. In fact, the ancestors of most of the big men of a decade ago were old soldiers who had had stern training and brought discipline and seriousness into their home life. This same serious spirit will be carried into the homes of our soldiers. An odd soldier here and there will go wrong, but so does an odd preacher; but why blame the soldier any more than any one else? Why cannot a soldier have a good time once in a while if he wants it? I am not here to defend that sort of thing, but humanity is the same the world over. But that is no reason for coddling the soldier. Give the boys a chance. They have conducted themselves nobly as soldiers, and before they went overseas and will do so in the future. I do not share the fears of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), who the other evening seemed to apprehend some sort of danger from these returned soldiers. I have not yet found one of them who was not a law-abiding and thoroughly good citizen. I know that there has been trouble in Toronto over aliens, and in my riding also, where some aliens have as much as six or seven thousand dollars in the bank and a big roll in their pockets. When our boys come home, practically incapacitated many of them, and see that sort of thing ana the alien wanting to hold on to his job they do not like it. In my riding we have taken precautions to make the employers understand they had better get a move on. I understand that one minister of the Crown has been told to get rid of the aliens at his factory in Toronto and give the returned soldiers a fair show. The soldiers do not want to be coddled; they want an opportunity. Let us give them the opportunity to create new cities and towns and homes and farms, and they will gladly accept it in preference to a second or third class job in the Civil Service. If given the opportunity, our soldiers will prove themselves fit for the very highest jobs in the land.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

I hurried in the hope of finishing my address before six o'clock, and in my haste I did nbt say fully what I wished to say on one point about the returned soldiers. We need not have any fear whatever of the returned soldiers, if they are anything like properly used. Otherwise it is hard to say what we may look for. I anticipate-and I think the future records of this country, when they are written, will bear me out-that our returning soldiers, four hundred thousand or five hundred thousand are going to be the greatest thinking and acting asset of the Dominion of Canada in the years to come. Like all old soldiers they will be steady, hard men. I believe that the history of all the victorious and Allied countries will show that we are entering upon the Periclean, the Augustine



Age, the Renaissance, the Elizabethan period, the Reformation period, of our time, to be marked by a great outburst of literature, art, and general progress.
Now, I will only take a few minutes to touch upon an aspect of the case more practical than theoretical-the financial aspect. I would refer hon. members to the report of the Department of the Treasury in Washington, of 2nd December, 1918, the report of Secretary McAdoo to the House of Representatives. I have here the official document, but I read from copies that have been made. He refers to the raising of great loans and the advancing to allied countries of a sum upwards of $9,000,000,000 in cash. He said:
The fundamental fact underlying these great economic achievements has been the inflexible spirit and purpose of America to secure for the world the blessings of that kind of liberty and Justice in which America was conceived, and without which neither America nor civilization can exist.
Speaking of the third Liberty Loan he said:
(1) With the bonds of previous loans selling below par and industrial and other securities yielding a return much in excess of the interest rate on Government bonds, the question of the rate of interest on the new bonds became acute. It was the general banking opinion that the rate should be 4J per cent and few believed that it would be possible to sell the necessary large amount of bonds at a lesser rate. The Treasury on the other hand stood firm In the belief that,
1-	The rate of interest would not of itself maintain Liberty bonds at par in the financial market.
2-	That the price of Liberty bonds, even though quoted at less than par on the exchanges, would) not deter the American people from buying at par the same bonds when offered by their Government to secure the necessary funds to carry on the war.
In other words, they would show themselves patriots, not grafters.
3-	That the patriotism of .the American people was not measured by interest rates nor determined by the fluctuations in the market prices of Government bonds on stock exchanges.
, The situation was very complex. There could be no denying the fact that existing issues were selling below par, nor could there be any refutation of the claim, except by actual experiment, that the investing public would not buy the new issue at par when the same bonds could be bought in the open market below par. The Treasury felt, however, that to raise the interest rate to 4J per cent would mean a corresponding' increase in the cost of the war and force still higher interest rates on future issues of industrial and other securities as well as further to depress the price of existing long term bonds. On the other hand, it seemed clear that the time had arrived when every effort should he made to stabilize the interest rate on Government bonds and to reach a point where there would no longer be expectation of further Increases in rates.
It was decided, therefore, to recommend that the Congress authorize the issue of a ii per cent nonconvertible bond or an increase in the interest rate of one-fourth of 1 per cent instead of an increase of one-half of 1 per cent. Such a bond, it was believed, would result in accomplishing two things1,
1-The stabilization of the interest rate as far as it was possible to stabilize it in the extraordinary circumstances then existing.
and,
2'-The elimination of the conversion privilege, which had become no longer necessary for the sale of the bonds and which in itself had a tendency to create a demand for a constantly rising rate of interest on successive issues.
Speaking of the fourth Liberty Loan Secretary McAdoo said:
I have sought to avoid the issue of bonds at such a -rate and upon such terms as might result ultimately, when the war is won, in the accumulation of great wealth in the hands of a relatively small proportion of our population, carrying interest at a high rate and exempt from taxes.
The oversubscription of this largest of all loans was the greatest financial achievement in all history and a wonderful manifestation of the strength and purpose of the American people.
