wrong road, but it is very freely implied, and indeed it is stated, that we left Liberalism.
Hear, hear.

I think I hear a mild "Hear, hear" from an hon. gentleman opposite. Well, if the point I have already made has anything in it, it would be so much the worse for Liberalism. But did we leave Liberalism? Whence have we to derive our Liberal traditions? It would be no use asking my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), who takes an intimate and well-informed interest in old country politics, to derive any inspiration from Mr. Lloyd George, because I am quite sure that Mr. Lloyd George does not possess a particle of his confidence; but surely the case of Mr. Asquith is different with him, and Mr. Asquith was at the head of the Government in the old country which introduced compulsory military service there. I differed from my hon. friends opposite on the question of compulsory military service; I also differed from them, and was almost alone on that side of the House in that respect, on the question of the extension of Parliament. But Mr. Asquith was responsible for several extensions of Parliament in the old country.
He protested against an election up to the end of the war, and kept on protesting against an election even in the early days of reconstruction. So, after all, if I have fallen from the grace of Liberalism I have fallen in very good company, for I still have the company of Mr. Asquith and the entire Liberal party of Great Britain-and that is not a bad record for a Liberal who was raised in the atmosphere of British Liberalism. We do not admit that we left Liberalism-not for one moment.
There is a third thing implied in this invitation that has been extended to us from the opposite benches, and that is that we should turn to those on this side who were formerly known as Conservatives and say to them, at this moment in our country's history: We joined you amidst the storm, the strain and stress of a danger the most violent that ever threatened the world; we have weathered the storm with you; now that the sky is clearing and the sun is peeping out again, without a moment's hesitation or notice, we take leave of you. Would hon. gentlemen opposite respect us if we took that course at this moment? We are not built that way. We left our friends opposite for what we believed to be the national good, which the old poet Virgil

described as the noblest motive that could guide the citizens of any country. And when we make another alignment it will be because that same guiding star leads us. V e joined these others, and if w e can we will stay-if we cannot stay we will leave, but always for the good of our country. That is our Liberalism.
There is another implication-and it would be a most important one if there was anything in the invitation to go over-and that is that there is something to go over to.
Air. AlcMASTER: The portfolios are all on the other side.

I did not catch my hon. friend's remark.
Air. AIcAIASTER: You say you have nothing to come over to. I say, the portfolios are all on the other side.

I have no portfolio. And I did not say even that I have nothing to go to. I said there was an implication that there was something to go to -I was stating the opinion of my hon. friend, not my own. He had better not reply to mine until he hears it; he might show less temerity after hearing it. I have tried to image to myself that little home shack that my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition drew to our attention, with the latch, and the string, and the light. I followed the description, for I listened carefully to every word of my hon. friend's speech. I am bound to say, having regard to that speech from the point of view of constructive ideas or political policy, that I think he ought to have added to his figure -when he told us that the lamp was burning in the kitchen and the string was on the outside of the door, he ought to have added the warning: " Bring your own provisions."
Now, I ask any hon. gentleman on either side of this House to read the speech of my hon. friend if he has forgotten it and to find out what constructive planks of Liberalism were set forth in that speech. Why, Sir, there is far from being a fatted calf awaiting those who return.
Little Mary was rich by comparison, for she at least had a little lamb.
What was the main feature of my hon. friend's speech? It was: Why does not the Government do something? He seemed to find some complaining tones in the speeches of the mover and seconder of the Address, and he asked: Why does not the Government do something? That was not a new cry on his part. We on this side can remember him saying that same thing at

any time when it occurred to him while the war was on. He demanded to know why the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) did not do something. I suppose that hon. gentlemen pleased him in the end,-he left his portfolio to some one else. Why does not the Government do something, was his plaint during 1917. And the Government did something; they brought in the Military Service Act during that session. Then the hon. gentleman changed his question to; Why in the world did you do it? On this side of the House hon. gentlemen did not want to have an election; they thought it was not good for the country. I was alone on the benches opposite in supporting that view. The Conservatives on this side of the House were the true Liberals according to the Asquith view, for they did not want to distract the country with an election during war time. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) said: Why don't you do something; have an election anyway. Well, he had his election, and no doubt while that election was going on, down on the rocky coast of Cape Breton he repeated his plaint to the sad sea waves: Why doesn't the Government do something? Surely, they did plenty during the election; I believe my hon. friend himself only held his seat by the skin of his teeth. And now we re-assemble in the second session of the new Parliament, and again he says: Why doesn't the Government do something? Why does not he tell the Government some of the things he would do? Has he done what every fair opponent should do-and I do not wish to attribute unfairness to my hon. friend; he has been extremely good-tempered and well-conditioned in his new position-has he informed himself of what the Government is doing? Was it nothing to do, as I have said, to stand by the Allied forces until the end? Do these hon. gentlemen opposite think that these shiploads of men are being brought with unexampled rapidity overseas, demobilized and sent to their homes, without the Government doing something? Is he informed as to what the Government are doing in the noble and God-like work of looking after the maimed and the blind, and fitting for new occupations many who can never work at their old trades again? I cannot recall that the hon. gentleman in his speech even gave us an opinion on what the Government proposes to do as outlined in the speech from the Throne. I may be doing him an injustice, but I cannot recall that he said a word about building ships, about constructing roads, about building houses for our people. I am not now either commending or condemning these various projects; but at least when the Government is taking these new departures in the life of the nation and making these proposals, it is not in order to come and say: Why does not the Government do something?
Now, my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster), who made an interruption just now the relevance of which I fail even yet to see, furnished us with a kind of plank. He made some considerable reference to the tariff, and indicated, what I am very glad to know-, that he has low-tariff ideas. Well, I will say to my hon. friend that, portfolio or no portfolio for me, or for h;m in the future, he had better get busy and instruct his own leader about the tariff. I have been in this House for ten years with the leader of the Opposition; I have listened to nearly all the speeches he ever made and I cannot remember ever having heard him say " tariff He probably has done so but this is a subject that he fought shy of. There is a reason and my hon. friend from Brome knows it. He will not get up in his place now and assert that there is quite the enthusiasm for tariff reform manifested in the speech of the leader of the Opposition that there was in his own speech. On the question of the tariff, in my humble judgment-and I have tried to inform myself-those who represent what was formerly the Liberal party occupy a less advanced position than did the whole Liberal party of a quarter of a century ago, so far as their policy has been stated up to the present time. What was the policy of the Liberal party oveT twenty years ago? I think I can state it from an authority that will not be disputed. I want to give a few extracts, if I am permitted, from some speeches delivered in the year 1893 or between 1893 and 1896, and that is just about a quarter of a century ago:
I submit to you that the ideal fiscal system is the British system of free trade.
That was a statement of the policy of the party 'that would at once have attracted all British Liberals under its banner.
"Let it be well understood that from this moment we have a distinct issue with the party in power. Their ideal is protection; our ideal is free trade.
"I come to expose to you the policy of the Liberal party. Let me tell you that the policy may be summed up in the good Saxon word 'Freedom,' in every sense of the term-freedom of speech, freedom of action, freedom of religious life and civil life, and last, not least, freedom in commercial life."

"I denounce to you the policy of protection as bondage; yes, bondage, and I refer to bondage in the same manner as American slavery was bondage; not in the same degree, perhaps, but in the same manner. In the same manner the people of this country, the inhabitants of the city of Winnipeg especially, are toiling for a master, who takes away, not every cent of profit, but a very large percentage, a very great portion of your earnings for which you toil and sweat."
That was the official statement of the policy of the Liberal party given more than twenty years ago by an authority that no one can dispute. Is that their policy to-day? My hon. friends opposite are silent. Is that the policy of the hon. member for Brome?
An hon. MEMBER; Yes.

But my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) said that he was in favour of tariff for revenue. He is a product not of a quarter of a century ago but of the intervening period when the policy which had formerly been enunciated was lost sight of or not pursued with any great degree of enthusiasm. Now, I mention this as showing that I was rightly informed when I stated that the invitation of hon. gentlemen opposite implied that there was something to come to.
As a matter of simple fact, Mr. Speaker- and this is a statement which I make very deliberately and of set purpose, and it is important that it should be made in this period of the history of Canada-the great majority of the people of that part of Canada from which I come have been able to see, in the history of the last twenty-five years, very little difference, if any, between the records and performances of the two parties. Difference in profession there has been but in performance there has been very little difference and the sooner that it is authoritatively stated, so far as I have the authority derived from constant observation to state it, the better. That is the view of a large majority of the people of western Canada.
Mr. MoMASTER:	What about recipro-.
city?

My hon. friend, of course, and I, supported reciprocity. We did not get a chance of performing on it. But, has not the present Government performed on it; has it not given free wheat and free potatoes; so that, as I hinted, the profession was on the one side and the performance on the other.

May I may be permitted to interrupt the hon. gentleman? I would like to know

	.

My hon. friend has already spoken in this debate at considerable length. I listened to him for an hour and a quarter without interruption and I must ask him- although I do not want to be discourteous -to give me time to get out of the way for another fellow. I do not want to go at any great length, or at any length at all, into the programme which the Government has put before us. But I would like to be permitted to lay down what I conceive to be important principles that ought to guide us irrespective of all party names in the very serious work of trying to " reconstruct " Canada-if you will allow the word. Mr. Speaker, I am afraid, from the speeches to which I have just made reference, that hon. gentlemen opposite are more concerned about the reconstruction of a party than about the reconstruction of the country; I am afraid so. I wish I could think it otherwise, but there has been a good deal of .evidence that that is their frame of mind,: That was the meaning of the invitation to which I have referred at such great length.
We, on this side of the House I claim, are more concerned about the reconstruction of the country, and let me say to my hon. friends opposite that there is no earthly chance of their getting the high encomiums and support of the people of this country until they change their policy if I have rightly diagnosed and described it. In the months and years immediately ahead of us, the first principle of reconstruction that I would lay down is, that we ought to endeavour to keep up the same patriotic fervour as we displayed during the war. If it was then worth while getting fervid about sending our sons by the hundred thousands across the seas to fight for great principles and to fight for liberty, it is worth our while in Canada surely to be equally fervid about fighting and struggling for the good of our own country.
And, let me say at this point, that I think we ought to cultivate the sacrificial spirit of the men who went across the seas-we ought to cultivate the spirit of those men. Mr. Speaker, there is a frightful moral chasm between nearly all of us who stayed at home and enjoyed in varying degrees the prosperity of war times, and those boys who went across the seas to die, if need be, for $1.10 a day. They have done their work. It is now up to us, as civilians, to do ours; and if, for the rest of our lives, we have to make sacrifices in this country from the humblest workman to the richest plutocrat-if we have to make sacrifices of the very strongest and most drastic kinds-

our shrinking flesh should suffer all that is coming to us in that regard.
With that spirit of sacrifice should go the spirit of helpfulness, and here I would like to make an appeal to my hon. friends opposite. I do not intend to specify members, but there have been hon. members opposite who seemed to me to have pursued an unworthy line of talk in this House. One wonders what is their motive in saying words here wThich can possibly arouse discontent among our returned boys and their relatives. Some one talked about Canadians having been made a spearhead in the recent war. Why, Sir, that is surely an unworthy thing to suggest. I have met lots of men from the trenches, the best of the world's manhood, and I have not found that in the trenches there was the slightest jealousy, or envy, or rivalry between the sons of Canada, and the sons of Ireland, Scotland, and England. I have not found anything but unstinted praise on the part of Canadian soldiers for what Tommy Atkins did in the war, and I am perfectly sure that Tommy Atkins has been equally generous to Canadians. I should be glad for the sake of the fair name of our country, that there was no more oratory of that particular kind. I do not for a moment fear the political consequences of such talk, because no one will be quicker than our returned men to recognize that there might be just a shade of suspicion about such solicitude expressed in such terms by men, who, to say the least of it, were not too enthusiastic to keep these same men, when in the fighting line, from being overrun by the Huns. I do not think it will be easy to infuse a doubt into the minds of returned men as to the willingness of those for whom they voted in such numbers in the last election,-because they knew that they were behind them in this fight without a doubt, and to the finish-I do not think it will be easy to infuse a doubt into those minds as to who is willing to do the best, the very best that the country's resources will allow us to do, for these men now that they have come back to our shores.
Now, if I might, I would like td say to the Government, and to the members of this House, irrespective of the side upon which they sit, that I think those of, us who really want to face reconstruction intelligently and wisely, should be prepared to remind ourselves, and our entire people, that the great problem of reconstruction is a world in debt,-not a nation only, but a world in debt. That is the problem that to-day faces us and all the belligerent countries. And I think that if we can keep
that in mind it will modify the relationships between parties in this House, it will modify the asperity of the criticism which we might be inclined to heave at the heads of the Government when they are not doing what we think they ought to do. It will modify tlie attitude of the various classes of the community in presenting the claims of their particular class upon the Government and Parliament of the country; it will modify the strength of the application of men for an immediate raise in their salaries; it will help our national life all round, and will help to our higher and better citizenship if we can keep it continually in mind that the nation and the world are for the moment heavily in debt.
If I were to venture to undertake to say a word of advice to the Government, I should say that they would be wise if they avoided palliatives and half-measures; they would try as Parliament ought to help them to try, to get down to the roots of things, and to look for a period-which perhaps we have not quite arrived at yet,-when we shall undoubtedly have industrial depression and great economic and national difficulties to face. I do not think there is the remotest doubt about that. If we do not have it, Mr. Speaker, then history has taught me nothing about the economic consequences of war.
I am not going, as I said before, to mention in detail the measures referred to in the Speech, and I am at least to that extent following the example of my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition. The legislation with respect to roads, and these other matters that I have spoken of, it will be the duty of this House to discuss; and so far as this side is concerned, I think I can guarantee my hon. friends opposite that all these measures will be discussed with a degree of independence that will surprise them, because we are not dominated by party spirit on this side. That does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that we are prepared at a moment's notice to vote this Government out of power until we see something to take its place-I put in that saving clause. So far as my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Joseph Read) is the particular spokesman of my hon. friends opposite, he declared the other night-contrary to the spirit of a year and a half ago-: "We cannot possibly have an election until the boys come back." So up to that extent, I take it, hon. gentlemen opposite are in absolute agreement with me. I do not want to go into these things in detail, but I might for the sake of illustra-

tion say, that, in my judgment, the making of roads is not a basic occupation. That is true of the building of houses, it is true even of shipbuilding: the basic, economic occupations of a country are those which go down into nature and take the wealth out of the soil, out of the timber, out of the rivers and the lakes, and the oceans; if you like, out of the mines. Those are the basic occupations of this, or any other lands.
There is another principle of reconstruction that I am sure we want to deal with in this House-I shall do so at any rate, and I think we all of us favour free discussion of public questions, and in this .respect I agree with my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) that this talk of shelving the'tariff, or not speaking of the tariff, can only be compared to the man who wTanted to build a house without discussing the materials of which he was going to build it. I am a hundred per cent with my hon. friend from Brome on that subject. I am not going to try to anticipate the Budget, but I am going to refer to some of the fundamentals of reconstruction, and to do so by the use of a few words which will suggest thoughts and show how absurd it is to think that for any length of time we can avoid the discussion of the tariff or any other subject.
Whether we are going to supply pensions and look after the sick and maimed and the injured^and mutilated, whether we are going to supply employment to all our people, I think it will be agreed that one of the things we must do in the face of our great national debt is to produce wealth in the country. Now, no one will have the temerity to say that the tariff has nothing to do with the production of wealth. We may take one view or another of what the effect of the tariff is upon the production of wealth, but that it has a bearing on the subject 'I think every one will agree who thinks about economic subjects at all. It is, of course, open to any hon. gentleman to argue that Great Britain in this war- and we must learn the lessons of the war- was a remarkable example of financial failure under free trade. I do not know that any one who would argue that would carry the mind of his hearers very far. It is equally open to anybody to argue that Germany was a remarkable example of financial success under protection. But whatever we may think about that point, I want to make it clear to the 'House that if we are to learn the lessons of the war we cannot postpone the discussion as to which view is right along those lines.

Allied to the question of wealth is surely the question of trade. .Now, our trade has been remarkable during the war. What is the lesson of the war on the question of our trade? What *was the economic cause of the extraordinary amount of trade we did during the war? It is possible to answer that question in one word: markets. We did the business because we had the markets. We produced to an extraordinary extent; we got the prices; we had safe customers in the shape of foreign governments; we had the markets, and we did the trade. I never could see it myself, but I suppose it is a debatable point whether you will do the most trade with obstacles or without obstacles. The member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) believes in the obstacles, to a certain extent; he believes in a tariff for revenue. Well, the tariff is an obstacle to trade whether it is for revenue or for any other purpose. I am one of those who is advanced much further than the member for Brome on the trade question. I am innocent enough to believe that you will trade better, just as you will run a race better, if you do not have obstacles. But whatever the views of other hon. gentlemen may be, we cannot avoid discussing that question.
Then, about the industries of the country. We have been told that tariffs are necessary to build up our manufacturing industries. Why, Sir, this war afforded the remarkable spectacle in Canada of industries turning their plants around to produce things that they had never produced before, producing them in enormous quantities, and selling them at tremendous and immediate profits. Why were we able to do that during the war? The answer is the same as I gave a moment ago in regard to our trade; we did it because we had the markets. That is to say, the exigencies and the pressure of the war overcame the obstacle, or any obstacle that there was in the way of the tariff. I take it that is the lesson of the war on this particular point.
The Government are interested in shipping. I do not blame them. We have to discuss shipping on the estimates of the Minister of Marine during this session, or on some other occasion. I have always believed that shipping is in the same position as these other matters to which I have referred. If you have a purely protectionist country, I think it must be evident to the most casual observer that you do not need any ships. If you have a perfect wall around your country and cut yourselves off

thoroughly from other nations, it is obvious that however you might need cathedrals or jails or anything of that kind, you would not need ships. Well, the converse also would seem to be true; if you want to have successful shipping you will not put up a wall of that kind. But this may be my insular stupidity which I have brought from England with me. It appears so simple to me that a child would accept it for the truth the moment it was presented to it. I wish hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House would, on this question as on the others to which I have referred, cultivate the teachable spirit of the child.
I suppose we shall have to discuss taxation, Mr. Speaker. I am afraid so; it will be a prominent subject of debate for many a long year. And it is absurd to talk about discussing taxation without gradually coming to discuss the tariff, because, for better or for worse, the tariff has been our main method of taxation in this country. We shall have to discuss tariffs when we come to taxation, or else we shall be parliamentary ostriches, and that would not be complimentary to us.
The cost of living is a question which this or any other government and this or any other parliament must tackle in the immediate future. Notwithstanding the large wages which have been prevailing in this country, I am afraid it is too true that a considerable number of our people have been living from hand to mouth in spite of the artificial good times that have been created by the war. If you cut down the cost of living, you would help conditions very much all round; you 'would lessen the rapacity of people for large profits and increased salaries. That question must be attended to; it is vital, and its solution would solve very much besides.
We are going to discuss the possibility of settling soldiers on the land. The tariff has a direct bearing on that question. It was argued by those who had carefully studied the question before the war that it was impossible to produce the splendid wheat that we produced in western Canada at a paying profit, at the price we were getting for it. Wheat in southern Alberta was then, I suppose, bringing about 65 cents a bushel, and having regard to the price of implements and the price of land, it was argued by many economists and men in the business that wheat could not be produced at that price to pay. If there be anything in that contention-I see that my hon. friend the President of the Grain Growers' Association of Manitoba approves of what I am
saying-then at the very threshold of land settlement for soldiers we are met with the question: Are you justified in putting soldiers on the land to produce wheat or to produce any other agricultural products under these conditions? _ We must not try to settle any of these problems on war conditions-and war conditions as to prices largely remain at the present lhoment-because it is impossible that war conditions in these regards are to continue.
I have mentioned these things just to indicate some of the questions that will be before us in this period and to try to guide the House, independent of any old party affiliations, to right lines of thought. I cannot forget, Mr. Speaker, that I come from western Canada It is impossible to hide from our eyes the fact that in western Canada at the present moment there is this remarkable state of opinion to which I have referred. A few days ago I had a letter from a valued constituent touching on many subjects. That letter began with the statement to me, for my guidance as his representative, that in. the part of the country in which he lived he rarely met a man who described himself either as a Liberal or as a Tory. That is a remarkable indication of the state of flux in which the opinions of men are in this country. The fact of the matter is that, perhaps, the most important thought for our guidance in this whole reconstruction period is this: that while it is a truism to say that the external forms of government and external conditions of countries have been tremendously affected by the war, it is quite as significant that everywhere men's thoughts are in a state of revolution; they are everywhere prepared to accept new ideas. And that is the frame of mind in which we should, either as members of the Government or as members of Parliament, approach public questions.
When I say that I am from the West, I want to add this: that I am no sectionalist. I could not be as a western man, if I wished at the present moment, because one of the most remarkable features of our internal politics just now is that the West is rapidly making converts to its views in the province of Ontario.
I notice that my friend from Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Joseph Read) who has very large way of doing things, said the other night that there was no distinction between the farmers' movement and what he called the Liberal party. That is ndt my recollection. I think the hon. member was speaking outside the patent facts of comparatively

recent political history. Long before the reciprocity pact, the farmers of the West were asking for free agricultural implements, but the reciprocity pact, if I remember it correctly, proposed a reduction of 2h per cent on agricultural implements which would not have meant very much to anybody. There is a great difference between free implements and a reduction of 24 per cent from fifteen per cent, so I shall not allow my hon. friend to mop up, so to speak, this support of the farmers. It would be a very convenient way of doing party business, but my hon. friend says he is a patriot and stands for the nation first, and I am not sure that he was not thinking of a party when he made that statement, because it is not quite correct. I do not stand for any section in this country. Our boys fought for a united Canada and I believe in a united Canada. I believe in this nation from shore to shore, and I believe that we shall fight our difficulties as a united people just as our sons have fought the battles across the sea. But I think all the same that if I were in the cabinet, or even if I were an eastern manufacturer, I should keep a sharp outlook on what the West is doing.
I want on this head to make a special appeal to the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White). He knows I have a great affection for him, and when we sat on opposite sides of the House, I had such an affection for him that I undertook his tuition in economic affairs. And he is by far my most promising pupil. He is not only my most promising, but is my most influential pupil. I need scarcely tell him to keep a sharp lookout on the West because he has already shown in his brief but brilliant political career, that he does keep a sharp lookout everywhere and that he has a teachable mind on these economic matters. He is sometimes a very much 'traduced man. We hear it said sometimes that he is connected with corporations. I have known some of the people that threw these stones, and one would want to throw a good brick back at them one's self if one wanted to go into that kind of politics. I wish, however, to claim for my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) that he has as free a mind as I have found anywhere in the public life of Canada, I have great pride in my pupil's mind. It is a penetrable mind, and it has been penetrable to western ideas. That is why I talk to him at this particular juncture. It would be no use my starting on a hard case like the leader of the Opposition (Mr. 
McKenzie). At the beginning oi the war, I myself, was responsible for bringing western economics into this House in a very pointed form, and I told my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) to put on an income tax. That was new to my hon. friend and he did not see his way to do it, and he made some speeches, saying what was quite true, namely, that it was a difficult tax to collect and you could not jump at these things like a bull in a china shop. But my hon. friend came on, and he told us in several speeches that an income tax was, he feared, impracticable, but not impossible. Why, the fact now is that he remains a member of the Government which imposed an income tax, and the head of the department which did it, and I believe he is very proud of it now. I was, therefore, not wrong in describing the Acting Prime Minister as being a teachable and penetrable man and being my most hopeful pupil'. It is no discredit to him to change his mind. The man who, in the course of a great war, does not change his mind, has no mind to change. It is only hon. gentlemen opposite who held false ideas of Liberalism to the point at which they joined a choir with the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) as choirmaster, and chanted "As it was in the beginning, is now and ever shall be." And they thought, when they were doing it, that they were Liberals. That is the chant of the oldest fashioned Tories.
It is in the English church prayer-book.

When Sir Robert Peel, one of the greatest financial leaders of the nineteenth century, was elected in England in 1341, he was elected to maintain the Corn laws. In 1846, without again going to the people, he abolished the Corn laws. Like a wise statesman, he saw the conditions changing, the country needing different things-just as those of us who left my hon. friends opposite saw what these hon. gentlemen could not see-and he abolished the Corn laws which he was elected to maintain. So my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) is in apostolic succession to some of the greatest statesmen. Lord Beaconsfield, when Mr. Disraeli, was member of an administration which destroyed the Liberal Administration of that day on the question of franchise, and then within a year he came in and introduced a franchise more drastic than the franchise of the Government he had destroyed. Dis-

raeli changed even more rapidly than did Sir Robert Peel.
Pardon me, the hon. member is hardly right. He accepted an amendment proposed by John Bright. That is the way "he dished the Whig.s."
My hon. friend is dealing with a later period in history than that with which I am dealing.

1867. In 1868 there was a general election in which Mr. Gladstone was returned to power. My hon. friend must study history a little more before he is so cock-sure of himself. We will, however, accept the phrase and take our history as being roughly correct, and my hon. friend is not disputing that Disraeli did "dish the Whigs" and that he did change his mind. I am not scoring any arithmetical success, as two and two is four and one is five; I leave those phases of politics to my hon. friend.
Well, now, these changes of thought are not put down in history to the detriment of the reputation of the statesmen who changed their views. On the question of free wheat my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister also showed that he had an open mind. He delivered a long speech in which he said that during the war he did not believe in giving free wheat; but he remained a member of the Government that did. I have very great hope that I do not appeal to him in vain to keep his mind still open. Let the western breezes blow through it; they will blow away some of the cobwebs he picks up in Toronto, and he will do clearer and better thinking and proceed to a position in Canadian statesmanship that he has not yet attained. I feel sure of it. I feel most hopeful of my hon. friend, for he is not only a statesman with a capacity for changing his mind. I cannot think he is absolutely impervious to political conditions. il am sure that every man in Government and Opposition circles must have regard to this fact about the people of the West; they can demonstrate on occasion their ability to stand as one man when the national good requires it. They stood as one man in December 1917, and if I were an eastern stateman or an eastern manufacturer I would say:	" These are people
that we had better keep our eye upon; they are worth watching; they are a faetor*of increasing numbers and increasing strength in the political life of Canada, and we must watch what they are doing."
There is another consideration about the West that I want to urge. The West wants no special favours whatsoever. We are asking for no special or class privileges. I hear people talking as if the farmers of the West were selfish men who wanted the Government to do something for their particular industry. On the contrary we are so confident of our ability to build up our own industries that we defy and challenge the world. We produce better wheat in western Canada than they can produce elsewhere in the world, and we are prepared to sell it against all comers. The same is true of our beef produce. Anything we do in the West we do well, and we defy competition. We want no special favours, and I take it that in that respect we are good Canadians. I do not understand the Canadian who says: I cannot compete. When I was quite a young man in the Old Country I remember a sculler named Edward Hanlan coming Over to England and beating the Englishmen so easily that he stopped in the middle of the race to scoop some water out of his boat. He did not say he could not compete! Did the men in the trenches in the recent fighting say they could not compete? They were never content unless they were right at the front. They did not complain of being made a spearhead. You could not help them being spearheads. That is the kind of Canadians I believe in, and that is the kind of goods we produce in western Canada. The Canadian who says, I cannot compete; I must have special help, special pap from the Government is a kind of Canadian that should be put in a glass case and exhibited in the British museum. He is not in full line with the manhood of Canada. I am sorry if that seems an extreme view, but after all it does not seem a very special request to make of a Parliament or Government to ask that we be put on exactly the same footing as others and that others be put on exactly the same footing as us.
And if I may speak for western Canada I of Canada will come to my views all at once. I have far too good an understanding of the difficulty of making progress to expect that, but I do say that I have brought before the House considerations which are well worth the attention of both parties in this House.
And if I may speak for wesern Canada I would say: Take off our shackles, and give us the freedom that our boys fought for. Our courage and our energies are as great as our prairies are wide, and we believe that our economic views are as clear as our atmosphere. Regardless of our political



future, when occasion required it we in the West stood as one man and voted as one man behind the men who stood in the breach for the world's liberty.
We are grateful that we share in Canada to-day, through the providence of the Almighty, the security and the freedom which has been purchased by blood. We want to go into the future animated by the same spirit that has animated us during the war, and we in western Canada will be found giving unstinted support to the men who are prepared with courage and with clear-sightedness to build an edifice of happiness, prosperity, and the highest manhood on the foundations laid at such tremendous cost.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address on the ability and success with which they have accomplished their task. In this I only endorse the unanimous opinion of this House and of the press of the country.
I desire also that my first words should be words of thanks and congratulation to the brave soldiers of our Canadian army. I yield to no man, not even to my eloquent friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) in my admiration of the boys who have represented us at the front. In the terrific struggle which the victory of the Allied armies has now ended, our soldiers have heroically done their duty, and more than their duty. Always in the front line, amongst shells and bullets, amidst clouds of deadly gas, under a rain of iron and fire, they have unceasingly given to the Canadian nation and to the whole world numberless examples of collective and individual heroism. The gallantry, moral energy and physical courage of the Canadian soldiers have become a tradition in the Allied armies. Our soldiers have written a glorious page of history. To the families of those who have fallen on the field of honour 

and my hon. friend from Red Deer is the head of one of those families-let us extend our deep sympathy. Our dead heroes rest in a far-distant land, but we must not forget that they are not buried on foreign soil, for it has been well said that every man has two mother countries-his own, and France.
In order that the terrible sacrifices which have been made shall not be in vain, statesmen are now assembled at a Peace Conference to frame policies and devise means to prevent a recurrence of such a cataclysm as we have just passed through.

I am glad indeed that the speech from the Throne refers to the founding of a League of Nations, and that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has declared himself in favour of such a league. The democracy of the world is rallying behind President Wilson in support of that great project, and in some cases doing so despite rulers and kings, and compelling the doing away with the old order of things. The peace that is to be achieved must be a peace that regards the future instead of the past; it must not be only a lull in the storm, as was said by one of the Allied statesmen recently. This war, as we have often been told, was a war to end all wars, and wars cannot be ended unless the old system is changed. The mere fact that the Turkish state, a disgrace to civilization, had to be maintained to ensure what was called the balance of power is, to my mind, a sufficient reason to discredit the old system. Some fear that by entering a league, nations may lose part of their freedom and even their separate entity. They say that internationalism will replace nationalism. That is a mistake. You cannot be an internationalist unless you are a nationalist; there cannot be a League of Nations unless there are nations. The control of armaments will inevitably mean a certain limitation of national freedom of action. But where will be the change? Who shaped the British naval policy before the war? Sir, the naval programme of Britain was determined by the naval programme of Germany. The British tax payers had to submit to larger taxes at the whim of the Kaiser and Von Tirpitz. Likewise the military programme of France was dictated by the military programme of Germany.
The hon. Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) said that to assure the power of the league a military force will have to be maintained. I should have liked my hon. friend to be more expliicit. It will be a sad disappointment to many if military expenditures have to be maintained after this war. Sir, the people of the world are to govern themselves. For some of them the period of transition will be a period of struggle, of agitation, of chaotic disorder, but mey will adjust themselves to the new conditions, and order will ultimately prevail. Russia, Austria-Hungary, and Germany were the only remaining absolute monarchies in Europe. They lie in the ckust. Their disappearance makes international agreements possible between people and people, and the democracy of the world will see to it that no " scrap of paper "

shall again be torn. The peace of the world will be guaranteed, not by military power, not by naval power but, I hope, by the supreme moral power, which in democratic countries is public opinion. The evils of war are great enough to warrant great efforts to free the world from them.
The hon. Acting Prime Minister also stated that Germany must be compelled to pay the fullest indemnity, and he very properly referred to the fact that Canada did not desire the war, and that her war expenditures ought to be reimbursed by the German people. I should be glad indeed if the wishes of my hon. friend could be realized; but I cannot think that the Canadian people ought to rely too confidently on the payment of that indemnity. The indemnity as stipulated to be paid is not merely an arithmetical operation, it is not a mere arrangement of figures. A large indemnity such as that which Germany would have to pay if Canada's claim is to be considered-for we can only come after the devastated territory of France and Belgium have been repaired-cannot be paid in cash. Germany could only pay by producing and exporting goods that would otherwise have been produced by England, France, or some other country. Mr. Lloyd George said during the recent British elections that Germany must pay, but she must not be allowed to dump her goods upon England. But she must dump goods upon England or dump them upon neutral countries, and so displace the British goods, or the indemnity payments cannot be made.
The hon. gentleman said that the ablest statesmen of the world are assembled at the Peace Confeience. Let me here express regret for one thing and the sad circumstances under which we meet this session induce me to speak with the greatest moderation. There was a great Canadian statesman who should have been at the Peace Conference. Sir, President Wilson has amongst the members of his deputation there a political opponent. On the main committee the British Empire is represented by Sir John Simon who was defeated on December last as a political opponent of Mr. Asquith and who has been throughout the war a consistent opponent of conscription in Great Britain. But here of course we have a "union" Government, and only friends of that government were qualified. The fact lemains that minority parties, parties not actually in power, are part of a nation and should have a voice in decisions which will affect the rights of
16J	.	[DOT]
those nations for generations after their existing governments have given place to others.
While I believe that Canada has to be represented at the Peace Conference, I just as strongly believe that the Prime Minister of Canada should be at home now conducting the affairs of the country. The Prime Minister of a country is not an ambassador. Last year, Parliament had to be prorogued somewhat early to allow the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues to proceed to London for the Imperial Conference. We were told that there was urgent need of their immediate departure. Important business was hurried on in this House without due consideration, so much so that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) had to register a vigorous protest. Our distinguished representative had to wait for weeks before the Conference actually met. True, the wires were kept busy recording their very strenuous work there for a time, especially that of my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) whom I see taking his seat. At times there was not much to report. We were told that the President of the Privy Council was getting older every day, and that the Prime Minister of Canada was impressing England by being favourable to that now almost extinct garment, the frock coat.
This year our representatives left Canada when the armistice was announced. I am not sure that the armistice was actually signed when they left. They were the first representatives to arrive, but their presence did not prevent Mr. Lloyd George from running an election campaign or the President of the United States from conducting public affairs at Washington for many weeks after our representatives had crossed the sea. The Prime Minister has had all the time and opportunity necessary to press his views on the Conference, and he should now come home to look after the tremendous task which confronts him. Surely, one of his colleagues might be left there to meet the Bolsheviki if the conference finally takes place. I would respectfully suggest that the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) should have the appointment. He would be the best man to handle the situation if they tried to put up any raw deal over on him. The Montreal Star was telling its readers some time ago that the Prime Minister was coming home for a holiday. I hope his colleagues will persuade him to work here and go holidaying elsewhere.

This leads me to a subject with which I desire to deal bi'iefly. In the absence of the Prime Minister, the Acting Prime Minister should give us a full and comprehensive statement of the history of the constitutional changes which have been created by the formation of the Imperial War Cabinet and by the adoption of various policies formulated at the last Imperial Conference. The press of this country, .supporting the Government, is not in agreement as to the meaning and functions of the Imperial War Cabinet. The Toronto Globe, which has still a modicum of Canadianism left in it, contends that it is a mere consultive body and not at all an executive body. The Toronto News, the organ of Imperialism in Canada, states that it is an executive body. Speaking at London before the Imperial Parliamentary Association on June 21, 1918, the Prime Minister said:
A great step in the constitutional development ot the Empire was taken last year by the Prime Minister-
That is the Prime Minister of Great Britain.
-when he summoned the Prime Ministers of the Overseas Dominions to the Imperial War Cabinet.
Later on he said:
If I should attempt to describe it, I should say that it is a Cabinet of Governments.
I venture to believe, and I thus expressed myself last year, that in this may he found the genesis of a development in the constitutional relations of the Empire that will form the basis of its unity in the years to come.
Ambiguous as the language of the Prime Minister is it conveys the meaning that a constitutional change has effectively been made since he says that a great step in the constitutional development of the Empire was taken last year when the Prime Minister of Great Britain summoned the Prime Ministers of the Overseas Dominions to the Imperial War Cabinet. Furthermore, *we have been told that the functions of the War Cabinet would not cease with war but that this body would remain a part of the constitutional structure of the Empire. If that be so what right and what mandate had the Prime Minister of Canada to accede to this scheme? Canadian policies have been framed and decided upon in Canada since the days when responsible government was granted and they must continue to be framed and decided upon in Canada. Is it that Canada's policies are to be decided in London by a body of men in which Canada would have one representative out of twelve? True it is that the decisions arrived at would have to be rati, 
fled by the Canadian Parliament but that is a somewhat illusory safeguard as it would be open to the Prime Minister to use his influence to place the decisions of this body upon the Statute Book of Canada and he might always rely on his parliamentary majority to enable him to do so. The words of the Prime Minister that the new body upon the statute-book of Canada and loquent catch words, and nothing else. There' is no such thing as a cabinet of governments. According to strict constitutional rules and practice there cannot be a cabinet unless there be also a parliament to which that cabinet is directly responsible. I do not wonder that the Round Table should be delighted and should regard that new .scheme as a distinct advance, for they fully realize that an Imperial cabinet cannot exist without an Imperial Parliament and that is their ultimate game. Sir John Willison is a consistent advocate of Imperialism. The following quotation from a letter written by him is very significant.
My imperialism means equal citizenship for Canadians in the Empire. That we have' never had. That we have not yet secured. Nor do I believe that we can acquire such citizenship through War Cabinets or periodical Imperial Conferences. For the time these are useful as means to an end, hut we know that, after all, actual ultimate control over peace and war rests in the Imperial Parliament.
According to Sir John Willison the Imperial War Cabinet is a means to an end, namely, the creation of an Imperial federated parliament, of which Sir John Willison is a consistent advocate, a Federal Parliament in which Canadians would be in a small minority and which would levy taxation on Canadian citizens.
Sir, Canada is a nation and she will never become a province. At the Imperial Conference of 1917 a resolution had been adopted that all discussion and constitutional changes should be postponed until after the war when a conference for the purpose of considering these matters was to be called. I exceedingly regret that this resolution should not have been adhered to and that our Prime Minister should have agreed to a scheme which he has himself described as an important step in the constitutional development of the Empire. May I also point- out, and it will apply to other matters as well as to this-that'Confederation is an agreement. It was the result of the agreement of four colonies. It is in effect a treaty, and that treaty cannot be altered nor modified without the consent of all the contracting parties to it. The provinces have agreed to part with many of their rights, and to entrust them to the

Federal Parliament, but the Federal authority has no right to delegate any of its powers to another body without the consent of the parties to its original contract.
I now come to our internal affairs, and I have a word to say to my hoh. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) at the beginning. 1 have not much to criticise in his speech. Indeed, I congratulate him upon many things he said. His eulogy of his former leader was a masterpiece of eloquence such as I have seldom heard in this Chamber. But what I object to is the somewhat patronizing attitude that the hon. gentleman look ,a little later on. We, the Liberal parliamentary party, are a contemptible little army according to the Hindenburg of Red Deer. We all thought when he crossed the floor of the House that the heavy artillery was going, and I am sure he agrees with us on this. But, Sir, there is something we can say, with all modesty. We are not so numerous as the gentlemen on the other side, but we have some qualities. The first is that we are a united party. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition can sit there with a sense of security which I am sure the Acting Prime Minister would like to enjoy. It is the sense of security which is produced by the certainty that nobody, either behind him or alongside of him, has a knife or a dagger. My hon. friend has declared himself as concerned about the Late of our party. Our future appears to him very dark. I thank him for his solicitude, but will he permit me to remind him that he may be mistaken. What has taken place in a constituency called Red Deer, very recently, might have taught my hon. friend the wisdom of modesty in prediction. I hope my hon. friend will not take these remarks otherwise than in good part. He knows that he and I have always been friends, he knows that I am a great admirer of his, in spite of the slight imperfections he may have. I will now proceed with my remarks.
I believe that the first war machinery that should be demobilized is the present Government. Self-destruction is a painful operation, but in the interest of the country my hon. friends ought to make the sacrifice and demobilize themselves. Theirs is an unnatural alliance at the present juncture. The doctrine that a political truce should exist during the period of reconstruction, and that the great questions of policy should be left aside and untouched, is sheer nonsense, and my friend from Red Deer demonstrated that himself in part of his remarks. We are not living in Utopia. The very fact that the resources
of Canada, as the result of our war effort, have been strained as they have been, compels us to face grave and great problems, and the two traditional opposite sides, which are the interests and democracy, cannot but face each other when the settlement is effected. One or the other must give way; it is impossible for gentlemen of different ideas on those problems to sit with each other, and be consistent with their ideals and principles. Principles are eternal, expedients are temporary. Burke has said that inconstancy is a sort of natural corrective to folly and ignorance. This, under ordinary circumstances, is not flattering, but it is still worse when inconstancy is forced upon unwilling people in order to allow them to perpetuate or prolong an equivocal situation. I agree with the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, that all citizens at this period must be animated by a spirit of pure patriotism, and adopt as their goal the welfare of the country; but in order to reach that desire they must strive to assure the success of the policies which they, in their conscience, deem to be the best to obtain that result. The idea of reconstruction means that a new order has to be created, and that changes have to be made to build up the country upon new and firmer foundations. How can it be done if the reformers and the progressives of the country stand pat and let the opportunity pass by? I fully understand that the reactionaries, the Tories, the protected monopolies-all those whose private interests lie in the perpetuation of the present order of things- should advocate political neutrality. Political neutrality means no change at a time when changes are possible and even necessary, when the democracy of a country asserts its right to shape the policy of government, when every nation is bent upon discarding the privileges of the few and safeguarding the interests of the many. But political neutrality on the part of a reformer is a crime against his country, and a betrayal of his principles.
The people whose voices are most loudly heard about reconstruction are those who do not want reconstruction at all. They claim that during the reconstruction period nothing should be done; things must not be disturbed; methods of business should not be changed; tariff policies should not even be discussed. They instinctively feel that the fewer innovations just now-with these people it is always " just now "-the better. They have mobilized under their banner all the appetites, and they masquerade as reconstructors. But, Sir, it is imperative that
*246

new policies should be devised. The Minister of Public Works (Hon. F- B. Carvell) *told us the other day that when all the revenues of the country shall have been used to meet the obligations of the present year, we shall still be short $100,000,000. Where shall we get the money to pay this enormous amount? Still, Canada must not be bankrupt and shall not be bankrupt. It is indeed unfortunate that to a large extent our financial situation is the result of extravagance and maladministration. I would need only to quote the speeches of the Minister of Public Works to show that for every dollar of legitimate war expenditure, another dollar has been given to graft and profiteering. Still, all our obligations must be met, and a new system of taxation must be devised.
Sir, a protective tariff ithat is so high as to prohibit goods from coming into this country is not a fair method of producing a revenue. I have a word to say here to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Hon. J. A. Calder); I regret that he is not in his seat. He stated that there was a cleavage on the tariff as between the East and the West; that the two sections of the country were practically arrayed against each other. This I emphatically deny. Eastern Canada is not an adjunct of Toronto. The minister is very clever, but he cannot bind me with what he used to call the financial rings of Toronto. He cannot do it; he is bound with them, I am not. The voice of Toronto-I would like my friends from the West to put this into their minds-is not the voice of the East. Toronto is making a noise altogether out of proportion to its importance. The rural interests of .eastern Canada-and they constitute the great majority of the people,- are prepared and willing to work with the western farmers to obtain a lowering of the tariff. And, unless I am much mistaken, my fellow citizens of the prairies will not sacrifice their right of redress for the mess of pottage which the Minister of Colonization and a few others are enjoying in the Union Cabinet.
The tariff question must be settled now. I take this opportunity of asking certain members of the Government, those who have been called the " separated brethren," to apply to the consideration of this question that sort of mind described by Milton, namely: " A mind not to be changed by time or place."
There was a statement in the remarKS of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization with which I entirely agree. He said 
that Canada will never be a great country unless we put an end to national strifes and a better union of her citizens is secured. Every true, patriotic citizen of Canada realizes that national unity is indeed necessary. But such unity, Sir, cannot exist without liberty, without justice, without respect of the rights of all citizens. Let every Canadian respect his fellow citizen, whatever his race, creed or nationality may be. Let us do away with the spirit of race domination and national exclusiveness. Sir, the war should help the solution of that problem. Prussianism has been crushed in Germany; Prussianism should be crushed in all the countries of the world. Down with this Prussian spirit of domination ,n Europe; but down with it, too, in Canada. , Let us all do our share to accomplish the great work of national union and harmony. We who have had the privilege of learning our political doctrines under the guidance of the great statesman whose loss we mourn, shall endeavour to remain true to his teaching and inspiration. From the grave where he has been laid, Sir Wilfrid Laurier still leads us. We shall never forget his great lessons of tolerance, moderation and equal justice for all. " Live and let live" ought to be the standard principle of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, one of the great reforms to be accomplished is the re-establishment of government of the people by the people and the full restoration of the rights of citizens. The press must be free; censorship must be done away with; freedom of speech must be revived. Certain restrictions were justifiable during the war, but the condition of war no longer exists, and I cannot conceive that any' democratic man in Canada would approve of such an act, for instance, as the imprisonment on the eve of Christmas day of a Canadian citizen for the crime of having in his possession an edition of Plato's Republic. Sir, this is an outrage to liberty and decency. The press should be free; the control of the mind of the whole people by way of censorship or otherwise is the very method, in all its purity, pursued by Prussia.
It is that nefarious system that has so moulded the conscience of her people as to produce that moral spirit which has startled the world. No such system should be tolerated in Canada, and the industry of shaping public opinion must be abolished. In that regard, I advocate the disappearance of the new national newspaper under the President of the Privy Council.
It is a useless waste of money and its existence creates a dangerous precedent. In this connection, let me say, not only for

this newspaper, but for all sources of information, that a lie is always a lie and never constitutes a truth even when it masquerades as propaganda. Moral unity and true progress cannot be brought about by arbitrary methods and compulsion. Liberty alone can achieve that result. In that respect I do not hesitate to say that in Canada as elsewhere, the strongest bulwark against Bolshevism is Liberalism and the principles for which it stands. Canadians who would spare their country the violence of revolutionary changes, that great mass of the people which is between the opposite sides, namely, the interests and Bolshevism, will wish God-speed to the forces of reorganized Liberalism which will ultimately unite for political action.
Having mentioned the word "Bolshevism," I wish to express my regret that speakers on the other side of the House should have seen fit to represent in a most unfair manner the remarks of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) the other day. The methods of cheap political agitators and yellow journalism should not be emulated in this House. It is always their tactics to disqualify in advance the person they purpose attacking by branding their victim as a crook or a coward or a traitor. By abusing their opponents, they endeavour to prejudice the issue and close discussion. Profiteers, monopolists, trust magnates, the protected interests, have always tried to associate reform and progressiveness with revolution and crime.
I regret that some of my friends who still call themselves Liberals should have shown, to such a degree, the influence of their present association. That the Tories should adopt such methods, I do not wonder. It is the old game. The next election cannot, of course, be fought with the slogan "A vote for the Liberals is a vote for the Kaiser." That fellow is out of business now. A new cry must be found, and evidently it will be "A vote for McMaster is a vote for Lenine and Trotsky." Is it not possible to place Canadian politics upon a higher and moie honourable level?
There is another matter to which I wish to refer in connection with the Address. A new Franchise Bill is announced, and when it is brought down we shall discuss it. But I regret that the Government does not immediately repeal the War-times Election Act, that iniquitous legislation which will ever be a blot on the fair name of Canada. The late Government, before going to the country, ran away from the
judgment of those who had elected them and were their natural judges. They resorted to closure for the purpose of tampering with the electoral laws of the country and manipulating the franchise. In order to frustrate and thwart the will of the people, they proceeded to disfranchise Canadian citizens entitled to all the rights of British subjects in this country.	It
was merely an act of political gambling. All citizens must be equal before the law. Every citizen of a democratic country has a right to his proportion, an equal share in the Government of the country.	As
Jefferson said, "Governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed." Those are the principles of liberty and responsible government. And the Allies have proclaimed to the world that they have been fighting for the maintenance of those principles. When President Wilson, on April 2, 1917, made his famous speech before the two chambers of the United States Congress, requesting them to declare war on Germany, he uttered the following words:
But the right is more precious than peace, and we shall fight for the things we have always carried nearest our hearts-for democracy, for the right of those who submit to authority to have a voice in their own Government, for the rights and liberties of small nations.*
And he added:
To such a task we can dedicate our lives and our fortunes.
But here in this country out Government had to be judged by a sort of family jury and citizens who did submit to authority were deprived of their rights and have no longer a voice in the Government of this country. They are not represented in this House, and nobody has a right to speak for them in the Parliament of Canada. This House is not the true expression of the popular will. I am speaking only of the principle of the legislation. In practice, it was a still more damnable machinery, and in point of fact citizens of friendly or neutral countries were, under that law, actually disfranchised and could not record their vote. That law was a crime against popular sovereignty. All Liberals resented and opposed it. The Toronto Globe and the Toronto Star fought a vigorous campaign against it. They said that it was most undemocratic, arbitrary and Prussian in its character. The Toronto Globe has for its motto those words of Junius;
The subject who is truly loyal to the chief magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures. [DOT]
But the Toronto Globe and its friends submitted to the arbitrary measure they

have condemned and they were quite willing to profit by that measure. It was most unfair to enact that legislation, but it is not any fairer for gentlemen who have denounced it as a fraud and a crime against liberty, to help carry out the very same legislation. And yet the good old Toronto Globe said after the election that the victory achieved with the help of that Prussian law, as the Globe itself styled it, was a victory for democracy. I urge the Government to repeal that law. Let us see it wiped off the statute-book this session.
There are other subjects I should like to discuss, but I shall have an opportunity later on. In conclusion, I would assure the Government that we on this side of the House are only too willing to co-operate with them and do all in our power to help solve the great problems that confront the country in this trying period. Our only aim is the good and prosperity of our common country, but we shall always follow the course which we conscientiously believe to be the best means to reach that happy end. We may not be successful, we may fail in our endeavour, but we are working not merely for political successes, but for the upholding of the great principles of Liberalism by which we shall always stand.

Mr. Speaker, J desire to add my humble tribute to the eulogies that have been passed on the late leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I also desire to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address. It seemed fitting that both the mover and the seconder should have worn the khaki. Both had done good service for the country, both had fought the enemy, and were therefore peculiarly qualified to give expression to the desires and ideals of the returned soldier. At one time, when the 'Hun was pushing forward, liberty, civilization and everything we held dear trembled in the balance, but now the war is happily over. It is not necessary to dwell at any length upon the causes that have brought the war to a successful conclusion. We all realize the genius of Marshal Foch, and Marshal Haig and the ability'of the other Allied generals. It was, however, the hammer blows of the Allied armies that did the actual fighting, and in this the Canadian armies had their full share. The brave sons of Canada were in the van in all the big attacks, and wrote the name of Canada in letters of gold on all the battlefields of the great war.
Another factor without which victory could not have been achieved was the 
British Navy. W7e have all heard of the freedom of the seas. It was the navy's part to preserve the freedom of the seas both before and during the war, and we all know how well it accomplished that task, enabling the soldiers and the munitions of war to be safely transported from all parts of the world towards the places where they were required.
Important and onerous as were the duties cast upon this Government during the war, equally important and onerous are the problems that will have to be solved in the period of reconstruction, but we need have no fear that the Government which has conducted so well the affairs of the country and Canada's part in the war will not be equally successful in the work of demobilization, repatriation, and reconstruction. The period of reconstruction calls for the exercise of the greatest wisdom, prudence, and foresight, but the resources of.Canada are so ample that with wisdom and good judgment all the problems confronting us will be satisfactorily solved.
The war, and the conduct of Canada in the war, and the conditions arising out of the war, inaugurate a new departure. Canada has shown what she is able to accomplish by furnishing the best soldiers that took part in this world war. In consequence of the war, or at least concurrently with the war period, Canada has .risen to eminence and distinction so far as finances are concerned, and takes her place side by side with the Mother Country in the matter of furnishing the loans to government to carry on the public business. And now, while the subject of peace and of peace terms are considered, now that the Peace Conference is in session, the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues of the cabinet sit there with full powers as representatives of this country, side by side with the diplomats of the great nations of the world, negotiating a world peace. That surely is an advance, a marvellous advance for Canada. She has risen to new heights, to a new plane of importance. And these new conditions, this rising to new heights, involves equally new and great responsibilities. All this is a new departure and old ideas and old methods will have to give way. We must look to the future, and not to the past; we must consider the present, and take advantage of and exercise the privileges that are afforded us, while looking forward to even greater things. Not only did our soldiers, many of whom made the supreme sacrifice of life itself that we might enjoy liberty and freedom, not only did these men do nobly, but our civilians

as well, men and women, did their share nobly and well in supporting and carrying forward the necessary work for those who were fighting abroad.
The programme set forth in the speech from the Throne is varied and ample.
I have no intention to refer at any great length, even in my own humble way, to many of the matters in that programme. But I think we shall all agree that nothing too good can be done for the soldiers who have fought and bled and offered their lives for our liberty. Whatever measures the Government can devise within the bounds of the resources at their command,
I am sure, will meet with the full endorsement of all the members on this side of the House.
Then there is the question of alien enemies in Canada. I, for one, sincerely hope that the Government will exercise its utmost powers in carrying out whatever regulations may be enacted to drive these people out of the country. They have no right here, and they have done much harm; I hope the Government will leave nothing undone to suppress them. As to immigration, that is a very important question, and I am sure the Government will exercise the greatest possible care with regard to it. We want no immigrants in this country except the very best, and we want none here who are tinged with any ideas of the alien enemy, the Bolshevists or any of that description.
At a time like this, when there is so much to be done, when such great responsibilities rest upon the Government and Parliament of Canada, one might naturally expect our friends of the Opposition to assist in solving the problems that confront us, Brat they would be willing to lend their aid to bring about the best conditions, that they would throw out from time to time some hints, some elements of a platform that they would be willing to stand upon, and so assist the Government in carrying on their work. But, so far in this debate, I do not think anything of that kind has been offered. -It is true, one hon. gentleman made an apology for the Bolshevists, but I do not think that is a very encouraging or satisfactory means of assisting in the work of reconstruction in Canada. Another hon. gentleman thought well to sneer at the King, at the Prime Minister, and at everything pertaining to the Government of the Dominion. That is the second plank of a platform, so far as we have heard. And there has been another: my esteemed friend the hon, member for Prince (Mr. Joseph Read) last night seemed disposed to extend the friendly hand to the alien enemy. He expressed the wish that a warm place should be found in the hearts of the people of Canada for those who had done so much to injure our cause. These, as far as I have been able to observe, are the three planks of their platform as they have thus far been made known to us in this House.
I wish to say just a word more about my esteemed friend the Ron. member for Prince, he was prolific in his advice and he pronounced very strong censure upon those who had at some time sat upon the other side of the House but who had come over here. He thought that their conduct was somewhat inconsistent. You would almost imagine from the way he developed this feature of his speech that he himself had been most consistent in his political allegiance. No one would suspect from what he was saying that he had been boxing the political compass, that from being an ardent Conservative he, without very much notice, became a very extreme Liberal. It is said that it was no question of public policy that brought about this remarkably quick turn in his political affiliation. It was, as far as I can understand, a grievance regarding a damaged cargo of potatoes.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
