speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext: I desire to direct the attention of the Government to a matter of importance as set forth in a letter written by a Canadian soldier in England and published in L'Acadien, a French paper published in Moncton, N.B. I have translated the letter into English in order that it may be better understood, and I will read the translation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member desires information from the Government on a matter of importance?

maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
I desire to put a question to the Government on a matter of importance. The letter is as follows:
Knotz, Ash., Eng., February 15th, 1919.
*Ml-, the Editor of L'Acadien:-I do not believe I am a grumbler, but when it comes to injustice committed1 towards the French Canadian soldier, I cannot do otherwise than indicate the facts to L'Acadien which is ever ready to defend our rights. Perhaps I will be able to call the attention of some members of Parliament to the injustices which are done to us in the Canadian Army, and have them claim from the authorities the justice and British fair play for their fellow-countrymen.
I understand, by the English papers, that the Canadian troops in France have crossed to England where they will have a leave of eight days to visit their relatives and friends, before coming to Canada. But the French Canadian soldier who asks for transportation to see the land of his ancestors In France, to spend a few days with some friends he has known in his mother country, or even the Canadian soldier who has chosen a lifetime companion amongst the good girls of France, sees himself refused the privilege of going once more into the country for the defence of which he has sacrificed everything. It is said that the transportation is difficult.
Is that fair tpliay, especially when a great number offer to pay their expenses? There is an order according to the Canadian soldiers who have relatives in England, wives, mothers, daughters, the privilege of bringing to Canada the said relatives at the expense of the Canadian Government, the soldier having only to notify the military authorities of the fact. That is also very well. But why is it that the same privileges are being refused to the French Canadian soldiers who have relatives in France?
I know that my assertions are true, such privilege having been refused to a soldier.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
Order. I am unable to follow the reading of the letter as carefully as I would wish, but I have followed it suf-

ficiently to be able to say that if any meaning is to be taken from it, it involves an attack on the Government for its policy in respect to the treatment of soldiers. In no case would that be permissible on the Orders of the Day. There is some question as to how far an hon. member should go in laying the ground for a question, but certainly the hon. member is not in order in reading a letter of that character which involves practically an attack upon the policy of the Government. If he wishes to direct a question to the Government, it seems to me he ought to be able to summarize the complaint or to put it in the form of a question.

maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
My question is whether the Canadian soldier, before returning to Canada from England, has the privilege to go back to France on a visit.
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia):	I think I can answer the question of the hon. gentleman, and I wish to thank him for his courtesy in sending me a copy of the letter he has just read, which I got only a few moments ago. It appears to be a complaint from a young French-Canadian soldier who was in England, and I may say that I have every sympathy with this young man when he says in his letter that he desires to revisit France for the purpose of visiting the girl who is his choice amongst the good girls of France as his life-time companion.

maintopic: FURLOUGHS IN FRANCE FOR CANADIAN SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
Send him back at once.
Major-General MEWBURN: In that letter he says that he understands the Canadian troops have returned to England. That is not quite correct. The Third Division has returned to England * and part of it is on the ocean now homeward bound. In the first instance, it was expected that the Canadian Corps would embark from a French port direct to Canada. That was found impossible for various reasons which I shall be glad to explain to the House later on. Since the armistice, I understand that as regards the troops in England, before embarkation, the men on application have been given a short furlough or leave. I know that the difficulties of transportation across the channel are very acute owing to demobilization and every discouragement is given to men wishing to return to France. This man does not say which unit he is with. If he was with the celebrated 22nd in France, as I presume he was, I understand certain leave was given to that unit in France, and I understand the 22nd Bat-

talion is still in France. I have no personal knowledge of men who have made application being refused permission to return to France on furlough; but if the hon. member so desires, I shall be very glad, if he will give us fuller particulars in regard to this young man and the unit he is with, to pass the information to the Overseas Minister.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. D. L. Redman (Calgary East), for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Thursday, March 6.

Mr. Speaker, I intervene in this debate primarily for the purpose of making some observations in respect of the statements made a few days ago by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) in reference to the Civil Service Commission and its work. This debate has been a very long and interesting one, interesting because of the many subjects dealt with by the various speakers and also because of the unfettered expression of the individual views of members of Parliament. As was suggested by an hon. member who spoke last night, I have no doubt that the war will affect our parliamentary institutions just as it affects many other things which concern us. As I listened to the concluding remarks of the hon. member from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) last night, as he championed the cause of free speech, a free Parliament and an uncontrolled press, I could not but reflect upon the last ten days proceedings in the House and come to the conclusion that he was endeavouring to champion a cause whose victories were won many years ago and that all these matters are more strongly entrenched and rest upon stronger foundations to-day than ever before in the history of British representative institutions.
Before addressing myself to the subject of the Civil Service Commission and its operations, I wish to refer very briefly to one or two other matters. I would gather from the concluding remarks of the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) which I chanced to hear the other day, and from the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), that some hon. member had entered a protest against tRe visit of the Prime Minister and his colleagues to the Peace Conference at Paris. Protests of

this nature have, from time to time, appeared in the Canadian press. 1 am unable to understand how any Canadian could object to Canadian representation at the Peace Conference now sitting at Paris. Further, I do not believe such protests reflect in the slightest degree Canadian opinion. Every Allied nation is represented there; every portion of the British Empire is there represented. Upon what basis or reasoning it can be argued that Canada should not be there represented is something absolutely beyond my comprehension. This is the judgment day in the history of nations and institutions. The Peace Conference now sitting at Paris marks, probably, the greatest event in human history, and it would be a strange thing, indeed, if we, as a nation, were not permitted to participate in those proceedings.
Can it be rationally contended that Canada, which fought in this war to the end that some day a peace conference would be convened, shall be written down in history as an absentee from the conference? When we entered the war we had in mind that some day victory would be achieved and that a conference would be held in some part of the world to settle the terms of peace, and to provide, if possible, appropriate means to prevent the recurrence of such another war. That day has come, and it is suggested that Canada should not be represented at the conference. I must express my surprise that such a view should be taken by any hon. member or by anybody in Canada.
If Canada should not be represented, why should the United States? Our effort in man-power, in money, and in everything else, relatively equalled their effort, and I am unable to comprehend the process of reasoning which would lead anybody to the conclusion that the great nation to the south of us can with propriety be represented at that conference, but that Canada should not be represented. We fought as a nation. Our political sovereignty is almost as complete as that of any other nation which fought in this war. We are not a subject power. Our political status is not that of a colony or dependency, and I submit that it would be a great offence to'the spirit and pride of the people of this country if for a single moment it were seriously urged that we should not be represented at the Peace Conference as we are to-day. Speaking for myself, I should be ashamed of my country if at this period in her history and that of the British Empire our political status were such
that we could not with perfect propriety and as a matter of right sit side by side with every other nation which fought in the allied forces, in settling the terms of peace and the other questions arising out of the war.
It must be a matter of pride to us that we are able to take part in this great world constructive and reconstructive programme.
A new map of the world, and particularly of Europe, is being made to-day. New nationalities are being established, on the principles of self-determination or otherwise. New political systems are being framed and the old systems are being destroyed. The terms of peace with the enemy are being settled, and there is being organized a League of Nations which we trust will maintain the peace of the world for many, many years to come.
Furthermore, many material problems of inteiest to Canada and all parts of the world will be the subject of discussion at the conference. For instance, efforts are being made to solve labour problems upon an international basis. The conference is ' also considering questions affecting the distribution of shipping, of food supplies, of raw materials, as well as economic and financial questions of vital interest to every nation of the world. I cannot take the time to enumerate the different matters which will very naturally and very properly be the subject of consideration by the conference. In view of the world-wide importance of the questions that will be considered by the conference, I say that it is hardly proper to suggest that Canada should not be represented there. And if we are to be represented, what more appropriate than that the Prime Minister of this country and some of his colleagues should represent Canada? How else could we be represented? If anybody had a right to enter a protest, surely it would be the colleagues of the Prime Minister remaining here, upon whose shoulders further responsibilities have been cast in consequence of the absence of their colleagues.
The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) argued last night that Canada is no longer in a position of political dependency, that it is not a colony in the sense in which it was some years ago. I thought he approached that question cautiously and with some reserve. He took a view which was quite correct and I thought he might have shown a little more confidence in his position. To suggest that the political status of this country to-day, politically or otherwise, is comparable to our position



fifty years ago would be to interpret wrongly the organization and constitution of the British Empire and of the several Dominions and to disregard recent political developments. I do not think it is worth my while to pursue the matter further. I merely wish to enter my solemn and emphatic protest against the proposition which has been made by some hon. members to the effect that the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues should be in Canada to-day, instead of representing Canada at the Peace Conference.
I wish to refer very briefly to a matter which was discussed on Tuesday last by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) in his remarks upon the Address. In discussing financial matters he particularly referred to the flotation cost of three different Canadian loans. The figures which he gave are so palpably in error and do so manifest an injustice to the Department of Finance and the (Government that I think a few words should be said upon that point. I shall not, however, refer to any other portion of his remarks. I have not the slightest doubt that the hon. member himself is anxious to have the exact facts.
Did the hon. member say that my figures were in error?
Yes.
My figures were correct according to the Auditor General's Report.

I think I shall be able to show that the hon. gentleman was in error in the statements which he made. He referred to the flotation costs of three public loans. First, in respect of the 5 per cent Public Service Loan in New York, in 1916, for $75,000,000, he stated that the cost of flotation was $4,098,580, or $5.46 per $100.
The fact is that the cost of that loan was $2.70 per $100, and not $5.46 as the hon. gentleman states. In calculating the cost of this loan, he permitted to enter into his calculation the discount of the bonds, amounting to $2,022,927, so that his calculations are obviously wrong by that very substantial amount.

Will Canada have
to pay that amount of over $2,000,000?

Upon the maturity of the bonds they must be retired at cost. That is quite correct. But the hon. gentleman was discussing the cost actually paid for the flotation, and obviously and beyond dispute, the discount upon the bonds

should not be taken into account in calculating the expenses of the flotation itself. If the bonds were sold at a premium, my hon. friend, according to his method of calculating, would be driven to the conclusion that the loan had cost nothing- even less than nothing. That, certainly, would be a strange conclusion to reach.
You must balance one account against another.

No, because the hon. gentleman was discussing the cost of flotation. Of course, the discount on the bonds must be taken into consideration in the bookkeeping, and it of course represents the difference, between the par value of the bond and the issue price, but it has no reference whatever, I submit, to the cost or charges of the flotation. Again, the hon. gentlemen referring to the cost of the "Dominion of Canada war loan, 1915," states that the cost was $3,408,358, or almost $3.41 per $100. The fact is the loan was issued in Canada at the price of 97J. The total cash expenditure for remuneration of bankers and brokers, printing, advertising, salaries, contingencies was $425,677, so that the percentage of cost was 42J cents per $100, considerably less than one-half of one per cent. Now, my hon. friend, I know, will be one of the first to admit that there is a very substantial difference between a flotation cost of 42| cents per $100 and $3.41 per $100. Again the hon. gentleman referred to the " 5 per cent Dominion of Canada War Loan " of October, 1916, a loan of $100,000,000. He stated that the cost was $3,539,410, or $3.54 per $100. The fact is that this loan was issued in Canada at a price of 97i, and the total cash expenditure for remuneration of bankers and brokers, printing and other expenses was $797,468.27, a percentage cost $0,792 slightly over 79 cents per $100-less than four-fifths of one per cent.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to read from the Auditor General's Report which he has before him the figures given for this loan?

My hon. friend
made the mistake, quite unintentionally, of taking the statement as it appears in the Auditor General's Report without discriminating between the actual expenses in connection with the flotation of the loan and the discount upon the bonds. If he had merely subtracted from his figures the discount, he would have reached the cost of floating the loan. His remarks the other evening made it appear that the discount

upon the bonds was an actual expenditure of money.
May I be pardoned another question? I am very dull witted, no doubt. Do I understand that we arc not to pay these discounts?

The 5-year term bonds of the 5 per cent Public Service Loan, 1915, were sold at 99.56, which represents the amount investors were willing to pay. The discount merely expresses the fact that investors wished a higher rate of interest than that offered for the bond at par. If the bonds are issued at five per cent and the investing public desire a higher yield of interest than that, they must offer a price below par. The hon. gentleman is perfectly right in saying that ultimately the bonds must be redeemed at par but that is another matter. At the same time I would impress upon him the fact that in his speech he was clearly discussing the cost of floating the loan and he calculated the discount upon the bonds as an expenditure in connection with the floating of the issue. It went into Hansard and to the press in that form, and I merely wish to make the correction so that there may be no misunderstanding on the part of the public as to the actual cost of floating these loans. When securities are offered the seller must accept the price offered by the market, or not dispose of the securities If less than par is offered and it is accepted, it means that par was not obtained for the bonds, but the difference between that and the issue price is not a charge or disbursements in connection with the flotation of the loan.

Mr. Speaker, as I am drawn into this through no action on my own part, I ask permission to submit a question to the hon. gentleman. How can he get round the statement made in the Auditor General's Report, and also in the Public Accounts, where the figures are to be found exactly as I gave them and include all these items as part of the cost? He will surely admit that I am correct-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is going beyond his privilege under the rule.

I think I have
fully answered the question of my hon. friend. Upon reference to the Auditor General's Report it will be seen that the discount at which the bonds were sold is treated as discount, and not as a flotation charge or expense, whereas my hon. friend was confusing the discount with the costs
184 .
of flotation. That is the point I wish to make.
My hon. friend referred also to the fact that the 15-year bonds of the " Public Service Loan," which sold at the figure of 94.94, shortly after the issue went above par, and he infers that the bonds were sold at too low a rate. I would point out certain facts with reference to the money market at that time. The Government were unable to make this loan in Canada, at least it was not thought that a market existed here, and the Finance Minister was obliged to go to the only market then available in the world, New York. In that market Canada had no preference over any other country, and other countries were selling securities there at that time. Canada had to accept the best market price offered or not sell at all. The Anglo-French 5 per cent 5-year bonds had been marketed there about six months earlier. That was a five per cent bond and was offered to the public at 98, or to yield 5-45 per cent to the investor. The underwriting price was 96. This loan was not successful and had an adverse effect upon the market. When the Canadian loan was offered to the public it was selling at 95, yielding over 61 per cent. This, of course, affected the market for this particular Canadian issue.
My hon. friend thinks that because the ir>-year bond of this issue afterwards reached par and over, therefore, somebody made a great deal of money to the loss of the Canadian treasury. It is true that these bonds did reach par and over, but only for a short period. It is also true that very shortly afterwards they fell to 97. It is also true that in 1917 they were selling as low as 87J and my hon. friend might as well be solicitous about the people who lost when they fell to 87 as of those who profited when the price went above par.
If the hon. gentleman wishes I can give him the explanation of that although I do not want to interrupt him.

I do not wish to engage in any very lengthy discussion about this particular matter. It was perhaps peculiar that a 15-year bond should sell at a lesser rate than a five or ten-year bond. The fact is that at this period the shortterm securities were more in demand by the investing public than the long-term bonds. Short term securities were at that time more popular with investors. But it appeared later, that the long-term bond

was more in favour and had a wider market than the short-term securities. But that was a condition which nobody could foresee at that particular time in the United States.
The Public Service loan of 1915 was sold at what was then regarded as very favourable terms. The results were highly spoken of by the financial journals in the United States, Canada and Great Britain and I do not think there is anything in connection with it that is open to criticism. The only reason I entered upon this subject was to emphasize the fact that my hon. friend the other evening, in stating the expense of floating these loans, was very grievously in error and represented it at a figure very much above; and in excess of the actual amount.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In regard to the statement that I have been grievously in error, I would refer the hon. gentleman to page F-16 of the Auditor General's Report foT 1917, Volume 1, where he will find "Charges of Management, Loan Account." The identical figures that I gave are given on that page.

I am contending that my hon. friend is wrong in his method of calculation and that he has improperly taken into his calculation the discount of the bonds in reaching the actual cost of floating the issue. He has treated the discount as an expenditure or outlay of money, and in doing so I say he was in error.
I do not know about discount

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Now, I approach the subject for which I rose, namely, the statements made by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) in respect to the Civil Service Commission and its work. The statements made by the hon, member for West Toronto on Tuesday last involved very serious charges against the Civil Service Commission and the gentlemen constituting that commission. I do not know that any more serious charges were ever levelled against any Government, any branch of the Government, or any individual connected with the public service of the country. His charges involve the perpetration practically of crimes. If they are true it is serious; if they are true they are worthy of further investigation; if they are true the hon. gentleman should repeat his statement formally and ask for an investigation. It is hardly fair to the public
IMr. A. K. Maclean!
service that charges of this nature and character should be made unless the hon. gentleman making them Is prepared to substantiate them. I want to say to him that if he believes in the statements he has made, if he thinks that they are well founded and can be proven and if he desires a parliamentary, or any other form of investigation the Government will gladly accede to his request if he formally makes the application.
I regret, however, to say that I have come to the conclusion that his statements are not well founded, and that in not one . single instance can they be established or proven. I regret that my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) should have undertaken to make the statements he did concerning one of the important branches of the public service without first informing himself as to the facts. I do not question my hon. friend's motives. I know he is too honourable a gentleman to make these statements without believing that they could be supported by the facts but still I wish to say that in my judgment, after an investigation of them severally, they cannot be supported by the facts, that they are not well founded, and my hon. friend has done a grave injustice to the-public service, to that important body the Civil Service Commission, to the members of that commission and particularly to the . secretary of the Commission.
I wish to take these charges practically as they were made in the House the other evening, and I shall comment upon them as I go along. The first matter to which he refers is the appointment of the deputy postmaster in the city of Toronto, and I want to read to the House-and I would ask the House to carefully observe my reading of the statements made-so that my answer to those statements to-day will appear quite clear to hon. gentlemen. They will remember that the hon. member for West Toronto stated that the appointment of the present postmaster of the city of Toronto, in succession to his predecessor who had died early in the last year, was very properly made, and he commended the promotion of the then assistant to the position of chief postmaster of the city. He commended it further upon the ground that the appointee was the senior officer and was entitled to promotion under the principles of the Civil Service Act. He then proceeded to discuss the appointment made to the position of assistant postmaster which was rendered vacant by reason of the promotion of the then assistant to the position of postmaster. He made this statement-

My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard), In his speech the other day, approved of the appointments to the Toronto post office. I want to associate myself with him so far as the choice of postmaster is concerned ; the appointment was made promptly with the best man available. But when it came to the position of deputy postmaster, what happened? The postmaster, who had worked with the present deputy for twenty-five years, sent the recommendation to Ottawa for his appointment. That appointment was held up in this city for months. It was held up until I instituted inquiries to ascertain the reason for the delay, when I was told that it was due to the Civil Service Commission endeavouring to ascertain whether the official recommended was the senior man-. It was none of their business, Mr. Speaker, whether he was a senior man or not-he war! the one best qualified for the position. As it happened he was the senior official, but the commission refused to accept the recommendation of the postmaster, who knew all the men -that were available for the position, and spent some time before consenting to make the appointment. Why? Because the next man dn seniority was a friend of a friend of the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission.
That is the statement of the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). Now, what are the facts? They are as follows: That the appointment was not held up by the Civil Service Commission; that the man who eventually was appointed was not the next senior in the Toronto Post Office; that the Civil Service Commission did not refuse to accept the recommendation of anybody; that the Civil Service Commission does not know to-day, collectively or individually-or did not know until Wednesday last-the name of the man who was appointed. These are the facts and I propose to establish them. M3y. hon. friend says that the Civil Service Commission refused to make the appointment. Well, I will give him the reason why there was a delay in the appointment. He says that tEe Toronto Postmaster recommended, I think, Mr. Westman. The truth is that the Toronto Postmaster did not recommend Mr. Westman until months after the vacancy occurred. He recommended a man in Winnipeg whom he wanted transferred to Toronto. Now if the Postmaster in Toronto had his way, an official in Winnipeg would be the Assistant Postmaster in the former city instead of the one who was appointed, and my hon. friend might then have protested perhaps with some justice and some vehemence. I want to give the facts which relate to the delay in filling this position, and which are contained in a memorandum which I have received from the Deputy Postmaster General. Possibly I had better read from the memorandum
itself as it will present the circumstances to the House clearly and in order:
As regards the delay in the appointment of the Assistant Postmaster, Toronto, the following facts are submitted. The Postmaster of Toronto died on the 17th May, 1918, and the new Postmaster was appointed on the 15th June of the same year. As the Department expected the Postmaster to make a recommendation as to who his successor as Assistant Postmaster should be, no action was taken until the 3rd July, when the Postmaster was written to, asking for a recommendation in this respect. He replied on the 16th July recommending that Mr. Thomas T. Bower, Assistant Postmaster, Winnipeg, be appointed to the position, of Assistant Postmaster, Toronto. Nothing," further was done until the return of the Chief Post Office Superintendent, Mr. George Ross, who was absent overseas looking after the Postal Corps of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and inquiring into grievances complained of in that Force, as it was considered necessary to have Mr. Ross' advice in regard to whether Mr. Bower should be removed from Winnipeg. Mr. Ross recommended strongly against the removal of Mr. Bower, in the interests of the Winnipeg Post Office, and on the 5th November, the Postmaster, Toronto, was-written to, that the Department could not see its way to approve of his recommendation to remove such an important officer from his position at that time, particularly in view of the disturbed condition of the West. The Postmaster was then asked for a further recommendation, and replied on the 18th November, recommending Mr. Eldon Westman. This recommendation was forwarded to the Commission on the 26th November, and on the 30th November the Commission wrote the Department asking to be furnished with a complete statement of the clerks senior to Mr. Westman,, also the date of examination, date of entering the service, present salary, and any other information the Department might think justified, ignoring seniority. This information had to be obtained from the Postmaster, Toronto, and the reply was given to the Commission on the 21st December, approved on the 28th December, and the certificate of promotion issued on the 16th January, 1919-the promotion to take effect from the 18th May, 1918, the date the vacancy occurred.
My hon. friend charged the Civil Service Commission with delay in the making of the appointment to the assistant postmastership of Toronto for many months. The fact is that the commission was not responsible for the delay. The hon. gentleman also stated that Mr. Westman was the senior in that post office. As a matter of fact he was not the senior. The Civil Service Commission was justified in inquiring whether Mr. Westman was the senior officer before making his promotion. The Commission was "well within the law, and well within good practice in making the inquiry it did. Every single statement which my hon. friend made in reference to this appointment are not founded upon fact, and they are unfair and unjust to the com-

mission in every single particular. Now eventually the appointment was made. The senior officer was not appointed, hut I believe the best man was chosen, and in that belief the hon. member and myself are in agreement. That was the view of the Civil Service Commission, but the Commission was not responsible for the delay. The delay was due to the postmaster of Toronto, who wanted to transfer from Winnipeg to Toronto the assistant postmaster of the formtr city. Why blame the Civil Service Commission then for anything in connection with this particular appointment? The Commission is as innocent of any wrongdoing in connection with this matter as are the mummies in the tombs of the Pharaohs. I repeat, that not in one single particular can my hon. friend justify the statements he has made, and there is not the shadow of a shade of a reason for the complaints which he brought against the Commission in respect of this particular appointment.
Now everybody does not think that the Civil Service Commission did right in appointing Mr. Westman to the office of assistant postmaster, and a protest has been made by the Postal Service Association, I think, against that appointment on the ground that the official in question was not the senior, and that statement is quite correct. There was at least one other official in the Toronto post office who was entitled to that position ahead of Mr. Westman upon the ground of seniority, but upon the grounds of capacity, ability and fitness for the position he was selected.
My hon. friend next referred to an appointment made to the Custom House in Toronto, and this is what he said in relation to that particular matter:
The same thing happened in regard to filling
a position in the Custom House at Toronto. A hardware appraiser was needed there, and the collector of the port forwarded three names from which to make a selection. But, Sir, these three names' were taken by an official in this city, and cast into the wastepaper basket, and the Civil Service Commission appointed a man in the cdty of Victoria, B.C., to come to Toronto to take the position of hardware appraiser.
That is the charge, but the fact is that the Civil Service Commission did not make the appointment at all; they were no more responsible for the transfer of that man from Victoria to Toronto than I was, or than was the member for West Toronto. Yet my hon. friend accuses the Commission of wrong-doing in connection with this particular appointment. I say with confidence that this accusation is not founded upon fact. Indeed, it is not founded upon any-

thing; it is a dream, a vision, on the part of somebody-I am sure not on the part of my hon. friend. The matter never came before the Civil Service Commission; I am sure that not one member of the Commission could give the name of the man who (was transferred from Victoria to Toronto. What more can I say about that charge?
Why, then, was this man appointed?

Well, I am going to tell you. The transfer was made by the
Customs Department, and its authority for so doing was Section 17 of the Act, which reads, in part, as follows:
Subject to the provisions aforesaid and to the provisions of section 15, nothing in this section or in this Act shall prevent the deputy head from transferring any officer, clerk or employee from one part of his department to another.
It was under the authority of that section of the Civil Service Act that the Customs Department, not the Civil Service Commission, made the transfer in question.
Was it the deputy in that case?

I do not know,' it does not matter what he was. The official in question occupied the position of appraiser or valuator in the Customs Department at Victoria, and the Customs Department transferred him from Victoria to Toronto. It is a serious thing to charge the Civil Service Commission with the transfer of this man when they had nothing to do with it, never heard of it, and could not even give the name of the man who was so transferred. It is not humanly possible that they could know the name of that man, unless by virtue of the publicity which has been given to these matters during the past few days they had occasion to refer to some documents or were enabled to secure the information from some other source.
Now, if my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) had attacked the practice of transferring officials he would have been upon safe ground, and he might have been justified in attacking that practice. Speaking for myself, I do think that the Customs Department were hardly justified in making that transfer. I do not think they were justified. They should have known that the doing of that thing would prejudice the Civil Service Act just at this particular stage when it is being tried and when it has many critics and few friends. I think that they are deserving of some castigation

on the part of members of Parliament for doing that. True, they were well within their powers, but I think they did not exercise a sound discretion.
Who is ''they?'*

The Customs Department. I do not say that there are not occasions when it is good business and good practice in certain departments to transfer persons from one place to another. I have particularly in my mind at the moment the Customs Inspection Service. I think it would be perfectly justifiable practice to keep the Customs inspectors moving from one province to another. I believe that a Customs inspector should not long remain in one province. But that is a matter worthy of the consideration of hon. gentlemen. The practice I refer to might very well be attacked, but if it is wrong, if it is open to criticism, surely Parliament itself, not the Civil Service Commission, is to be blamed for it. But it is within our power and our jurisdiction to amend the Act so as to prevent transfers by any one department from one point to another, if we think that the practice is wrong. I do protest, however, against such a body as the Civil Service Commission being blamed for something for which they should not be blamed.	i
My hon. friend next referred to the matter of advertising for applicants for certain positions and the making of temporary appointments in the meanwhile; and he drew the conclusion that invariably the temporary appointee would secure the permanent appointment by virtue of the prestige given to him through his selection by the department. Again I say that this is a fair matter for discussion, but I protest against charging the Civil Service Commission with the building jup of this practice. They are in no way responsible for it; it is unfair to accuse them of it. I myself think that the several heads of the departments should resort to temporary appointments as little as they possibly can. Every minister and every deputy minister should anticipate his departmental needs in respeot to the appointment of officials, and only under circumstances of urgency and grave necessity should he recommend a temporary appointment to the Civil Service Commission and subsequently ask the Commission to advertise for applications to fill the vacancy. I say this because such a practice lays the whole Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission open to suspicion. In that
connection I am not disposed to be too censorious or too critical of the remarks of my hon. friend, because I can quite understand that in the multiplicity of temporary appointments followed by advertising, my hon. friend or 'any other hon. gentleman in the House might well become suspicious of the practice and might well conclude that improper influences were operating somewhere and at some times.
Now, what occurs? Why are temporary appointments made preceding the publication of advertisements calling for applications? It is invariably due to the fact that a department often requires men possessing special qualifications to discharge special departmental duties. Moreover, the Civil Service Commission has been in operation for such a short time that they have not been able as yet to build up an eligible list from which it can select temporary appointees to meet the needs of the several departments of Government. Therefore, when a vacancy occurs or a new office is to be created and the needs of the department are urgent and cannot wait, the practice is for the deputy minister to make a recommendation to the commission for a temporary appointment, and to ask them to approve temporarily of that appointment. The Commission is not to blame; it is unfair to cast that burden upon the Commission. If anybody is open to criticism, it is the minister or the deputy minister or some departmental head, and I repeat that my hon. friend, in his criticism in this connection against the 'Civil Service Commission and the Secretary of the Commission, was unfair and unjust to them.
Yesterday evening the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) referred to the appointment of a publicity agent required by the Department of Immigration and Colonization. He stated that Mr. Donald Tuck was an applicant for this position. In his application, Mr. Tuck set forth his qualifications and the hon. member thought that he was entitled to the office. Mr. Tuck's letter is used to support the complaint that the Civil Service Commission should not delegate its powers of appointment to a Board of Examiners. Mr. Tuck, however, was himself a beneficiary of this, because not very long ago he was an applicant for the position of head of the Publicity of the Vocational Branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and his name went before a board of examiners and he was selected. He was, therefore, a beneficiary of the prevailing system, and if he

is to-day complaining of that system, I say that he cannot do so fairly. A publicity agent was required by the Department of Immigration and Colonization and the qualifications necessary were set forth in the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) last night, and I might read them:
A Publicity Agent to take charge of the Publicity work of the Department of Immigration and Colonization at a salary of $4,000 per annum. Candidates should possess the following qualifications:-Ability to prepare and direct newspaper, magazine and farm journal advertising campaigns, both in Canada and elsewhere, in setting forth the settlement opportunities in Canada; knowledge and experience with (a) follow-up systems, (b) the production and circulation of motion pictures, and (c) the natural resources of Canada; ability to direct lecture campaigns ; a personal acquaintance with writers, publicists and organizations now dealing with the opportunities and land settlement problems of Canada.
There were, I believe, some seventy-nine applicants for this position. The Civil Service Commission felt that they were hardly capable of deciding, amongst the seventy-nine applicants, who was the man most capable of doing the work. Accordingly they called to their assistance a board of examiners composed of Sir John Willi-son, of Toronto, Mr. P. D. Ross, of Ottawa and Mr. A. D. DeCelles, Librarian of Parliament. These gentlemen were called together and the applications were put before them. In the end they decided that a Mr. R. J. E. Stead, of Calgary, Alta., was the best qualified amongst the applicants. Will hon. gentlemen be disposed to say that the board of examiners selected were not honourable and capable men? Were they not just as capable of making the best selection as would be the Commissioners themselves if they undertook to make it? Further, the Civil Service Commission is not a board of examiners. Examinations are held on behalf of the Commission throughout Canada from coast to coast. They do not attend those examinations in the capacity of examiners, but examiners especially for that purpose are selected and appointed, and they take charge of the examinations. This was an examination. The statute permitted it. It need not necessarily have been a written or an oral examination ; it might be a competitive examination, if in the judgment of the Commission that was desirable. The board of examiners selected Mr. Stead. My hon. friend from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) referred to the case of Mr. Tuck, a returned soldier, and he read his qualifications which are very good.
I think my hon friend thought they were
[Mr. A. K. Maclean.!
so good that he concluded that Mr. Tuck should have received the appointment. I do not say that Mr. Stead deserved the appointment, nor that Mr. Tuck did not deserve it. All I mean to say is this, that when you have seventy or eighty applications for a position, it is humanly impossible to determine with absolute accuracy that one man is much better than another, or that the man who eventually receives the appointment is actually stronger in his qualifications than the man who did not get it. It is difficult to determine matters of this kind to a nicety, and if in the end the Board of Examiners have made a wise and sound selection and have given to the public service a man who will discharge in a competent manner the duties and responsibilities attaching to that office then public interests have been fully met and no one having the public interest at heart can very well complain.
Was Mr. Stead a returned soldier?
I think not. Mr. Tuck was.
How does this committee proceed in order to reach a conclusion? Did these men appear before the Board of Examiners?

I understand
they usually take the applications made by the several applicants and get from them the qualifications as told by each applicant. They also take all such other means as {hey consider wise and necessary to afford them information as to the qualifications of the several applicants. They can, if they see fit, bring before them such of the applicants as they think might be best fitted for the position.
What is the alleged justification for overlooking the returned soldier if he possessed the minimum of requirements for the office?

I do not say that the returned soldier should not, in this case, have received the appointment. I am not undertaking to say that Mr. Stead should have received the appointment as he did. I am arguing to-day on behalf of the Commission and I am attempting to relieve them of the innuendoes and charges made against them the other day. I am more concerned about that than I am about the defence of the Government, of the departments, or of any system that has grown up or that prevails in the administration of the Civil Service Act. The question.

therefore, which my hon. friend raises, is hardly the one I am endeavouring to answer. But when the public service requires a man for a special duty, the Civil Service Commission is hound to secure for the public service the best man available. If that man can be found amongst returned soldiers, then he should have the preference.

Did we not, in passing the Act last session, adopt the principle that where a returned soldier had reasonably good qualifications, that is, where he could qualify, it was not necessary for him to have the highest qualifications of all the applicants, and where he had those qualifications, he should get the appointment?

Substantially that is quite true. I agree with my hon. friend. That is the principle set forth in the Civil Service Act as enacted at the last session of Parliament, and I am not disputing that proposition at all. However, there must, in practice, be some qualification to that very general proposition. The Department of Immigration and Colonization required a man for the position which I have already mentioned, and, as I have said, Mr. Tuck was an applicant. He appears to have had considerable experience in advertising campaigns. In the second paragraph of his letter he says:
I am at present in charge of the Publicity of the Vocational Branch of this department which involves considerable research work and feel that I have qualifications and experience which would fit me eminently for the vacant position.
In my late appointment (prior to the war) as manager of the Copy and Art Department of The Norris-Patterson Advertising Agency I was brought in touch with many of the leading Canadian advertisers, the preparation of whose copy was in my hands, and the continued success of these advertising campaigns is evidence of the quality of this copy. In many cases it has been my duty to advise on and instal followup systems, and especially in the preparation of catalogues and booklets, my experience has been very varied, embodying, as it does, a knowledge of the technicalities of the printing and engraving industries."
Let hon. gentlemen remember that the Department of Immigration and Colonization wanted a publicity man in connection with immigration and colonization work. Let us now look at the qualifications of Mr. Stead. Remember, I am not arguing in defence of the appointment of Mr. Stead or attempting to detract in the slightest degree from the qualifications of Mr. Tuck. I simply want to place the facts before hon. members, and they can make their own deductions. I want to place the facts before
them in such a clear way that they will be able to visualize the difficulties of the commission in selecting a man of the qualifications required by the Department of Immigration and Colonization. I repeat that 1 am only interested in making what I think is a deserved defence of the Civil Service Commission.	;
Was Mr. Stead holding this position when the applications were considered?

I think so. In fact, my hon. friend stated so the other evening. Upon the recommendation of the Department of Immigration and Colonization Mr. Stead was appointed temporarily early in January, and for that, of course, the Civil Service Commission is not responsible. I shall now read the qualifications of Mr. Stead:-
" Grew up on a homestead 120 miles from a railway, where he obtained first-hand knowledge and experience of the problems of pioneer life on the prairies, and personal knowledge of the practice of agriculture."
May I remark just here that a publicity man for the Department of Immigration and Colonization would naturally be expected to have a knowledge of the western country, where colonization is alone possible. To continue:-
"Was for 11 years a. newspaper editor in Manitoba, developing during that time a wide acquaintance with the problems of the West, and also with newspaper writers and editors. Experience includes the management of the advertising department of a paper, as well as its mechanical production, and the superintendence of a job printing department.
Was business manager of The Alberta Automobile Co., Ltd., from February, 1910, to November, 1912. During this period travelled many thousands of miles over the prairies increasing his knowledge of the Country's agricultural resources and business conditions.
In March, 1913, was appointed Assistant Publicity Agent of the C.P.R. Department of Natural Resources, and early in 1916 was placed in charge of all the advertising and publicity work of the C.P.R. relating to the colonization of its lands. Occupied this position until January 1, 1919, when he was appointed temporarily to position of Publicity Agent for Department of Immigration and Colonization. During employment with C.P.R., his duties included the preparation and direction of newspaper, magazine and farm journal advertising campaigns, both in Canada and elsewhere, setting forth the settlement opportunities In Canada. ; and the installation and1 direction of a follow-up system dealing with inquiries from prospective settlers."
The duties of the publicity agent required by the Department of Immigration and Colonization naturally had relation to the colonization of our western lands, and the

experience of Mr. Stead with the Canadian Pacific Railway was clearly in line with the duties of this new position. I repeat that the Civil Service Commission was in no way responsible for the temporary appointment of Mr. Stead. There was nothing else for them to do but issue a temporary certificate to him, as a request had been made by the department. Therefore, I say they are not chargeable with any recommendation. There were some seventy odd applicants for this position and the Civil Service Commission chose to establish a board of examiners composed of the persons I have named. The judgment of this Board was that Mr. Stead should be appointed. I have read both the qualifications of Mr. Tuck and the qualifications of Mr. Stead, and I leave it to hon. gentlemen to decide whether or not the Board of Examiners made a mistake. Perhaps they selected the very best man among the applicants; perhaps they did not. At all events, the qualifications of both Mr. Tuck and Mr. Stead were excellent, and I can quite understand how both would appeal to the board of examiners, and I think hon. gentlemen might very well forgive the board if they had selected either. However, they chose to select Mr. Stead, who had been in charge of the immigration and colonization work of the Canadian Pacific Railway-a man who was born and bred in the western country and who knew its needs and might, therefore, naturally be expected to make a very competent official in connection with the matters of immigration and colonization in the Prairie Provinces. That is all I have to say of that particular case.
As I said a moment ago, the establishment of a board of examiners may be open to criticism. But that system is used in Great Britain to-day and was frequently resorted to in the United States some years ago, although I understand they are gradually departing from this practice. I have discussed this matter in the last few days with the Civil Service Commission and they inform me that once they have perfected their organization and have a competent staff they hope, in cases of this kind, requiring technical qualifications, to be able to make the appointments themselves. I appeal to hon. gentlemen to extend to the Civil Service Commission an opportunity to build up an organization, and if this is extended to them I am sure the time is not far distant when they will be able to discharge their duties without deserving criticism on the part of the public. In the meantime, I do not know what else they
IMr. A. K. Maclean. I
can do. If the system is wrong, Parlia-can easily cure it by amending the Act.
Let me give another case. A few days ago, the Department of Public Works required a solicitor. Seventy-nine applications for this position were received from all over Canada and a committee of lawyers was appointed composed of Judge Audette, of the Exchequer Court, J. F. Orde and W. D. Hogg, of Ottawa, to consider the applications. These three men were all practicing barristers. Will any hon. gentlemen say that if he had been a member of the commission he might not possibly have resorted to the same method as the Commissioners adopted? No member of the Civil Service Commission is a lawyer and, therefore, they could not very well render sound judgment as to the ability of the several applicants for this position.
Was the solicitor for the Public Works Department appointed temporarily?

No, in that case no temporary appointment was made by the minister, and in that respect the case is different from some of the others we have been discussing. I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hocken) how he can reasonably criticise the action of the Commission in creating a board of examiners to select from the applicants one to be appointed as solicitor for the Public Works Department? Were not those examiners better fitted to make a selection than the members of the Commission? What better method of selection could one suggest?	,
The hon. gentleman then referred to the appointment of a fruit inspector for western Ontario, and he made very serious statements in connection witji his appointment. He said:
The man chosen had been an American citizen before the last election in Canada and could not vote in that election. True, he was Canadian-born but he went across the line and was naturalized there.
This was .really irrelevant matter, and many inferences 'may be based upon what my hon. friend said, none of which, I am sure, he intended.	[DOT]
He returned to Canada, and was not entitled, as I say, to vote at the last election, but he happened to become naturalized here since. Then he takes precedence of men who have lived here and have been serving the country, men who never ran away and were naturalized in a foreign country. This person is placed over qualified men because he is a friend of the officials.
A friend of somebody in the Civil Service,
I suppose he means.

The understanding is that the late Mr. Johnson desired this man to he appointed. That is the way the Civil Service is operated.
The hon. gentleman says further:
His name is Mr. J. R. Hastings. We have over the signature of Mr. William Poran, the chief guide of the Civil Service Commission, the statement that when the limit for receiving applications has expired the applications will be submitted to a competent board of Judges who will select a man who is in their opinion best qualified for appointment. Is that the way, Mr. Speaker, we understood that this thing was to be worked out. Are these commissioners Civil Service Commissioners, or are they not?
Now, what are the facts in this case? Mr. Hastings was born in Scotland, fifty-four years ago, and came to Canada in 1882. Later, he went to the United States, as have many other Canadians from every province of the Dominion. He returned to Canada thirteen years ago and purchased an orchard at Winona where he has since been engaged in fruit growing. Nine years ago he became associated with the Winona Fruit Growers, Limited, and during the past seven years has acted as secretary and managing director of that organization. In 1917 he became a member of the Fruit and Vegetable Committee in the Food Controller's office, and later, at the request of the Fruit Inspector of the Department of Agriculture was temporarily appointed by the Civil Service Commission. Again, the Civil Service Commission were not responsible for the temporary appointment, and it is unfair and unjust to attempt to use it against them. If the temporary appointment should not have been made, the Department of Agriculture is to blame, and if accusations are to be made they should be made against that department. I understand that Mr. Hastings is a veiy capable man and well qualified for the position. There are members of this Parliament who say that he is better qualified for the position than any other man in Canada. Certain persons in Ontario sent petitions addressed to the Civil Service Commission recommending another person, whose name I cannot recall at the moment, for the position; but when they learned that Mr. Hastings was an applicant, they wrote to the Civil Service Commission explaining that they did not know that Mr. Hastings was an applicant and withdrawing their support from the man they had recommended. Mr. Hastings was appointed temporarily for six months, and at the end of that time the appointment was enlarged for another period of six months. Before that time ends applications will be received, and I understand it to be the intention of the Civil Service Cbmmission to appoint a board of examiners made up of three of the leading fruit growers of the province of Ontario, and with them will rest the recommending of an appointee to the Commission.
Will this board be responsible to Parliament? If not, to whom will it be responsible?

The board of examiners will make the selection from among the applicants and will recommend one person to the Civil Service Commission. The Commission will act upon that recommendation, or not, as they see fit.
To whom will they be responsible for the appointment?

The board of examiners will be responsible to the Civil Service Commission to whom they act in an advisory capacity. The Civil Service Commission will be responsible to Parliament and to the country for the appointment they make. I may state that when the Department of Agriculture required the services of Mr. Hastings they thought they had the right under section 15 of the Civil Service Act to take him into the service and made the endeavour to do so. But the Civil Service Commission intervened and said: You must not do that; we will appoint Mr. Hastings temporarily, and we will issue a certificate to that effect; but applicants must be publicly called for, and from among the applicants we will make the appointment. That is a small circumstance, but I merely mention it to show my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) that he is not right in criticising on this ground the Civil Service Commission or its secretary. If anybody is open to criticism it is the Department of Agriculture. I do not say this department is open to criticism, but I do say, and with emphasis, that the Civil Service Commission are not in this regard subject to criticism.
The hon. gentleman next referred to a case which, I understand, has been the subject of a great deal of discussion outside; the appointment to the position of Superintendent of Penitentiaries. There has been a good deal of publicity about this matter, largely because one of the applicants, who was one of the Inspectors of Canadian Penitentiaries, belongs to a very distinguished family in this country; in fact he is a brother of the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), and as gallant a soldier as is that hon. gentleman. My hon. friend from

West Toronto, in discussing this particular matter, said:
And this is the very principle that was adopted when a Superintendent of Penitentiaries was to be appointed. The Civil Service Commission had not the knowledge or the intelligence or the courage to make an appointment, and they selected three men to deal with it, at least one of whom was known to be hostile to the best qualified man in Canada for the position of Superintendent of Penitentiaries. What chance did he have? Among one hundred applicants his qualifications were the best; but this committee says: None of these candidates are quite satisfactory ; we throw them all out and we will advertise afresh. You see how they double-cross the soldier; how they whip-sawed a qualified man who is a returned soldier, who fought with the Canadian army at Courcellette, who was promoted on the field of battle to the rank of Brigadier-General and who had had twenty-six years of experience in the very work for which applications were being sought.
I would like to point out that my hon. friend has brought into the argument a great deal of irrelevant matter but which at the same time is calculated to prejudice many members of Parliament and a great number of people outside. If this evidence had been given in a court of law, I am afraid the court would have ruled that my hon. friend's testimony was not relevant and could not be accepted. But, anyway, it has been read into the record and you must deal with it as it is. At the last session of Parliament a statute was passed changing somewhat the administration of the penitentiaries of Canada. This was Chapter 36 of the Acts of the Parliament of Canada for the year 1918. Section 3 of the Act is as follows:
Sections fourteen to twenty-three both inclusive. are repealed' and the following are substituted therefor:-
"14.	(1) The Governor In Council may appoint a Superintendent of Penitentiaries, who shall be an officer of the Department of Justice, who shall, under the Minister, direct and superintend the administration and business of the penitentiaries, and perform such other duties as may from time to time be assigned to him by the Minister."
Then it is provided that:
"The Governor In Council may appoint not more than three inspectors of penitentiaries, who shall perform such of the duties by this Act required to be performed by an inspector as the Minister may assign to them respectively."
It is also to be observed that:
"(f) 'Penitentiaries' includes not only the penitentiaries hereinafter mentioned or described, but also such other prisons and public institutions as are from time to time designated for that purpose by the Governor in

Council by proclamation in the Canada Gazette."
In due course that Act was assented to by His Excellency the Governor General and became law. Later the Department of Justice were required to fill the position and they thought they should promote somebody in that department. The Civil Service Commission took the ground that there was nobody in the department who should be promoted as there was nobody engaged in that particular line of work, or in work which bore any resemblance to institutional work and they said that this position must be advertised. My hon. friends should not and, I believe, would not object to the course taken by the Commission. I am speaking on behalf of the Commisison this afternoon. The Commission are not open to criticism in reference to anything in connection with this particular matter at all. They deserve commendation for every step they have taken in the matter from beginning to end. In the end, an advertisement appeared in the public press asking for applicants for the position of Superintendent of Penitentiaries; a great many applications were received and later a committee was appointed to consider the applications. The members of the committee were as follows: Dr. C. K. Clarke of Toronto, late superintendent of Kockwood Asylum, Kingston, later superintendent of the Toronto General Hospital and, I am told, one of the best recognized authorities in Canada on institutional work; Mr. C. A. Magrath, of Ottawa; Mr. F. H. Chrysler, K.C., of Ottawa; General Fotheringham, of the Department of Militia and Defence, and Dr. Paget, of the Dominion Immigration service. This committee sat to consider the applications received. They concluded that the advertisement calling for applications stressed too much the business qualifications and did not give sufficient prominence to the technical qualifications. They were of the opinion that anybody responsible for the administration of the penitentiaries in Canada, and for any other institutional work that might later be placed under him, required certain technical qualifications. That was their view. It impressed the Commission and the Commission decided to readvertise, setting forth more clearly the technical requirements for the position.
It is a fact that the man who is in charge of penitentiaries, or who is responsible for the superintendence of penitentiaries in Canada, does require special technical

knowledge. The science of criminology in modern times is based upon the theory that all, or most, criminals are insane and that they require special treatment. The modern theory as to the care of these people is entirely different from what it was thirty, forty or fifty years ago. A new conception has arisen regarding the administration of institutions for the care of these unfortunate inmates. I am not going to decide whether the committee or the board of examiners were wrong in recommending that other applicants be advertised for and I am not going to decide whether General Hughes, as the hon. member for West Toronto says, is the best qualified man in all Canada.
There are three of that brand; would you kindly be specific.

I can only refer
to the one who is the applicant for this position; I think he is William J. Hughes-
No.

William S.
Hughes. It is not my intention to decide whether or not he is the best qualified man in Canada, as my hon. friend says. He may be-I do not know-but I do say that, taking the course of action pursued by the Commission from beginning to end, it is hardly open to the very harsh criticism which it has been subjected to by the hon. member for West Toronto. I think the Commission were to be commended because they were perfectly right in saying that the position should be open to public competition and, in insisting upon that, they were perfectly right. There will be always be some doubt really as to who is the best man for this position. But the friends of General Hughes are not the only people in Canada who say that somebody is being railroaded into this position and that some improper influences are operating in this matter. I have a letter which was addressed to me the other day by a man whose name I cannot give, but I propose reading to you just a little portion of the letter.

We will have to
get the whole of it.
I will give it to my hon. friend privately.

I do not want to
see it. I am not interested in the matter particularly. The only reason I asked for it was that I got into trouble by saying " Mr. Gundy " the other day. Every Gundy in Canada but the right fellow has protested.

This letter was
addressed to me the other day from Montreal and attached to the letter was a little leaflet issued from the Grand Army Headquarters of Canada. I see on the first page of the leaflet, underscored in blue pencil: "We ask no favours from politicians; they need not expect any from us." That, however is by the way.

Does that refer to any particular politician?
Mr. A. II. MACLEAN: I do not know to whom it refers, and I am not going to give the name of the writer. I am reading this letter in order to indicate to the House that when these positions are thrown open to public competition every candidate thinks he is qualified, and his coterie of friends think his qualifications are the best. I do this' merely to point out to hon. gentlemen the difficulties confronting the Civil Service Commission in filling appointments which are thrown open to public competition. This letter is addressed to me, but personally I do not know the writer, and it is in part as follows:
Hon. anti Dear Sir,-With reference to the appointment of Superintendent of Penitentiaries, which, originally, was advertised on' November 14th, 1918, and for which appointment I am led to believe my application is still under consideration.
I beg to invite your attention to the following facts:-facts, concerning this appointment which you must admit has been kept open for the appointment of Brig.-General Wm. St. Pierre Hughes, following the resolution adopted by the G.W.V.A. Cornwall Branch.
This applicant is of the view that the Civil Service Commission is improperly manoeuvering in this matter so as to secure ultimately the appointment of Mr. Hughes.
