The publicity given to this resolution is clearly a forerunner of coming events and an announcement to other applicants that the appointment has been now filled.
I do not dispute the right of any man, be h6 a private or a brigadier-general, to make application for any appointment if he is qualified to hold1 that appointment, but, as a returned soldier and also a member of the Great War Veterans' Association and the Grand Army of Canada, I do dispute the right of any association or society endeavouring to force the Government to place any of its members when the appointment is open to competition throughout the Dominion, and especially when the appointment is likely to be given to a returned soldier who has every qualification for the position.
My original application was submitted on November 18th, 1918, and my references were taken up by the Civil Service Commission, and X know for a fact that these references could not

be anything other than satisfactory as I am fully qualified to hold such an appointment and am without prejudice.
Will the hon. minister be good enough to state the name of the writer?
I am not going to disclose who the letter is from.
It is the custom of the House to give that information when it is asked for.
It is not the custom of the House when, as in this case, the document is not a public one, and furthermore it is not of very great interest.
I want to know to what Orange Lodge the writer belongs?
I do not know that he belongs to any Orange Lodge.
May I direct the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that it is with difficulty members on this side of the House are able to follow the interesting family quarrel going on on the other side.
There is no quarrel on this side of the House with reference to this matter and so my hon. friend opposite need not worry.
At all events we should like to hear what is being said.

I read that letter just to indicate to hon. gentlemen the difficulty which confronts the commission in making appointments of this kind, and in the circumstances I say it may well be justified in calling together a board of competent men and asking that board to recommend to them whom, in their judgment, among the seventy or eighty applicants is best qualified for the position. Whatever may be the merits or demerits of the system now prevailing in making appointments to the Civil Service, whatever may be wrong in the practice of the Civil Service Commission, I want to again say that in so far as this case is concerned the Commission has acted, in my opinion, with perfect propriety, and in an absolutely honourable manner from beginning to end, and in no respect do I think the Commission's conduct is open to adverse criticism.
Again, my hon. friend referred to the appointment of a Chief Clerk of Files. The Soldiers' Settlement Board required a Chief Clerk of Files, and in the advertisement calling for applications it was stated that candidates must have five or six years' ex-
perience with files and records in a Government department, and must be thoroughly familiar with such a system. The member for West Toronto in tliis connection spoke as follows:
I am informed, and I believe, that a man can begin and complete his studies in medicine in five years; that a man can begin and complete his studies for the Bar in four years; but to be an efficient and capable filing clerk, a man apparently requires five or six years' experience. Is there any intelligent man in this House who will say that that length of experience is requisite for that kind of position?
He proceeds to say there are young officers coming back so broken that it would be impossible for them to take up their former avocations, and that it is the business of the Government to see that they are offered opportunities of this kind. He goes on to say:
My deduction is, I think, reasonable, namely, that a man who is now in the Government service has been picked out for that position. The job is practically filled before the advertisement is put into the newspaper.
Later he states:
If we have a Civil Service Commission that is going to cut men out of all opportunity of obtaining such positions, what is the use of putting in the Act the statement that the returned soldiers shall be given a preference?
Such is the hon. gentleman's statement. What are the facts? The Soldiers' Settlement Board, which is administered by the Minister of the Interior, recently required a filing clerk and they were obliged to ask the Civil Service Commission to advertise for one. An experienced man was required, I am informed, for the reason that the Soldiers' Settlement Board is a new 5 p.m. branch of the public service. In the meantime, pending the receipt of applications in response to the advertisement, the Soldiers' Settlement Board recommended the appointment of a man temporarily.
Did the advertisement call for five years' experience?

Yes, and the advertisement was prepared by the Soldiers' Settlement Board, not by the Commission. Again I say it was unfair to blame the Civil Service Commission for this advertisement. If there is any criticism to be made it should be directed against the proper body. I complain therefore of the generality, the vagueness, and the unfairness of the charges made by my hon. friend from West Toronto. Now, five or six years' experience as Chief Filing Clerk does seem a rather extended period of service to me. I would

be rather disposed to agree with the criticism of my hon. friend from West Toronto, but I do not know whether I would be right in so thinking. For the time being I would rather take the judgment of the Minister of the Interior and his officials who must have believed that they required a filing clerk of certain experience and ability, or else they would not have asked for a person possessing such qualifications and experience.
Does not that blow the whole thing sky-high?

I do not think so. Now, what happened? As a matter of fact the person filling the position temporarily is a returned soldier who served three years overseas as a private, and who has had a son a prisoner in Germany since the beginning of the war.

Hear, hear.
(Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: At one time he was in the public service, and had experience as a filing clerk, for I do not know how many years.
He will have to get out then according to the advertisement?

I do not think
he will have to get out if he is competent, even though he did not have the five years' experience. I wish to impress upon hon. gentlemen that I am not taking the responsibility of saying it was proper to insist upon five years' experience.
I merely wish to insist that the Civil Service Commission be not held responsible for that portion of the advertisement, and that criticism, if any may justly be made, should be directed against i.he department responsible for the issuance of the advertisement. However, no injustice has been done to any one. In the meanwhile, the department have a man whom they consider quite capable of discharging the duties attaching to that particular office. Fortunately, it happens that he is a returned man. In due course his application, with many others, will be considered, and in any event the department is assured of having a competent man and one who is a returned soldier. Consequently, so far as this charge is concerned, every criticism which my hon. friend made falls to the ground.
Then, my hon. friend made reference to the appointment of a man named Michael Dryden to one of the employment bureaus at Halifax, stating that on February 3rd
Mr. Dryden was advised by a telegram from one W. B. McCoy, of Halifax, who is in the employ of the Industries Department of the Government of Nova Scotia, that he, Dryden, had been appointed to the office, whereas advertisements calling for applications had been inserted in the public press only on February 18th. I have made some inquiry into this matter, and again I find that in not a single particular is the statement of my hon. friend correct. Mr. Dryden was selected by a committee appointed as a Board of Examiners after advertisement. The names of the members of the board of examiners are:	Mr. Bryce M.
Stewart, editor of the Labour Gazette; Mr. G. C. McNeill, representative of the Great War Veterans' Association, and Mr. R. H. Coats, Dominion Statistician. After considering fully the applications, this Board of Examiners selected Mr. Dryden of Halifax.
Who appointed the board?

They were selected by the Civil Service Commission. I find also on inquiry that Mr. McCoy did not, on the 3rd day of February, wire Mr. Dryden that he had been appointed, but that he did, on the 23rd day of February, wire Mr. Dryden that he had been appointed, after he, Mr. McCoy, had been so advised by a representative of the Labour Department. The purpose of Mr. McCoy's telegram was to inquire when Mr. Dryden would report at Halifax to engage upon the duties of his office.
What had McCoy to do with those duties at Halifax?

I did not carry
my investigation very far, but I understand that the provincial governments and the Labour Department are co-operating in the matter of the Labour Employment Bureaus which are being established throughout Canada and that Mr. McCoy is in the employ of the Industries Department of the government of Nova Scotia, and, I imagine, was being interviewed by the representatives of the Labour Department who were sent down there from Ottawa. Therefore I say that so far as this particular charge is concerned, the statement of my hon. friend falls absolutely to the ground.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? I am prompted to do so because I have received a letter from Nova Scotia stating that a roster of names was prepared by Mr. McCoy in January; that this list was forwarded by Mr. McCoy

for the guidance of the Civil Service Commission, and that Mr. McCoy's recommendations were approved by the commission and his nominees appointed. Has my hon, friend any information on that point?

I have absolutely no information on that point. Again I say that the only thing I am interested in this afternoon is that of making a proper defence of the Civil Service Commission in respect of the charges made against it the dther day. The Civil Service Commission made a selection from among all the applicants who responded to the advertisement. Evidently representatives of the Labour Department were in the Maritime Provinces prior to the making of the selection by the board of examiners. What they did or what they said I know not and I care not.
My hon. friend made some reference to schools which, he supposed, were specially created for the coaching of candidates for the Civil Service examinations. He said:
I am credibly informed that in this city of Ottawa there is a certain school. Nobody knows where this school is unless he is directed to it. It does not advertise; the name is not on the door, but candidates who are fortunate enough to be directed to this school are always able to pass with the highest marks. The system has been explained by one of the pupils, a young lady, in this way.
Then he proceeds further, but I shall not quote his remarks at greater length. The innuendo of that statement is that somewhere in this city, in some dark, hidden recess, there is, to the knowledge of the Civil Service Commission or its secretary, a school to which favoured and selected candidates are directed and at which they can be specially coached for approaching examinations. A species of nepotism and favouritism is suggested in this connection on the part of the commission.
Is that in my statement?

That is not in my hon. friend's statement, but one cannot refrain from drawing inferences. I do not want to interpret wrongly my hon. friend's remarks; I do not want to read into them innuendos which he never intended. But, the effect of that statement upon the public is to give them the impression that in this city there are schools for the coaching of candidates for examinations, schools which are specially favoured by the Civil Service Commission, the students at which receive an advantage in one way or the other over other applicants for admission to the Civil

Service. Now, I hope that I do not wrongly interpret my hon. friend's remarks. That is a serious accusation to make against the Civil Service Commission or against anybody connected with it. If it is not true, it should not have been made; if it is true, my hon. friend should go further, should give to the House further facts and ask for a searching and thorough inquiry into the matter. Everybody knows that there are in Ottawa, and have been for years, schools specially organized for the instruction of candidates for Civil Service positions. I remember that six or seven years ago somebody in the Customs Department was dismissed from the service because he was conducting at night a Civil Service school, or a school for the preparation of candidates for Civil Service examinations. .1 should be surprised if there were not half a dozen such schools in Ottawa. Such schools are to be found in Cornwall, Brockville and Toronto; if they are not to be found in every city in Canada, they will inside of twelve months. There are scores of them in the United States. My hon. friend seems to think that in this particular school somebody knows the particular questions that are to be put to the candidates and the particular subjects upon which they are to be examined. Well, everybody in Canada knows the subjects upon which the candidates are to be examined. The curriculum is published and made known to the public; the subjects are set forth on the notices which are sent to the candidates giving the date of examination. The subjects are also mentioned in the regulations of the Commission.
Any one conducting a Civil Service school could go over the examination papers of the last ten years, and I suppose he could approximate any possible question which could be put by the examiners. Again I say, that was an unfair imputation to make against the Civil Service Commission. They are not responsible for Civil Service schools in Ottawa. Such schools may be here by the dozen. I have no doubt there is more than one here. They will grow up in every city and town in Canada from now on, just because there is a wi3e open opportunity to every boy and girl in Canada to enter as a competitor in the Civil Service examinations and aspire to an appointment in the Civil Service of this country. The Civil Service Commission are not responsible for such schools; they know nothing about them. No information reaches the persons who conduct these

schools as to the subjects. Such information is of a public nature. The subjects upon which candidates are to be examined are very few and everybody who wants to know the subjects, may know 'them. Therefore I say the accusation made in this respect against the Civil Service Commission is unjustified and unfair.
The last case to which I desire to refer is that in the concluding remarks of my honourable friend's speech, when he referred to the unfortunate theft of examination papers by some means or another. My hon. friend almost directly accuses the secretary of the Civil Service Commission for the fact that in some way or another these examination papers reached the hands of two or three candidates at an approaching examination. Why is the secretary of the Civil Service Commission blamed? Will any hon. gentleman answer that question? Why not blame any hon. gentleman in this House? Why not anybody else in the world? Perhaps it is a fair presumption to suspect some person connected with the Civil Service Commission rather than somebody unconnected with the Commission and whose work has no relation whatever to the work of the Commission. The secretary of the Commission never sees the examination papers. They are prepared by certain persons appointed by the Commission, and are educationists of some standing and repute.

Will the Minister name them?
A. K. MACLEAN:	I am sorry I
cannot. Their names were given to me but I have not now their names before me. When the questions are set, the papers are put into the hands of the confidential printer of the Commission and they remain in his possession. My hon. friend says: Where are you going to place the responsibility for this? Surely it must be upon the secretary. Under the Statute and under the regulations the secretary is not charged with this responsibility. If he should be charged with the responsibility, then let us make him directly responsible by passing an amendment to the Act or by suggesting an amendment to the regulations; but do not let us make him responsible for this particular offence when he was not responsible. He is the chief executive officer of the Commission and not the custodian of the examination papers. Perhaps he should be. Perhaps the practice of making the confidential printer of the Commission responsible is wrong. I am prepared to hear an argument in support of that contention.
Perhaps it is too great a responsibility to leave upon one man, and I am inclined to think so. The member for West Toronto in this connection stated: " If there are clerks under him who are handing out these papers for consideration and they would hardly do it if there were no consideration-he is the man who must be held responsible. If in your business, Sir, you had a man whom you had placed in a chief position of responsibility with regard to a thing of this kind, would you go on down the line and pick out the office boy for dismissal, or would you pick out the man who is primarily responsible?" If my .hon. friend's argument is sound he would act as follows: If an employee in the post office committed theft he would say: dismiss the postmaster. If the teller in the bank stole money he would say: Let the bank manager be charged with the crime and dismissed from office. If a deacon of the church committed a sin he would banish the minister from the precincts of the congregation and rob him of his pulpit. Surely there is a great fallacy in the argument which my hon. friend makes in this connection. I am not going to say much about this particular incident. It was unfortunate, but, perhaps, it is fortunate in the sense that it will cause the Commission to take greater precautions in the future in the care of examination papers. These things have occurred in other countries, in connection with examinations of the Civil Service. The same thing occurred in Ottawa years ago, when examination papers were printed at the public Printing Bureau. Personations at Civil Service examinations occurred at Toronto some years ago, and this has also occurred at Montreal and other places in Canada. In connection with Civil Service examinations, it must be remembered that there will always be some persons doing their very best to obtain information about forthcoming examination papers, and personation will be frequently attempted, but, of course, it will be the duty of the Commission to prevent this as far as possible. In this particular case the Commission are doing everything they can to bring the culprits to justice. Already one man has been arrested and his trial is now in progress. The case is in the hands of the secret service and is under the control of the Department of Justice. Everything that should be done is being done, and I do not think any hon. gentleman could suggest that anything be done which is not being done in the case. My personal judgment is that these papers



were not stolen from the premises of the Civil Service Commission. The evidence indicates that they were abstracted from a postage parcel en route from the city of Ottawa to another place in Canada. I would like to give my hon. friend my personal view and judgment in this matter, namely, that no person in tne Civil Service Commission is responsible for this, and much less is the secretary responsible. I am very sorry that my hon. friend attempted to leave upon the House the impression which he did, particularly in reference to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission.
Just a few words of a general nature and I have done, and I am sorry to have detained the House so long.
May I ask the minister a question?
Certainly, but I do not want to discuss discounts.
I do not want to raise a question of privilege. The point is that I do not want to stand before this House and the country as having attempted to mislead the people, and I am not going to.
I did not say you did.

I want to ask a question. If not, I will take the matter up with the question of privilege. It is to be found on page F-16 of the Charges of 'Management Loan Account, New York Loan, $4,098,580, but I want to know from my hon. friend if the Minister of Finance returned to Canada with the $75,000,000, less the Morgan's commission, or did he return with the $65,000,000, less the discount and the commission? Did we get $70,901,420 out of it, or did we get the $75,000,000?
We received the latter amount.
He came back with $70,901,420.
The difference represents the discount and all charges of selling the issue.
I want to know how much money went into the Treasury of the Dominion of Canada.
$75,000,000, less the cost of charges, less whatever the discount on the bonds was.
$70,901,420. Then I was right.

It would have
been easy to receive $75,000,000 if the rate of interest had been about 6 per cent.

The paint I make
is that I was charged with making a misstatement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
not in order in entering into a discussion or argument. He would not be in order in rising to a question. of privilege even if he had one, because the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has the floor. The hon. member's speech is on record and it is not competent for him to interrupt.
It is competent for me to ask a question if the hon. member is willing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With the consent of
the hon. member.
How much did the Dominion of Canada get from that loan? Was it $70,000,000 or $75,000,000?
Even if I answer that question it would not follow that my hon. friend's statement was correct.

I got my figures
from the Auditor General's Report.

I understood my hon. friend to say that the loan cost a certain rate per $100 and I think I have demonstrated that his statement was not correct. My hon. friend does not desire to misrepresent the facts. I know he would like to have the figures correct, just as I would myself, and having that high regard for him I ventured to correct his statement.

How much money
did we get?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Paragraph (2) of section
39 of chapter 12 of the statutes of last year reads as follows:
Immediately after each examination, a list of the successful competitors in the case of a competitive examination, and of the successful candidates in order of merit in other examinations shall be made out, and the list of successful competitors and1 candidates shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
(a) Provided, however, that in all examinations persons who have been on active service overseas on the military or naval forces of His Majesty or of any of the Allies of Hiis Majesty during the present war, who have left such service with an honourable record or who have been honourably discharged, and who obtained sufficient marks to pass such examination shall irrespective of the marks they have obtained be placed in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates.

What construction does the minister put upon that section?

I think the proper construction is the obvious one, namely, that a preference is to be given to returned men, and I think that the Civil Service Commission are following out that policy. I have not followed the work of the Civil Service Commission very closely and am not in a position to discuss individual cases with my hon. friend. But if the Civil Service Commission are not observing this section of the Act they would of course be open to criticism.

I understood my hon.
friend in answering my previous question to say that the returned soldier got no preference.

Oh! No. I did not mean to say that. What I meant to say was that in the case of a position where technical qualifications were absolutely necessary the iCivil Service Commission might select a man who was not a returned soldier if he alone possessed the proper qualifications. Reverting to my subject, the hon. member for West Toronto made very, very serious accusations against the Civil Service Commission. I do not believe that ever in the history of this Parliament has any man made more grave accusations against any Government bureau or government service than he made, and I doubt if ever in the history of the Canadian Parliament such serious charges were made against any one man as my hon. friend made against the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission. I have dealt with the cases specifically, and think I have demonstrated beyond controversy that the statements of my hon. friend were absolutely unfounded in every case and cannot be supported by the facts. In concluding his remarks my hon. friend from West Toronto said:
I have just one suggestion in closing, and that is that the Civil Service Act should be amended at a vital point. I would have every position in the Outside Service filled upon the recommendation of the man who sits for the constituency in which the appointment is to be made.
Mr. Speaker, I quite understand the opposition that exists on the part of some hon. members to the Civil Service Act. It was inevitable that there should be opposition, and I am not surprised in the slightest degree. There have been similar complaints in all countries which have taken the step that this Parliament decided to take at its last session. If the objection
19}
to the Act is that the recommending power has been taken away from members of Parliament and the appointive power placed in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, all right. That is a fair matter for debate in this Parliament, and if Parliament wishes to reverse the position it took last session, well and good. Nobody could complain about that because it would be the will of the people, as expressed through its representatives in Parliament, which mu3t ultimately prevail. But if that be the objection I do not think an hon. member should attack the Act through the Civil Service Commission. I think he should attack the Act itself, and on the floor of Parliament, and not make such serious charges as he has made against the commission and its secretary. Last session Parliament unanimously supported the principle of appointment by competition; and promotion by merit. I know the Act is unpopular in many parts of Canada. I have heard many of my political friends on the other side of the House say: This is not a Civil Service Act at all, because no Liberal ever gets a position. The only thing that will satisfy them, I assume, will be the filling of every office by a Liberal. On the other hand I have heard the same complaints from members of the Unionist party, some of whom are not satisfied unless every appointment goes to friends of the Government or of Government supporters. It might be well for us to appreciate that members of both political parties will not all be satisfied with the present system, and if this Act was accepted by Parliament upon the theory that the old conditions would still prevail, it might be well for us to consider at the earliest possible date the propriety of continuing this Act; but so long as it remains on the statute books I say it must be observed. The old conditions will not prevail so long as this Act remains in force. I can quite understand how representatives of Parliament find pressure from their constituents and political friends very embarrassing indeed with the present Civil Service Act in operation. I have sympathy for them. I have been embarrassed on that account myself. But the question is: Are we to have a different system from that which has prevailed in the past in making appointments to public office? Is it desirable in the interest of the public sendee that appointments to office be made on the recommendation of members of Parliament, or shall they be made by an independent tribunal such as the Civil Service Commission? I am very glad to

find so many members on both sides of this House approving, after all, of the principle and expressing their sympathy with the Act and their desire to see it continued. I believe it will only be a short time before every member of this Parliament, or of future Parliaments, will say that the present system is better than that which obtained in the past, and when every member, regardless of the name of the party with which he is affiliated or the constituency which he represents, will be anxious to preserve the principle of the Civil Service Act which leaves appointments in the Civil Service with an independent commission.
My own opinion is that it is by far the better system; fairer, more just, more democratic. It is hardly worth while to boast of democratic institutions unless you follow out the principles of democracy; and it is nothing but tyranny which gives to any party or to any member of Parliament the right to make recommendations to office which are virtually conclusive. I have made many recommendations to office myself during the many years in which I have been in public life, and I have seen the present Civil Service Act in operation; and I have no hesitation in saying that it is in the interest of the public service, it is in the interest of Canada, that the method of appointment which now prevails shall continue.
I trust this Parliament will never again revert to the old method of making appointments. I had intended to refer to the many anomalies and injustices which issue from the past system, but I shall not take up the time necessary to refer to these matters. I trust, however, that Parliament will continue to support, as sympathetically as it did last session, the principle of appointment to the public service by an independent commission.
Now, just a word or two as to the Commission. I have already said more than once that the criticism of the hon. member for West Toronto may have a very disastrous effect upon the work of the Commission and upon the progress and development of our public service under provisions of the Civil Service Act. I know that he did not intend to do injury to so important an institution as our Civil Service Commission, and it became necessary, therefore, for some member of the Government to speak in answer to the accusations he made and in defence of the work of the Commission. He has referred to the fact that the chairman of the Commission, Hon. Dr. Roche, is not a very strong man and has been more or less ill, and consequently 
has been unable to devote the time to the work that the work deserved. As a matter of fact, Dr. Roche has enjoyed better health during the last year than during many years previous. It is unfortunately true that Mr. Jameson has been seriously ill during the past few months. He became an influenza victim, in the month of November, I think, and has been obliged to spend the winter in the southern states. But, after all, the criticism which is made of the Commission was not directed, in the main, against the capacity, integrity and character of the Commissioners but rather against the work done by them as a body, and the suggestion was, not of incapacity or inability, but of something worse-a desire not to observe the provisions of the law or to carry out the Act honestly. I do not suggest that the Civil Service Commission must be free from criticism; but, I do state frankly that I think the work imposed upon the Commission is excessive, and that Parliament should consider the question of increasing the Commission during this Parliament. I know that the duties of the Commission are so onerous that much of their work must be neglected. They have not devoted sufficient time to the proper organization of the Commission as they should have done. But there was a reason for that. The statute passed last session imposed upon the Commission the duty of reclassifying all the Inside and Outside Service. In conjunction with a body of experts whom they brought to Ottawa they have been engaged in that work of reclassification ever since Parliament rose last year. I say on their behalf-for it should be said of them-that it has been impossible for them to discharge the duties pertaining to their office in the manner and with a despatch, which, I know, they would have desired. I am not pleading for mercy for the Commission, and I would be the last person to say that they should not be criticised. All I ask of Parliament is that fair play and ordinary justice be extended to the Commission and its members. I do not ask more on their behalf; they would not have me do it; they would not do it themselves.
I wish to say a word particularly as to the secretary of the Commission, because I feel that my hon. friend for West Toronto has done that gentleman a great injustice, unintentionally, I believe. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) speaking last evening objected to some statement made by Mr. Foran in commenting on the

statement made in Parliament by the hon. member for West Toronto. It is to be remembered that the accusation made against the Secretary of the Commission was a very, very serious one indeed-one who reads the hon. gentleman's speech carefully must be seized of the seriousness of his statements. Accusations made against any man, if the person accused believes them to be unfair, naturally provoke recrimination. In this particular case the recrimination has brought forth a reference to matters of religion and creed, which have nothing to do with the question of Civil Service-and I doubt if they have anything to do with Christianity. Perhaps the statement made by the secretary was unfortunate. I think the statement made by the hon. member for West Toronto will, some day, be regarded by himself as unfortunate. I think the secretary of the commission and the member for West Toronto will, some time, come to understand one another better with respect to these matters, and that each of them will forget some of the remarks that have been made.
My personal acquaintance with Mr. Foran is very limited indeed; in fact, I have never had the opportunity of meeting him in my life until the Civil Service Act was under consideration at the last session of Parliament. But, I do know that he is a strong friend of Civil Service reform and of an efficient public service. I do not believe there is a man in Canada who is so strong a friend of Civil Service reform, and of an efficient, capable public service, as Mr. Foran. He is so regarded by Civil Service reformers in the United States as well as by those in Canada who know him in connection with his work.
I must speak of him as I know him with my very limited experience. I have no hesitancy whatever in expressing to the House my own view, and that is, that he is a capable public official interested in building up a strong and efficient public service. I do not believe for one single moment that the secretary of the commission would be guilty of doing any of the acts which were charged, or suggested, against him in the remarks made a few days ago by the hon. member for West Toronto.
Mr. Foran has been in the public service for thirty years. He has been connected with the Civil Service Commission since 1908 and he was secretary of the Board of Civil Service Examiners from 1895 to 1908. Therefore, he has been intimately connected with, and has intimate knowledge of, everything that relates to the Civil Service of
Canada. I think he is trusted by all who know him. I believe his services to 'the public are appreciated by all who have had an opportunity of knowing him and I think I can safely commend him to Parliament, as a capable and trustworthy secretary of the Civil Service Commission.
I feel called upon in justice to say these few words for the secretary of the commission, and I do trust that the member for West Toronto will be able to revise his opinion of that gentleman and of the work of the commission, and that before this session closes we will have from him an admission that in regard to all, or practically all, of the statements which he made against the commission and its work the other evening, he, unfortunately, was misinformed. Having said these few words on behalf of the commission, the members of the commission, and its secretary, I finish.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I trust that you and the House will pardon me if, in the course of my remarks, I frequently refer to my notes. Wishing to be understood, and desiring to make a modest but active contribution to national harmony, I address the House in English, which is not my maternal tongue. For this reason I ask your indulgence.
I will make only a very brief answer to the speech which was delivered by the hon. minister representing the city of Halifax. First of all, I wish to assure the hon. gentleman that nobody on this side objects to Canada being represented at the Peace Conference. On the contrary, we say that Canada should be represented at the Paris Conference, but surely my hon. friend from Halifax will not support the idea that nearly one-third of the iCabinet should be overseas while there is so much to be done in Canada, and when ministers remaining here follow, according to the Globe, a policy of " putting off " concerning all important matters.	[DOT]
As to questions relating to the cost of war loans, and the conduct of the Civil Service Commission, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the debate, and I do not wish for the present to interfere in this family quarrel. I have only one word to say about the Civil Service Commission: I hope that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) will take advantage of

the opportunity which has been given to hint by the Government, and ask for an investigation in order to prove the charges which he brought to the attention of the House the other day. Speaking for myself, having heard from the gentlemen opposite contradictory statements on the matter, I shall reserve my judgment until this investigation has taken place.
Mr. Speaker, it is stated in the speech from the Throne that " important measures, designed to promote the welfare and prosperity of the people in the new era of reconstruction, social as well as material, upon which the world has entered, will be recommended for our consideration." This paragraph is very general, indeed, and enunciates a very large programme of action. For my part, I would have preferred to the word " reconstruction " the words " readjustment," or " co-operation," which seem to be more applicable to our country. However it may be, the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) the other day exemplified this programme in a very magnificent, descriptive definition. He summed it all up in this telling sentence :-
Reconstruction means a going forward, not a standing still; it means progress, not stagnation.
Let us see, Sir, if the Government has realized such a definition. Is it true that by their actions they have justified the laudatory speech of the hon. minister? In answering this question I wish to be fair, and I will give the opinions of friends of the Government itself. The fact that the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy), who was Parliamentary Under-Secretary for the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment, has resigned that position is very significant. Why did he resign? His motives were explained in a statement issued to the press and which has been already read to this House. It is a clear statement, and coming from such an authoritative source it proves conclusively that in matters of reconstruction the Government, completely and absolutely, lacked initiative, method and courage. Moreover, another good friend of the Government, Senator Nicholls, in a letter published by the Globe of December 4, 1918, said the following:-
The Government has been repeatedly warned to prepare for after-war conditions, but the war is over and little 6r nothing has been done, although every other civilized nation has been mobilized for trade purposes long since. Better late than never is an old proverb, but "a stitch in time saves nine," is a much better one.

These opinions are confirmed by the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization himself, who said the other day that " there was not very much talk at that time-that is to say, last July-about the preparations for after the war, and we must not be very much surprised in this country if in that respect the full duty of the Government was not completely performed." Then a little further on the hon. minister went on to say:-
We always understood that the war was going to end, that it would not last forever.
Again he said:-
We were not all adrift.
How can the hon. minister reconcile this last statement with the first one? I do not know, but what I do know and say is that the Government has failed in its duty regarding reconstruction.
They were repeatedly warned to prepare for after-the-war conditions, but when the armistice was signed, according to the Minister of Immigration (Hon. J. A. Calder) himself, little had been done. Surely this is not a progressive policy; it is rather Stagnation. Read carefully, Sir, the entire speech of the minister and you will see that while set phrases were coming forth fluently and eloquently, actual facts were standing still.
I will deal in the course of my remarks with three subjects: the returned soldiers, the labour question, and the tariff and agriculture.
As to the returned soldiers, many say to them that they are heroes. That is perfectly true. Many tell them also: we owe everything to you. Perhaps the desire is all right, but they speak from the generosity of their hearts, not with due regard to the financial possibilities of the country. Too many transient favours can only make sufferings more acute. Everything which is promised to our returned soldiers and not given to them will he considered by them as a robbery. The Government must take care not to make of each of those whom they help a kind of perpetual pensioner who may become all too easily a rebel or a beggar. On the contrary, it is our imperative duty to afford to these veterans an opportunity at the earliest possible moment and in the most extended manner of resuming their pre-war activities and acquiring, as a consequence, a greater dignity and the right to greater independence. To give to disabled soldiers artificial limbs is good, because you release their bodies of many hardships. But that is not enough. We must secure for them also calmness of heart and soul

and inspire in them a high idea of their dignity. Has the Government succeeded in this noble work of raising the morale of our returned soldiers? As you read the newspapers, Sir, you are obliged to confess that the numerous troubles caused by some returned soldiers in Toronto and in other western places seem to suggest a negative answer. This is a great source of regret to every law-abiding citizen, and I earnestly request the Government to adopt proper measures not only to assure material help to our heroes, but also to provide for their intellectual and moral welfare.
I truly believe, Sir, that the principle of granting pensions to returned soldiers according to their rank in the army and proportionately to the pay they were receiving as such is not just and fair. I do not advocate uniformity in the rate of pensions; I only submit that you must not create distinctions and privileged classes among the veterans. Moreover, the Pensions Board should not consider only the gravity of the injury, because the injury may not of necessity bring about a change in the earning power of the man. For instance, an accountant with a leg taken off at the thigh will be able, without suffering any decrease in his salary, to continue to do his book-keeping, while a pianist, deprived of the use of only one finger necessary to the exercise of his profession, may fall into poverty. Consequently, it is the relation between his infirmity and his ability to carry on the work or practise his profession which is the essential factor to be considered in determining the pension of the returned man. Each case, therefore, should be dealt with individually, separately, according to the particular circumstances, on its own merits, and not according to specific rules, rigid regulations, or the rank held by the man in the army.
The Minister of Immigration and Colonization told us the other day that we have, scattered throughout every province of Canada, something like 150 institutions for disabled soldiers. This is very well, but if these institutions are managed according to "the arrogant and insolent system" described by the Globe, "which regards the continued interest and concern of civilians in their sons and brothers after they hav.e become part of the military forces as presumptuous and calling for reprimand and punishment;" if the Administration maintains the conditions tnat-and here again I quote the Globe-"permitted Ottawa-behind the anonymity of which guilty officialdom now seeks to hide-to utilize a building"-the Base Hospital at Toronto- "which the Medical Officer of Health testified was in a disgraceful and unsafe condition, to house more than double the number of' patients it was properly capable of accommodating in a sound and safe condition;" if there is no better accommodation for soldiers in these institutions than in the Toronto, Montreal and other military hospitals; if, as asserts the Globe, of October 30th, 1918, Canada, in its fifth year of war has yet made no attempt "to provide adequate modern hospital accommodation and equipment for the men of Ontario's biggest military district;" and . if these conditions prevailed all over the country, well, Sir, to use the expression of the Minister of Colonization (Hon. J. A. Calder), we are nearly all adrift. I am afraid that our returned soldiers will not be cared for as they deserve, and the Government will be held responsible for this bad treatment.
We Liberals are true and sincere democrats, and as such are supporters of responsible government. We desire that the people should govern themselves in accordance with the Constitution, through the intermediary of their representatives. But a reasonable use of political rights demands a political formation, a political organization. How is it that to-day in our country a large number of citizens are sick of politics and apathetic to it? Evidently there is a close connection between this condition and Government by Orders in Council. It is not sufficient to say to the people: You are free according to the law; you are, by the universal franchise, the leading authority; by your vote you are the masters of the country. How can the people be sovereign when we are not permitted, in a meeting of free citizens, to speak freely on matters concerning the interests of the country? Do we sincerely desire to be a nation politically free? Do we sincerely desire that all classes of society, with diligence, energy and thoroughness, should take an active part in active political fights for the defence of their most sacred rights? We must immediately abrogate the Orders in Council repressing the freedom of speech and freedom of the press. These are political liberties for which our forefathers have fought, and I feel it is my imperative duty earnestly to urge the Government to repeal without delay all regulations encroaching upon that liberty, regulations which entail autocratic Prussianism in this Dominion. It is time,

Sir, to practise in our political life the democratic ideals which have triumphed on the battlefield.
There is now in our Dominion a general industrial unrest. Its principal sources are: the abuse of Orders in Council, the high cost of living, the scandalous war profits and the social strife between the different classes of the community. During the last four years and a half we have been the sorrowing witnesses of the most bloody war in the history of the world. In our country we have also had our internal difficulties. There has been a general struggle between manufacturers and labourers, between producers and consumers. The result has been the triumph of the powerful over the weak, of the unscrupulous man over the honest man. The rich have become richer and the poor poorer. What has the Government done to help the Canadian people to recover all the rights of which they have been deprived by capitalism under an economic sphere? Has the Government proved to the working people that not only do the labouring men work for a salary, hut they perform in our community functions of general interest for the accomplishment of which they have a right to gratitude? Has the Government been progressive in this matter? The strike of the postmen last July, the difficulties of the Government with the Civil Service, the strike of the employees of the Public Printing Bureau which began to-day, are good answers to this question. They prove conclusively that as regards labour the Government has been inconsistent, autocratic and stagnant.
Ministers of the Crown were responsible for this strike and postponed a decision until they were forced by public opinion to make one. Let me quote an article from the Globe under date of July 25, 1918, which explains the situation very well:
It is impossible to avoid accepting the verdict of the man on the street that responsibility for this dislocation of business rests primarily with the Government at Ottawa. The bonus passed to the letter carriers by Parliament has never been paid. The Government either neglected the repeated petitions of the men or refused to take them seriously. The Premier, the Postmaster General, and several members of the Cabinet were overseas. Those remaining at Ottawa followed a policy of " putting off." The result is the strike, the tying up of much important business, and general public inconvenience and loss.
The plain truth of the matter is that the Post Office Department has been practically neglected for months, while the'Labour Department, which should have properly also interested itself in the situation as it concerned the carriers, is headed with such hopeless inefficiency that nothing effective or business-like can be hoped for under existing conditions.

If the Government acted in the same manner towards the Printing Bureau employees, they must bear their responsibility before public opinion. For this reason, I blame the Government for its prolonged delay in performing one of its principal duties, that is, to guarantee and favour the development of professional organizations. The ministers who occupy the Treasury benches must remember the very object of the State, namely, that its principal mission is to protect all rights without exception.
If common law justly prevents the abuses of the less disputed power, the paternal one, much more should it do so when it is a question of labour contracts. A minimum must be guaranteed to the weakest contracting party. Liberty alone is not sufficient to solve the serious social problems.
As part of its so called progressive policy, the Government intends to confer upon women the privilege of sitting in Parliament. This reform is not asked for by women, and in my opinion is mere camouflage. Women will not avail themselves of this privilege. In Great Britain at the last election there were only a few women candidates and only one was elected. Does the Government really believe that it will be otherwise in Canada? If not, this proposed legislation is useless. Moreover, it is not demanded by the women, who in general have never claimed political rights, but have always firmly demanded laws which would enable them to be victorious in their struggle for life. In our modern society, working women have been exploited by the manufacturers. They receive no protection and work hard till they are exhausted, and it is well known that they are not sufficiently paid. What they demand in the name of justice and humanity is a minimum wage and the Government would serve the interests of women better by passing a law fixing a minimum salary for working women throughout this Dominion, than by giving to women the privilege of sitting in Parliament. Legislation such as I have suggested has already beep proposed by the Government of the province of Quebec, and I urge this Government to follow along the same lines.
Inasmuch as the labour programme claims the possession by labourers, including farmers, of their essential rights, the legal, proportional and professional representation of their interests, the protection of their homes, a sufficient salary to insure a decent standard of living for themselves and their families, guarantees by way of state insurance against accidents, illness and unemployment, old age pensions, the privilege of participating in profits and

even, by means of co-operation, in the capital of the enterprises to whose success they contribute by their work, to that extent I approve of it. Why? Because the labouring men constitute an essential part of the community and because the Government must solve the problems of our social life. The question is, not merely to provide against poverty, but to guarantee social rights; it is not a question of charity, but a matter of justice. It is important to limit as much as possible that unhappy class of our people earning a precarious wage. Having first admitted that the labourer is entitled to a just salary in proportion to the efficiency of his work we must then grant to him additional remuneration by means of sharing in the profits of the enterprise in which he is engaged. This is the future form of salary and perhaps it will take a long time before the rights of the labourer in this respect is recognized. There will undoubtedly be much objection to it but we know that the principal has been already applied in some measure and with good results in the form of co-operative farming, in the form of distribution of dividends or bonuses and of pensions proportionate to the size of the family. Remedies must be applied if we are to check effectively the industrial unrest which at present makes our national outlook very gloomy. What remedies have the Government proposed? The Minister of Public Works made two suggestions. By the first he declined all responsibility on the part of the Government, and wanted the capitalists to spend their money in industrial enterprises regardless of consequences. To my mind that suggestion is impracticable, because in financial matters there is no sentiment. Secondly, he intimates that the Government will spend enormous sums of money on highways, railways, shipping, etc., but that in consequence we shall face a yearly deficit of from one hundred to one hundred and fifty millions of dollars. This second suggestion is not the proper remedy, and if it constitutes progress at all, it is an uninterrupted progress towards bankruptcy.
What else is the Government doing? We have ministers giving interviews-talking always talking, but doing nothing in the matter of social reform. If this Government progresses at all it progresses in stagnation.
Speaking on the Budget in the session of 1916, the Acting Prime Minister said:
"The future of Canada rests with the development of its great resources, of which the greatest and most fundamental is agriculture, and this development is in turn bound up with the question of increase in population of the productive sort and the facilities afforded It
for the application of its intelligence and industry. It is probable that in the straightened financial conditions which may prevail for some years forward, the question of capital for the development of agriculture may be of paramount importance, and it is our intention to inquire carefully during the coming recess into this most important subject	
It is always the same song, Sir; it was repeated the other day by the hon. Minister of Immigration, when he said:
"A good deal of thought and study has been given to many of the problems that would naturally come up when the war would close."
But where are the results? Has the Government created a system of rural credits as requested by the farmers for many years? Not yet, why? Because the Government always studies but never acts. Since 1913 they have had before them a Bill regarding rural credits, and after six years of study and thought, they have not yet adopted it. They are not following on this great question, the bold example of France, of Great Britain, and of the United States, all of which countries have passed, even during war, progressive legislation to efficiently promote rural credits. I hope, iSir, that there will be no more standing still on this question, but that in the interests of the farmer the Government will establish rural credits in Canada, so that the farmer may not be at the mercy of accumulated capital in merged banks, but may be able, by means of co-operation, to finance and develop their own industry, the basic industry of our Dominion. II make this suggestion, not only for the good of farmers, but in the interest of the whole country; because, if agriculture progresses, there will be a decrease in the cost of living, and with such a decrease industrial unrest will soon come to an end.
Is the Government more active and determined as regards free agricultural implements, free food stuffs, reciprocity with the United .States, and tariff questions in general? The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) has admitted that " the Tariff forms a very essential part of the work of reconstruction." This opinion is general among the people; manufacturers await a decision on that important question, and are postponing improvements to their factories pending announcement by the Government of its policy. On this point I have only to read the circular of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, dated at Toronto, February 19, 1919, and numbered 174. It is entitled " New Factories and Additions," and says in part:
There is no doubt that a considerable amount of factory extension construction is held up

owing to the uncertainty prevailing in regard to what the Government may do with the tariff at the approaching session,

as a result of the demands of the Western Grain Growers and other farmers' organizations.
The demand for a decision by the Government on the tariff question comes not alone from the manufacturers of this country, but the Grain Growers, the United Farmers, the local legislatures of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and the rural population all over Canada, are unanimous in favour of an immediate and substantial reduction of the tariff. On the 4th of this month, Premier Norris, of Manitoba, according to a Canadian Press despatch published in the Citizen, expressed a strong opinion that never in the history of Canada was the time so opportune as now for a revision of the tariff on the lines of a substantial reduction. " The Government at Ottawa," said Premier Norris, " is not supposed to be a party Government, and should be in favour of dealing independently with the question."
Facing such a general demand for decision and action on the tariff question, what is the Government doing? Have they, as the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization said, " A true conception of what the people of this country demand in the way of progressive legislation?" No, Sir, they progress only in stagnation. They " wait and see." They should remember that this policy was disastrous in England, and that such standing still is against the public welfare and cannot be rightly supported. Allow me to quote on this subject the conclusion of a letter, dated Langvale, Manitoba, February 10, 1919, and published by the Financial Times, Montreal, of first March inst.
They argue for a "wait and see'' policy and for us to let this sacred national policy alone until they have had time to adjust themselves to peace conditions. What about time for us to adjust ourselves? Our point is that if the burden is not removed we farmers, on this drifting policy, will be, if not ruined, brought dangerously near that point. As I said before when wheat was too cheap years ago we were very near to a catastrophe. The life of Canada depends mainly on the basic industry of farming. Let them beware that they do not hill the goose that lays the golden egg. The manufacturers seem to see blue ruin ahead for them if Free Trade is adopted. This I do not credit, but I do know after thirty years' experience farming In Manitoba that if the burden is not eased the fa-rmwill be more and more forsaken, and I fail to see how we can possibly build up Canada fit for all classes without a prosperous farming community.
This statement is very accurate and I entirely concur in it. I said, last year, that I was in favour of free agricultural imple-

ments and free foodstuffs. May I add, Sir, that, following Liberal principles, I am a staunch supporter of the 1911 Reciprocity Agreement with the United States, of an increased British preference and of the immediate withdrawal of the war supertax. I greatly doubt that such an expression of opinion on my part can induce the Government to reach a conclusion on this question. They are too much inclined to stand still and stagnate in matters of progressive legislation.
We are jubilant. Sir, because the war ended with the triumph of liberty and civilization ; but we have another important duty to perform. Our delegates attend the Peace Conference. Let us pray the Almighty that their decisions be always and only guided by the eternal principles of justice and charity which have enlightened the world and which alone can ensure a lasting and profound peace for the universe. Let us learn the moral lessons of the war. Our gallant Canadian soldiers of all races and creeds have united their energies and thoughts, their experience and hearts, for the defence of a sacred cause. Let us imitate them and heartily practice for the progress and welfare of our beloved Canada the beautiful virtue of mutual toleration and the duty of national unity; let us be animated and inspired by the spirit of that illustrious and much regretted statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who during his lifetime always had an undivided affection for Canada and liberty, a profound respect for human beings and who always advocated " welfare in harmony."

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few observations in connection with the debate on the Address as the representative of the most northerly and most westerly territory of this great Dominion. The hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Trahan) has paid some attention to some incidents that have occurred in the present session and, before addressing myself to the subject matters of the speech from the Throne, perhaps you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, to make a few references to some of the things that he has said. He refers to what he is pleased to call the family quarrel and I presume he has reference to what took place in the House this afternoon when the hon. the Minister (Mr. A. K. Maclean) referred to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). One of the hopeful things about this Union party to me is, Mr. Speaker, that when a man who sits on your right

has anything to say in regard to the conduct of affairs by the men who sit on the Treasury Benches, he is not afraid to get up and say it in Parliament, or in public, and to have it carried on the wings of the telegraph to the uttermost parts of this Dominion. That is, I consider, good policy. Publicity is one of the great safeguards of democracy and I think it is just as well that members should express themselves here where they can express themselves.
My hon. friend referred to the speech made by the hon. Minister of Colonization and Immigration (Mr. Calder) and particularly to his remark regarding reconstruction that not all had been done that he wished they could do. Is that not all right? I do not suppose there is any minister of the Crown sitting here who is able to do what he would like to do, but it is at least a confession of interest for a minister to get up and say that he has done certain things but there are other things * that he has not found himself in a position to do. He shows the Tight spirit at least when he takes that position rather than attempting to defend what it is impossible to defend. The world is in a very chaotic [DOT]condition and great changes have taken place all over.
My hon. friend also paid his respects to the method of governing which this Government used to a large extent during the war and when resort was had to Orders in Council. I have heard other hon. gentlemen speaking from the other side of the House and criticising the Orders in Council as well. They have found fault with the Government for using that method of giving [DOT]effect to the will of the people in carrying on the war. I do not think that criticism is well founded. In my judgment, Orders in Council are an indication of the flexibility of our constitution rather than a symptom of the autocratic methods which governments use in times of stress. Orders In Council have been used by the British Government for more than one century at least. They were in existence at the time of the Napoleonic wars, having been used by the British Government of that day. I do not remember what their origin was, but I know they existed then. They are not used, generally speaking, except in times of stress. Where did the Government get its authority to issue these Orders in Council? Perhaps the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me will be surprised 9 p.m. when I point out to him that the authority which is carried by these Orders in Council is derived from the
War Measures Act, an Act which was consented to unanimously by the members of this Parliament, and an Act which was supported by the distinguished gentleman whose spirit has passed beyond and who led the party of which my hon. friend is a member. Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself supported that measure. I wondered when I heard of these hon. gentlemen referring to these Orders in Council if they had just thought back far enough to realize where those Orders in Council had their source. In my hand is the Hansard for the special session of Parliament in those fateful days of August, 1914. Sir Wilfrid Laurier is speaking
