Is my hon. friend satisfied? In that case I may be permitted to read the quotation:
The gravity of the occasion which has called us together makes it incumbent upon us even to disregard the formalities and conventionalities which in ordinary times the rules of the House, written and unwritten, enjoin as a wise safeguard against precipitate action, but which, on such an occasion as this, might impede us in dealing with the momentous question before us. This session has been called for the purpose of giving the authority of Parliament and the sanction of the law to such measures as have already been taken by the Government, and any further measures that may be needed, to insure the defence of Canada and to give what aid may be in our power to the mother country in the stupendous struggle which now confronts her.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier quoted the War Measures Act from which these Orders in Council spring. The Government is not attempting to get from under any responsibility that they have in this matter. In the final analysis they have to depend on the War Measures Act, and we are told that only those Orders in Council which are necessary to be retained will be submitted to Parliament. They will be brought down and Parliament will be asked to approve or disapprove of them. I do not see why it is necessary to criticise the Government for using an Order in Council as a method of representing the people during the stress of war.

My hon. friend referred to the extension of the franchise to women and criticised that act of the Government. Sir, it is too late to criticise the giving of votes to women. If there was one thing which impressed itself upon my mind during the war, so far as the Canadian people are concerned, it was the degree of organizing ability which the 'women of this country displayed, to say nothing of their heroism and patriotism during the great struggle. For my part, Sir, I welcome the giving of votes to women, for I feel sure they have well deserved it, and if they are not as thoroughly versed in the arts of government as the male members of our population they will very quickly learn.
I would like, Sir, to offer my felicitations to the distinguished gentleman who now leads the Opposition, and upon whose shoulders the mantle of the late distinguished leader of the Liberal party has fallen. He is an old parliamentarian, and I am glad indeed to find that he was selected as the leader of his party.
I am pleased to find that the speech from the Throne promises constructive legislation which will require constructive statesmanship to carry into effect. Perhaps never in the history of our country do we need more than now such statesmanship and such legislation. Some of the hon. members of this House in their conversations with me rather indicate that they almost fear the return of our men to this country after the cessation of the war. What were we fighting for four years in the great war for? Was it not for a victorious peace, and have we not achieved that triumphant result? Why then should we fear the return of our men from the front, or fear lest a chaotic condition of mind ensue when they do come back? Are these men strangers to this country? Are we bringing back from Europe four or five hundred thousands of aliens? No, Sir, they are our own people who understand the meaning of representative government and what the possibilities of Canada are. They are coming back to their own people, coming back to their own homes, and I have no fear at all as to what their attitude will be. I welcome them back because they have a tremendous flood of energy which, if properly directed, will result in great good to this country of ours. They are coming back to take part in the political life of Canada, and unless my judgment is altogether wrong the men who will govern this country, provincially and federally for the next decade or two are in the Canadian Army. I have no doubt that the Prime Ministers of Canada even will

be recruited from that source if history repeats itself in our country, as it did in the United States. In the course of the next ten or fifteen, or perhaps twenty years I have no doubt that the men who fill these positions in front of me in this House, the men who represent the Crown in this country, will be chosen, to a very large extent, from the Canadian Army which has brought such glory to our common country. There is no fear in my mind about the ideas these gallant gentlemen will bring home with them, because they have fought the fight, they have kept the faith, and they are coming back to the country which they love and which they may call their own.
Amongst the constructive legislation promised in the speech from the Throne is a measure to assist in settling the soldiers on the land. I am a great believer, Sir, in having among our population people who have a stake in the soil. Canada is an agricultural country, but we have different resources from which we derive our national life. They are four in number, the farms, the fisheries, the mines, and the forests, but of these four the greatest of all is the farm. It employs the greatest number of our people, it furnishes the largest number of tons of freight to our railroads-in a word, farming is the backbone of Canada. But you cannot convert four or five hundred thousand soldiers immediately into farmers. There are certain things which must be done, and done in unison, before a soldier can be made into a successful farmer. These things are three in number. First, you must have land for the soldiers, and I am glad to find that the Government has undertaken to provide land for our soldiers when they return. But that is not enough. We must also provide the soldier with a certain amount of capital- not very much, but a certain amount-so that he will be able to make a proper start. But there is another thing that is almost equally as essential as land and capital, and that is some experience or some knowledge of agriculture. These are the three things that are necessary, in my judgment, to start a soldier who wants to go on the land and become a producer, as we all want him to do. To give him land and money without knowledge or experience is not of much use, failure is almost sure to result. But if you give him a certain amount of training, which can be done by putting him through a course in our agricultural institutions, then I think the chances of hijs success are very greatly enhanced.
Another matter referred to is the permitr ting of desirable immigration. If there is

one thing that we have learned in the recent war, it is to be careful about the character of the people we permit to come into this country, and I hope the Government will see to it that the immigrants permitted to enter Canada will be men upon whom we shall be able to rely in any great national crisis in future. If there is one important thing we have learned from the experience of the past it is the necessity of having in this country men who will defend it if necessary with their lives, and that democracy which we nil stand for, and which we all believe in, and I hope we all practice. To bring men to this country who have lived their lives under institutions foreign to our own, would be a very doubtful asset in time of peace, and a heavy liability in time of war, as we have already found out. So I hope that the Government will be most careful to see that any men they bring into this country will be such as our free institutions will appeal to, and such as will defend democracy with their lives. The assimilative power of the Anglo-Saxon race has been one of the wonders to men who have studied the question of the assimilative power of races, but even that great and inherent 'quality of our race has been over-taxed in this country. Therefore, I repeat, let us be careful in the future, and see that we get the right kind of immigration into Canada.
Another matter the Government has taken up, I am glad to say, is the matter of public health. Mr. Speaker, the greatest asset any state can have is the people that compose that state, and the stronger those people are in body and mind the more valuable that asset is. A health department is capable of doing wonders in strengthening our state. In the matter of tuberculosis alone a department of public health, with headquarters in Ottawa, and ramifications throughout the country, can assist in saving-and I speak from knowledge, for I have had some experience in this particular matter-seventy-five per cent of those people in this country who to-day are suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis, called consumption. Such a department can do more than that; it can convert those people into active citizens, who will be a great asset to the country. There is another way in which the Department of Public Health can help our country-I mean in the matter of sanitation, providing a pure water supply for our cities and seeing that our streets are kept clean. In a word a department of public health can do an infinite amount of good.
A Department of Public Health can carry on and develop methods of decreasing the number of typhoid cases. Typhoid, so recently as the South African War, killed more soldiers than did the bullets of the Boers, though in this greatest war of all times typhoid has been practically wiped out. A good, active Department of Public Health at Ottawa can do a great deal towards reducing the mortality from typhoid in this country. The same is true of .smallpox. The same is true of venereal diseases, always following in the wake of the armies.
A Department of Health at Ottawa can do * a great deal towards reducing that danger ' to a minimum. Take the great influenza epidemic which is sweeping over the world at the present time and which caused the death of thousands of Canadian people within the few months that it scourged and ravaged this country. We do not know yet what the cause of it is. The greatest bacteriologists in the world have devoted their best efforts to the solution of that problem, but the medical profession is not united as to what the cause of this disease is. There is a field for a Department of Health; there is an opportunity for scientists to investigate and inquire into the cause of that fatal scourge and try to secure a remedy. So it is with cholera, that seaborne disease; so it is with bubonic plague. Because of the situation of our country in relation to the ocean highways of the world, these diseases may invade us at any time. They have invaded us in the past. Bubonic plague has been in Canada; cholera has been in Canada; smallpox has been in Canada; typhoid has been in Canada. I think, therefore, we should have a Department of Health, and I should welcome it now.
The speech from the Throne referred to the export trade of Canada. For fifty years we have been devoting our energies to spending money in the development of interprovincial trade, in creating manufacturing industries, in building up our educational and commercial institutions, in constructing our transcontinental railways, in digging our canals, in lighting our coasts, in providing means of transport for this sparsely populated country stretching from ocean to ocean. We have built up in Canada a very considerable manufacturing business, but we have never had our fair share of export trade. During all these years we have been creating, creating, creating. Now is the time, when -our statesmen are at the Peace Conference, when commercial treaties are being revised, when the name of Canada stands



further north-that ships are taking to-day. And why? Because the northern route is the shorter route. Why did the old Spanish merchant ships going to Manilla sight the Aleutian islands? Because that was the shortest route. These airships will cross the very section of country to which I am asking the Government to afford transport facilities. They will seeft the line of the mountain range where the winds are not great; they will cross the great section of this country between the Alleghenies and the Rockies, this great central plain, they will sail across to the Rockies, north along that great chain and down the Yukon valley and across over the Aleutian islands and thence by way of Siberia and China to Japan. And on this route from the mainland of America to Yokohama, there is not a section of more than 150 miles, perhaps not more than 100 miles, over which they will have to fly over water.
Why should we do all this that I am asking? Because, Mr. Speaker, we are a progressive people who have led the world in great enterprises. The first ship that crossed the North Atlantic was built by Samuel Cunard, of Halifax, Nova Scotia after whom the great .Cunard line was named and through whose genius that great transportation system was developed. In the old House of Commons you will still find the brass plate near the Library which gives the history of the first ship that crossed the Atlantic under her own steam -a Canadian ship. When my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) was Minister of Finance he did a notable thing. Senor Marconi came to America and tried to get the Newfoundland Government to assist him in erecting a wireless station. But the Newfoundland Government could not do as he requested because of a contract which had been made by them with a cable company, the name of which I have for the moment forgotten. Marconi came to Cape Breton. An officer of the Canadian Government, a member of the staff of the Post Oifice Department, Mr. William Smith, happened to be in St. John's, Newfoundland. He heard of Marconi's invention and of the difficulty that existed because of the contract with the cable company. He was enterprising and far-seeing enough to write to a gentleman here who told the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens about the matter. That hon. gentleman himself wrote and told Mr. Smith that the Government of Canada would be willing to assist Marconi. Marconi came to Ottawa, the Government did assist him with a grant, with conditions attached that the Canadian people should be given

low wireless rates for a certain length of time. The result was that Marconi towers were erected at Glace Bay and the wireless system became a fact-and perhaps there are few greater boons to the human race. To-day Canada has perhaps the finest wireless system in the world. And that reminds ' me that, under the scheme I am advocating, we could take the wireless plants that are being dismantled because of the cessation of war and place them at Hudson's Bay ports and other places in the north for the assistance of the enterprise.
Is there any other great enterprise in which we led the world? We built the first transcontinental road on this continent. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the first railway which connected tide-water on the Atlantic with tide-water on the Pacific, the first which ran from coast to coast, was built by the Canadian people, by the Canadian Government, namely the Canadian Pacific. There was no complete transcontinental road in the United States at that time-I do not know even that there is one to-day, and we have three of them.
We have never yet gone into any of these far-reaching enterprises without our action being justified by the result. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the great nickel and copper deposits of the Sudbury region were discovered by the engineers and contractors who built the Canadian Pacific railway. It was the building of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway which made known the great mineral deposits of Cobalt and that whole region. That road was not built with a view to opening up a mineral country, but was built to reach farm land in the northern portion of the Lake Temiskaming country. The same is true of the Porcupine and other great mineral fields opened in Northern Ontario. The sending of a squadron of Northwest Mounted Police to the Klondike, before it was discovered or heard of, helped very largely in the discovery of the Klondike which resulted in giving $200,000,000 of wealth to the world.
Is there anything else in which we led the world? Yes, we were the first people in the British Empire to federate great states, when we created the Dominion of Canada and thus established the model upon which every federation in the Empire has been moulded. Seeing, then, that we have the genius, that we have the country, that we have the people, I trust that this Government, in its wisdom, will see fit to consider some of the suggestions I have made. If they do, I promise you, Mr. Speaker, I promise the Government and the people of Canada, that it will be the sowing

of fruitful seed which will yield a hundredfold.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to address the House for the first time during the present session, my first word must be of deep regret at the loss of our great and beloved leader. And I cannot resist the impulse to extend my thanks, as one of the humble followers of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to the many hon. members on both sides of this House who have spoken in terms of eulogy of the life, character and achievements of that great Canadian. I must mention first, and with special appreciation the remarks of the acting leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) on the second day of the present session.
I also express thanks to two other non. members on this side of the House. I must more particularly express my sincere thanks and appreciation for the eulogy pro-, nounced yesterday by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in the speech delivered by him and in which the expressions of admiration and esteem for our revered leader reached a higher plane than has ever been attained in this House before. These remarks came from one who had been educated in the school of that great British statesman, Gladstone, who had dwelt with him in the city of London, who had heard him on many occasions and whose privilege it had been to listen to speeches delivered by him which had not only astounded his auditors but the whole world. I esteem particularly his likening of that great British statesman to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I have always believed that it was the ambition of our Canadian statesman to follow in the steps of such a great British statesman as Gladstone. On many occasions when I desired to impress upon my people in New Brunswick the talents and position of our great leader I have deemed it appropriate to compare him to some of the great British statesmen and I have often designated him the Gladstone of Canada.
Being left in bereavement and without a leader at the opening of this House, the first duty of the Opposition was to look for another leader, either permanent or temporary. It having been decided by the Liberal party in this House that the choice of a permanent leader should be left to the consideration of a Liberal Convention to be held as soon as possible, the choice has been made, I believe, for the time being, of a member of this House and of the Liberal party well known to every hon. member on both sides and well known not
20i
only in his native province of Nova Scotia but throughout the other provinces of Canada. He is known as a result of the long years which he has given to his people in this Parliament, by his standing as a lawyer, by the ability with which he discharged the duties that devolved upon him while occupying a seat on the Bench and many other admirable qualities which make him most acceptable not only to the Liberal party in this House but, I am sure, to the Liberal party throughout Canada. He also possesses qualities, combined with his experience, which may be of great benefit to the Liberal party, and to Canada at any moment. The hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) comes from a district where miners and steel workers are employed by the thousands in the great industries to be found in Cape Breton. His experience, as well as the place which he occupies in the confidence of those who know him best, give him the necessary qualifications to play an effective and useful part in the settlement of labour problems which this Parliament may have to solve before its prorogation. Therefore, he is well qualified for the position of leader of the Opposition in this House. The will of his people has guided every step of his career. He is an inhabitant of the ancient province of Nova Scotia where
10 p.m. the spirit of justice, liberty and harmony still prevails as it did in the days of Haliburton and Joseph Howe. He is imbued with that sense of British fair play and justice which he has displayed on every occasion in this Parliament.
Coming back to the debate on the Address, I cannot help but extend my sincere congratulations to the hon. the mover (Mr. Redman) and the hon. the seconder (Mr. Manion) of the Address. They are not in the House at this moment but I would point out that they have followed a direction new in this Parliament. They have not confined themselves to the old system by which it was considered the duty of the mover and seconder of the Address to speak to the House merely as supporters of the Government of the day. They have, in noble language spoken to us of the war and of the heroism, energy and valour of our Canadian soldiers. They have told us of the duty we owe to the returned soldier not only in the matter of increased pensions but in many other respects. I acknowledge the indebtedness of the House to them for the very admirable addresses with which they favoured the House in moving and seconding the motion.

Speaking of the valour of the Canadian soldier, I may say that he has not only done his duty but he has shown a spirit which elicited the admiration of every nation engaged in the war. He has won the respect and esteem not only of Canada but of the British Empire and the Allies by his valour and courage. At the very first of the war, on that great and critical occasion at the battle of Langemarck the Canadian soldiers displayed a superhuman courage and valour but for which the day would have been lost. With the knowledge that there was no possibility of reinforcements reaching them, rather than retreat they fought with splendid courage, the bodies of their dead comrades were used as a rampart against the enemy and whilst the souls of those who had fallen rose to heaven their surviving comrades rallied nobly, stopped the advance of the Hun to Calais and thus saved the Empire. In a great many other hard fought battles they distinguished themselves and brought glory to their native land. 'At St. Julien, St. Eloi and elsewhere their gallantry and courage brought victory to the Allies and on every occasion the Canadian soldier acquitted himself in such a way as to win the admiration of the civilized world. It remains for the Canadian people to show their gratitude to every one of those returned soldiers who fought for liberty, right and justice, for democracy and against autocracy.
Sir, I wish to be brief in my remarks with respect to the matters referred to in the speech from the Throne. The representatives of the allied nations, including the representatives of the British Dominions, are to-day assembled endeavouring to frame a treaty which we hope will ensure permanent peace to the world. Not only will that congress determine the amount of damages to be paid to the allied countries, but it will be its duty also to endeavour to see that we shall have peace for all time. Not only will that congress fix the indemnities to be paid, but it will endeavour to see that the German people shall divert the trend of the education of its youth from the muddied channel of arrogance, autocracy and Prussianism, to the limpid stream of fraternity and democracy, in the hope that that nation, after sincere repentance and enlightenment, will be able ultimately to join in the League of Nations and help to make the world immune from future wars. So long as Germany educates its youth along the lines which it has followed during so many years, so long will it remain a menace to the world, and the rest of the nations would have to continue the maintenance of

armaments, a thing which we would all deplore, and which it is certainly one of the chief aims of the League of Nations to put an end to.
I desire now to discuss more particularly the tariff question, and I am glad to see the Minister of Immigration and Colonization in his seat. That hon. gentleman the other day delivered a very remarkable speech, marked by some brilliant and patriotic features in discussing the intentions of the Government with respect to the returned soldier. But when my hon. friend came to consider the tariff question, he dropped to a lower level. In his opinion at the present time, when demobilization, reconstruction and re-establishment policies call for attention, we ought not to discuss the tariff question, but leave it in abeyance for some future time. Sir, in my humble judgment, the Government should have dealt with the tariff iquestion from the very first; but instead of that it pursued a policy of delay, and now calls upon us to wait a while longer. In my opinion, the very moment the armistice was signed the Government should have called Parliament together with a view to taking some action on this important question, which is the very foundation of our national prosperity, and yet even to-day we are not to see any action taken because of peace time conditions. My hon. friend declared the other day that he was now, and intended to remain, a Liberal. I believe I know my hon. friend as well as any member in this House, and I can bear testimony to his strong Liberal beliefs. I think he is still a Liberal, and I hope he will remain in that frame of mind, not so much from motives of expediency, but with a view to the application of Liberal principles in this great Canada of ours. Let me tell my hon. friend that the question of the tariff is the great overpowering question that a true Liberal of the English school should bear in mind, and therefore we cannot leave unconsidered the matter of tariff legislation, more particularly as we are in the transitionary period between war conditions and peace conditions. In my opinion, no reconstruction policy can bring this country safely from war conditions to peace conditions unless it is based on the economic principles held by the Liberal party. My hon. friend's uncertainty of mind on this subject is perhaps due to his failure up to now to convince his supporters on the Government side, and he, therefore, wishes more time to convince them. I maintain, Sir, that we cannot wait any longer. The people expected the Gov>
eminent to take action three or four years since, and not wait as it has done, and yet in the matter of the tariff it to-day appeals for further delay. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) yesterday gave the Government credit for having given a certain degree of reciprocity in the shape of free wheat and free potatoes. For six years my hon. friend had been lamenting the defeat of reciprocity and the loss of the advantage that would have resulted to the country had that policy been carried out. The same eloquent gentleman spoke of the efforts which he had been making for three years or so to induce the Government to have recourse to an income tax, and yet, after it has been so 'long urged when it comes to be introduced it is made as light as possible. But why stop there? My hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization always advocated Liberal principles until the day he joined the Union Government. I presume he entered the Cabinet from motives of conscience, and as to that I have nothing to say, but we on this side of the House also have a conscience which would not honestly permit us to cast in our lot with them. Instead of that we have remained true to our principles, to our policy, and to our revered leader. My hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, in giving a reason for postponing the consideration of the tariff question, said, in eloquent terms:	"There is
a cleavage between the East and the West'.' I think I can convince my hon. friends that there is no cleavage between the East and the West; that the policy of the West is the policy of the East; that the people of the Maritime Provinces are in harmony with the people of the West in demanding that the principles embodied in the reciprocity pact of 1911 be re-affirmed by this Parliament. The whole population of the Maritime Provinces is in favour of that pact to-day, as it was in 1911. The province of Quebec also is in favour of the reciprocity pact now, as it was at that time. If there is a cleavage it is between the people of Canada and a few financiers of Ontario and Toronto. To prove that the people of the East are in harmony with the people of the West in this matter, I have only to direct attention to a number of resolutions which have been adopted in the Legislature of Saskatchewan, a body which only a few months ago the Minister of Immigration and Colonization adorned with his talent and his ability, as he had done for twelve or fifteen years. There he made fame for himself, and was often justly extolled by the people of his province for his advocacy
of the true principles of Liberalism. I will read that portion of these resolutions which relates to the general interests of the country, leaving aside that which is of particular interest only to the province. These resolutions are in the form of a petition to the Dominion Government and were adopted unanimously in the Legislature of Saskatchewan, being supported alike by Liberals and Conservatives. The resolutions read:-
The immediate adoption by the Federal Government of an efficient policy of soldiers' settlement which will ensure the immediate settlement of as great a number as possible of our returned soldiers upon lands in Saskatchewan within reasonable proximity of railway facilities and community centres.
An immediate and substantial all-round reduction of the customs tariff.
The reduction of the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual uniform reductions be made of the remaining tariffs on British imports that will ensure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada in five years.
The acceptance by the Parliament of Canada of the reciprocity agreement of 1911, which still remains on the United States statute books.
The placing- upon the free list of all foodstuffs not included in the reciprocity agreement.	.
The placing upon the free list of all agricultural implements, farm machinery, vehicles, fertilizers, coal, lumber, cement, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils and all raw materials and machinery used in their manufacture.
The immediate extension to Great Britain of all tariff concessions granted to other countries.
This is the view of the Legislature of iSas-katchewan; indeed, of the whole of the people of that province. Only last Tuesday the sentiments expressed in these resolutions were adopted in almost the same words by the Legislature of Manitoba, where they were approved by every Conservative as well as every Liberal member of the legislature. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization knows that at many conventions of farmers and grain growers in Alberta the same sentiments have been expressed. The people of the three prairie provinces are one in their demand for the restoration of the reciprocity treaty. Had not the American Congress and Senate given Canada free lumber in 1913 the lumber industry in New Brunswick would have become bankrupt at that time and would have remained so ever since. In expressing these views I am sure that I voice the sentiment of the people of the Maritime Provinces, including members representing those provinces in this House. I know that these views are shared by the leader of the Opposition as well as by every

other member from the Maritime Provinces and Quebec. I need not say that they are entertained by my most esteemed friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Hon. Mr. Fielding), who was a minister of the Crown at the time this reciprocity agreement was entered into in 1911. Fortunately, the mott6 " No truck or trade with the Yankees " was not adopted by the Mother Country. If the Mother Country had taken the same position as that adopted by the Conservatives in 1911 and lacked consideration for the great nation to the south of us, where would we have been in this war?
Of course, these resolutions of the Legislature of Saskatchewan at once attracted the attention of the manufacturers of Ontario, and immediately, through the organ of the President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, they issued a statement of their position with regard to the matters dealt with in the resolutions. In their judgment the time had not come to consider the question of the tariff; it should be left over to the future. Here is what, on January 28, through their president, they say of these resolutions:-
Therefore, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association believes that the country should concentrate on the one main problem, with its attendant questions, and- leave the highly controversial problem of tariff revision to a time when it can be given the undivided attention it demands.
Of course, it demands attention. They give this reason why it demands attention:
It is a general and familiar law, that in any country, when fundamental tariff changes are anticipated, trade depression follows. During such periods of uncertainty, investment is curtailed, enterprise is limited, commerce lives from hand to mouth, consumers buy sparingly, and building languishes.
If it is a general and familiar law that when tariff changes are anticipated, trade depression follows, we should make haste and have the tariff revision made at once before trade depression takes place in this country. Now is the time to act. If we put the agricultural industry on a good footing, we shall be able to look after the returned soldiers. Agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. We want to sbnd the returned soldiers to the land. One hundred and fifty thousand of them have, expressed their willingness and their intention to go onto the land on their return. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) will, perhaps, tell me that the Government are going to be very generous to the returned soldier; that they will advance him a certain amount of money to pay for

the land he needs and also money to buy the implements he requires. At the same time, the soldier who wants to go onto the land, wants to see ahead of him a future livelihood. If the Government advance him money, he will have to make good every year the interest on that amount together with the annual instalment he will be called upon to pay. If he is discouraged and cannot meet his interest and instalments, his loan is bound to be forfeited. Unless he sees that he is really encouraged and gets everything he needs at the lowest possible price, he will certainly not go on to the land; or if he does, and is not able to get on, his land will be forfeited and will not be handed over to any returned soldier, but will likely go to some speculator in the West who is waiting for such opportunities. The time is most opportune for immediate revision of the tariff. The manufacturers of this country have, during the four years of this war, accumulated immense wealth through the tremendous profits on their operations. They are to-day in a better position than they have ever been before. They have to-day millions of dollars in the banks awaiting investment. They have millions of dollars worth of Victory Bonds at five and a half per cent interest, free of taxation. They are, therefore, in a position to face the situation to-day. They are in a position, not only to accept the situation, but to help the people of Canada and also to help the farmer to get what he wants so that he may increase the quantity of land under cultivation in this great country of ours. To-day, when I say that the East is in harmony with the West in their claim for reciprocity with the United States, -for free agricultural implements, and for having other articles put on the free list, it is because in the Maritime Provinces, as well as in Quebec, a new impetus has been given by the war to the industry of agriculture. Agriculture has doubled its production during the last four and a half years, and everyone of our farmers, with his son coming back from the war, is looking for the moment when he will again be able to increase his production. But to be able to do so he must be given every one of his implements at the lowest possible cost.
We have been informed by the acting leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) that the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) contemplates spending during the coming year $35,000,000 on railway rolling stock and steel rails; $20,000,000 on

railway extensions, and $10,000,000 on betterments. We have also been told that $25,000,000 are to be spent on housing. This makes a total of over $80,000,000 which will be spent on railroads and housing in Canada and which will give a new impetus to the industries which our manufacturers are well prepared to take in hand. Now is the time for the Governnnjnt to act. The problem of the returned soldier must be solved. In my county there are several soldiers waiting to get land somewhere in the county or in the province to which they belong. Owing to the still indefinite state of affairs, we have not been able to locate any of them and they are still waiting. After a few months it will be too late; a year will be again lost for the farmers in the West as well as for the farmers in the East. Therefore, I repeat that now is the time for the Government to take the matter into consideration.
It is true that a compromise is asked for by the manufacturers. They are willing to compromise and they will, perhaps, be satisfied with the elimination of the war surtax imposed by the Government at the beginning of the war on all importations including raw material. It was my lot at the time, amongst other members of the Opposition, to oppose as strongly as possible the imposition of a surtax of 5 per cent against products coming from Great Britian and 7J per cent on products coming from other countries. The manufacturers will accept the elimination of that war surtax which will give them the raw material. I see in that no great advantage to the producer or the farmer, for I was opposed at the time to the taxation of raw material just because it was hampering external trade, which was of first necessity, more particularly in war time and just now, and because it would also have the effect, with the maintenance of the tariff, of permitting the manufacturer to have the advantage of the elimination of the tax on raw material without giving the Canadian consumer the benefit of it. As long as there is a duty on goods manufactured from imparted raw material such as woollen, or linen, or leather goods, the manufacturer will raise his price in accordance with the duty. There would, therefore, be no benefit to the consumer.
There was an offer of compromise with respect to another matter by an hon. member to whose speech I listened with great attention. He suggested that we should have a tariff commission, and I was amazed at his suggestion. Surely, we have had commissions enough during the war. For
the last four years we have been governed by Orders in Council and by commissions. The Government would take away from Parliament all of its responsibility. A tariff commission would take a year or two to take evidence from the friends of the manufacturers and the protectionists before it would make a report. During all that time the consumers of the country would have to wait. If there is one thing which should be left to Parliament, according to all British traditions, it is the tariff, which has a bearing on the happiness or otherwise of all the people. I certainly hope the Government will not entertain the suggestion for a Tariff Commission. I would urge my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) to take the tariff question in hand at once, and if he can possibly succeed in bringing his supporters round to the Liberal policy on that question I shall give him great credit for it. I would also ask the Minister of Immigration and Colonization to take up with his colleagues another matter of vital interest to this country-the War-Time Elections Act. To my mind that Act should be wiped off the Statute Books at once and if there is one member of the Government who should initiate a movement in that direction among his colleagues it is the Minister of Immigration. He comes from a province where for long years he has enjoyed the confidence of the people who have come to this country at his own invitation and enjoyed the freedom of Canadian citizenship, who, according to his own testimony, have been loyal citizens of Canada and have voted for him every time he offered himself for election in the province of Saskatchewan. Will he go back to those people and tell them that he is going to keep on the Statute Book the WarTime Elections Act which disfranchises good, honest citizens who came here years ago? Will he tell them they shall no longer have the freedom of the country to which they are entitled? Speaking of this Act on September 11, 1917, just one month before he joined the Union Government, my old esteemed colleague from the province of New Brunswick, now Minister of Public Works, said: "I cannot understand the Government thinking that a Bill of this revolutionary character, which violates every principle of that British fair play which we have bragged about in this country ever since I was a boy, is going to be railroaded through Parliament." That is the way he characterized the Act. I would ask these two hon. members to get their heads together and when they are in

Councils to-morrow ask their colleagues to delay no longer but to bring down on Monday afternoon a simple Bill repealing the War-Time Elections Act.
There is another question on which I shall say only a word or two, and that is the question of assistance in the building of highways. We are very pleased that the Government is going to assist the provincial governments in the building of roads, but we on this side of the House wish to put the Government on their guard, as we did a few years before the war when the Government introduced a Bill with similar objects but which encroached on provincial rights. On that occasion we on this side of the House, and particularly my hon. friend the present Minister of Public Works objected to the method under which this money was to he spent. If there was one gentleman who had strong views on that subject it was [DOT] the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization who, at that time, had a resolution passed in the Saskatchewan Legi_-lature upholding provincial rights and declaring he would not accept any money for the improvement of highways under the terms laid down by the Federal Government. I ask him to see that in the framing of the Bill there will be no encroachment this time on provincial rights, ll do not object to there being an understanding between the engineers of the local Governments and the Federal Government, but there should be no pressure brought to bear on the provinces in the expenditure of this money.
While the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) is here, I shall take the liberty of drawing his attention to one or two matters which I have been asked to bring before him. I understand that there is a small number of printers, pressmen, feeders and compositors working in the Militia Department for a pittance which, according to my informant, is not worthy of the department. Sixteen of those men are working at a salary of $66.75 per month, working 42 hours per week, and receiving no extra pay for overtime, although they are often called upon to work overtime on Sundays. I do not know the facts myself but I have every reason to believe that the information given me is correct. I might say that the stenographers in the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch also make the same complaint of long hours and inadequate pay.
They have to work long hours at rates of pay not adequate to the service rendered.
I know that the Minister of Militia will

inquire into these matters, and if he finds my statements to be correct, I am sure he will give consideration to these deserving officials.
I close my present remarks with the hope that the result of this war may be to bring lasting peace and harmony among the nations of the world. And may that harmony be reflected in the relation between the various nationalities in this Canada of ours. We all share the same sentiments, a love of democracy, of freedom and justice, and I trust that, having these glorious ideals in common we shall be united in our appreciation of one another's efforts to carry them into practice.
On the motion of Major General Mewburn, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Burrell the House adjourned at 10.48 p.m.
Monday, March 10, 1919,
The House met at Three o'clock.

subtopic: STRIKE OF PRESSMEN-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BURRELL.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
subtopic: STRIKE OF PRESSMEN-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BURRELL.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Secretary of State if he has any information to communicate to the House in regard to the strike in the Printing Bureau and if he would tell us what progress is being made towards a settlement. I would also ask him if he would be good enough to lay upon the table of the House the report that I understand was made to the department by the men.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: STRIKE OF PRESSMEN-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BURRELL.
speechtext:
The report made by the committee

has already been laid on the Table. I have received no report from the men, although I understood that some report was to be made. As this is a matter of some public importance, perhaps I may be allowed briefly to explain the situation as it stands. The Bureau employees consist altogether of about twelve hundred. Of these the pressmen, comprising roughly about one hundred, have struck. The Act of Parliament lays down that current wages paid in commercial establishments shall form the basis of pay for similar work within the Printing Bureau, and it says: " For better guidance, the cities of Toronto and Montreal shall be taken, and those rates shall not be exceeded." The Act does not say that the highest amount payable in either Montreal or Toronto or in both of them may be taken, and the custom has been to take the average rate between Toronto and Montreal in commercial establishments. I might also state that the outside firms embody their rates in agreements which are entered into between the employers and the men. The present agreement, for instance, running until June 1, next. I might also point out that some outside firms, notwithstanding the fact that they lay down a rate to be followed in regard to the wages to be paid to the various services in their establishments, exceed that rate in the case of especially skilled workmen and in respect of various trades in those establishments. It has been contended by the Bureau employees that in fixing the rates for the Bureau, this excess rate for efficient employees in various outside establishments should be taken into consideration in applying a flat rate to all the employees in the Bureau. This, of course notwitstanding the fact, which will not be denied by any one, either employers or men, that the' efficiency of the Bureau is away below the efficiency of outside establishments. Indeed, the committee itself says that work in outside establishments is from ten to fifty per cent better than work in the Printing Bureau and the cost of production in the Bureau is unquestionably greater.
As the agreements were to expire next June and fresh agreements were to be made, and as we would then have to adjust the rates, it seemed best to the Government to leave all questions in dispute until those agreements expired and fresh ones were made. The question of a bonus also came up. As hon. members in this House know, the Civil Service were being given certain bonuses. It was thought by the Government-and I do not think it will be disputed by any one-that as a matter of fact or
right, the mechanical forces of the Bureau, which were paid according to outside schedules, could manifestly not participate in the advantages of an Inside Service, and that the bonus would not apply to them. But as some outside firms had paid a bonus, and as these differences of opinion did obtain amongst the Bureau employees and the minister, we concluded to pay a bonus, and accordingly a bonus of $2 a week was given to all the men in the mechanical forces and one dollar a week to the women in the bindery establishment. This applied to all of them and left the weekly pay received by the Bureau employees unquestionably somewhat higher than the average weekly pay received in all outside establishments. Moreover, this does not take into consideration, what the committee took into consideration, namely the question of holidays, for which they are paid $112 a year or $2 a week more, when outside establishments are not. This is all set forth in the committee's report. And whatever differences of opinion there might be in the employees' minds or in the mind of any hon. member in this House as to the accuracy of the various details of this report, I do not think that the substantial accuracy of this report will be disputed, and I think no member of this House will dispute that the closing words of the report must be accepted by all. They are:
We are firmly of the opinion that if our recommendations, arriving at a greatly reduced wage cost through the elimination of unnecessary labour and higher standards of efficiency are not adopted, the only recourse in the public interest is to close the Bureau.
In view of this report and in view of the obvious necessity of some reorganization of a government department which is running in this way, it was thought that as during this fiscal year anyway the Government Bureau employees, were in regard to their total weekly receipts, whether you call that bonus or wages, placed in certainly as good, if not in a better position, than all outside employees, they might very well wait until this report was considered before any increase of wages or new schedules in regard to hours were taken up. That was our position. That position was practically stated to the employees, that the matter should rest, as they were provided for fully, until the dispute was adjusted later on and the report was considered. I think it is the wish of the Government, as I am sure it is the wish of the members of this House that nothing less than justice should be done to the employees, common justice to the ratepayers of this country being kept in view. In the face of that report and my letter to

the mechanical department that the matter should be allowed to stand until the Government could consider the report, the pressmen, numbering about 101, have struck, while the rest of the mechanical forces have not struck.

On the Orders of the Day:

The Acting Prime Minister will have read in the newspapers of Saturday last an interview with Mr. F. P. Jones, from which 1 shall quote one or two extracts, upon which to base an inquiry:
Mr. F. P. Jones of Montreal, who has just returned from England and France, where he acted in an advisory capacity to Sir Robert Borden, says that the import licenses as they are administered in Great Britain discriminate against Canada and all countries that went to war in 1914.
Then comes the text of the interview, from which I quote these sentences:
The general election, followed by the Peace Conference, continued to occupy the minds of

the heads of the Lloyd George Administration, and evidently purely commercial affairs have been left to the Board of Trade. Now that the Canadian Mission in London have repeatedly and forcibly brought the matter to the attention of the British Government and also to the attention of our Canadian Ministers, in Paris, I feel confident the discrimination which does exist will be done away with.
Then, in the Evening Citizen of March 7th there appeared a further despatch on the same subject, purporting to give a summary of a discussion in the British House of Commons in these terms:
In the course of a speech in the House of Commons, Lord Wolmer informed the president of the Board of Trade that considerable feeling existed in Canada as a consequence of the policy of licensing prohibited imports. He asked whether licenses had been issued for imports from neutral Allied countries of goods which had been refused from Canada.
Under-secretary Bridgeman replied that it was true that, owing to their geographical position and to the difficulties of shortage of tonnage, a policy had been adopted respecting import restrictions which had had the undesired effect of discriminating against colonial goods. Now that the tonnage question was easier, he hoped that it would be possible to avoid this discrimination. The question was being considered and an announcement would be made shortly.
I desire to ask my hon. friend if he has any information as to the removal of the discrimination, and if not, whether he has any information in his possession to impart to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to say that I am able to set at rest any apprehensions my hon. friend may have with regard to discrimination, especially intentional discrimination, against Canadian trade by Great Britain. I have received two cables to-day on this matter. The first is from Mr. Lloyd Harris, of the Canadian Trade Mission overseas, in which he says:
In reply to question in House, this afternoon's Parliament, Secretary Board of Trade says:
The Government has decided no import restrictions shall be or continue to be imposed on goods coming from any part of the Empire without the assent of the Cabinet, which shall not be given unless some unforeseen necessity arises. It is not possible at present to remove all restrictions on imports from foreign countries because of the state of the exchange, but all raw materials will be free from import restrictions.
The other cable is from the Canadian Trade Mission in London to the Canadian Trade Mission here, as follows:
Board of Trade announced yesterday removal of all restrictions on imports from British Empire.
On the Orders of the Day:

Can the Government give the House any information regarding the cable reports of riots among the Canadian troops at Rhyl? Has there been any loss of life?
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia and Defence): Late on Friday evening I was informed that there had been some trouble in one of the camps in England and I immediately cabled the Overseas Minister of Militia for full information. My cable was crossed by his report on the matter, and which appeared in the Ottawa Evening Citizen of March 8th, as follows: (Reads official statement appearing in Ottawa Citizen, March 8th).
"Official statement of the disturbance at Kin-mel Camp. In view of the splendid discipline and record uniformly maintained by the Canadian troops since the beginning of the war, in England and Prance, the incident at Kinmel Camp is very deeply regretted at the headquarters of the Overseas Military Forces of Canada. It is considered that in comparison with others the discipline among Canadian troops has been of high order.
"It is greatly regretted that some of the reports of the incident have been exaggerated.
"Immediately after the armistice had been signed, Kinmel Park was secured as a concentration area, through which Canadian troops passed on their way to Canada, being situated convenient to Liverpool, their embarkation port. There all documentation is completed and troops sorted into drafts according to their destination in Canada.
"Considering the shortage of shipping, the Canadian authorities have congratulated themselves upon the splendid record which has been made, on the whole, as despatching troops to Canada in the month of February. However, the ministry of shipping were unable to furnish sufficient ships to carry out the programme, as promised to the Canadians. Owing to this, in ' February and early March the shipments of troops having fallen short by fully one-third, there occurred a backing-up from Kinmel Camp through the areas in England and through them to France.
"This has caused very great disappointment to Canadian soldiers who have been overseas for periods ranging up to four years or more without leave to their homes. The withdrawal of some ships and the postponement of sailings of others from time to time, particularly after soldiers had been documented and medically boarded in numbers based on the shipping allocated, has been very trying to the drafts, and this is what it is considered led chiefly to the disturbance.
"Immediately upon the matter being reported to the chief of the general staff, Lieut.-General Sir Richard Turner, V.C., K.C.B., he went to Kinmel Camp and addressed the men in fifteen different places. They seemed to appreciate his explanations and there are not likely to be any further disturbances.
"There are at Kinmel Camp approximately 15,000' troops, all ranks, who have been despatched there as being the last step before boarding ship for Canada. Had the number of men been able to embark in February according to the programme which it was confidently thought could be carried out, the trouble would not have occurred, but the shipping situation, owing to strikes and for other reasons, is admitted to be an extremely difficult matter to control. However, it is hoped by the Canadian authorities that there will not be a recurrence of the delays which have hitherto taken place.
"It is ifot attempted in the slightest degree to excuse the conduct of the men who took part in the disturbance. Many of the offenders have already been placed under arrest, who, with others involved will be rigorously dealt with.
"During the disturbance there was a certain amount of damage done and it was discovered that civilians were concerned. Up to the present time twelve of these civilians have been arrested and handed over to the civil authorities.
"During the disturbance there were killed three rioters and two men on picket duty. There were twenty-one wounded, of whom two were officers. There is no foundation for the report that a major who is a V.C. has been either killed or iniured.
" The troops at Kinmel Park are concentrated in wings representing the military districts in Canada to which they will proceed. They are not in their original units, these wings being composite formations consisting of personnel belonging to many different units. This sorting out is done in deference to the authorities in Canada to avoid delay when the men reach the Dominion. There has been some alleged dissatisfaction because of troops drawn from Canada under the Military Service Act getting priority over those who have seen longer service.
The troops who were in the Canadian corps at the time of the armistice are being returned to Canada by units in the formations that then existed, the first to return being a small number which were embarked on March 1. Soldiers not in the corps such as casualties, railway and forestry troops and others, where available, are demobilized on the principle of the longest service first demobilized, married men having the preference.
A court of inquiry has been convened to make a thorough investigation into all the circumstances in connection with the disturbance, of which Brig.-Gen. J. H. MacBrien C.B., C.M.G., D.S.A., is the president.
That is the official cable. I sent a furthei cable to the overseas Minister of Militia asking him to furnish us, at the earliest date, with any information he possibly can. He cabled:
All information that can be given out re Kinmel Park disturbance until court inquiry makes report contained in despatch to Government.
The moment that report is received the House will be advised. Later, if I may have permission, I will explain some of the problems of demobilization.

Does the minister know
if all the casualties are Canadians?

IMajor-General MEWBURN: That is not stated in the cable. I have cabled and asked for a complete list of the casualties.
Lieut.-General Sir SAM HUGHES:	1
was informed by an officer who has been at Kinmel camp that there was lack of fuel, lack of warmth, for the men there. I would ask the Minister of Militia to inquire into that. If there be any truth in it, why cannot Canadian coal ije sent in ballast in our ships to be furnished to the camp to keep the men warm?
On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: RECEIVER. STATEMENT BY SIR THOMAS WHITE-CORRESPONDEN CE.
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, II desire to make a statement as to important action just taken by the Government respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system upon which I think it desirable the House should have immediate information. The facts are fully set forth in certain correspondence which I shall read to the House, and an Order in Council which I have laid upon the Table, and which, as it is somewhat lengthy I shall summarize.
Under date of 25th February last, Mr. Frank Scott, Vice-President and Treasurer of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company wrote me as follows:
Montreal, February 25, 1919. Hon. Sir Thomas White,
Minister of Finance, Ottawa.
Dear Sir Thomas,-Referring to our recent conversations.
I am in receipt of a cable from Mr. Smithers, stating that in the anticipation of receiving the balance of the appropriation of $7,500,000, viz.: $951,911.33, to apply for interest on Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Debenture Stock due March 1st, payment was duly advertised. In consequence, however, of the remittance being coupled with the condition that it is to be used only for operating obligations, the company will be unable to meet the interest due on the first proximo, and serious situation will result.
I respectfully beg to direct your attention to the matter in order that the actual position, and possible consequences may be fully appreciated.
Yours very truly,
Frank Scott,
Vice President and Treasurer.
To this I replied:
Ottawa, February, 28, 1919.
Dear Mr. Scott,-I beg to formally acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 25th instant which you personally handed to me at my office here. I note what Mr. Smithers states in his

cable as to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company being unable to meet the interest due upon its securities on March 1st. With reference to the balance of the appropriation of the vote of $7,500,000 by Parliament, the sum of $923,311.26 was paid to your company on your certificate No. 10 dated January 28, 1919, duly approved by the Acting Deputy Minister of the Department of Railways and Canals. This certificate expressly states that this sum Is on "account of a cash deficit in the operation of the company from April 1st to November 30th, 1918, inclusive," and "is required to enable the company to meet its operating obligations." The small balance of the vote amounting to about $28,000 will, I understand, he required for the same purpose. There seems no doubt that the deficit in operation should have priority over all other charges.
I have already informed Mr. Kelley, President of the Company, and yourself that it is not the intention of the Government to ask Parliament to provide a further vote for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company while our negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company remain in their present unsatisfactory condition. As I indicated to you, it will be for the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to determine the question of their responsibility in respect of the interest maturing tomorrow upon securities guaranteed by their Company.
Yours very truly,
W. T. White.
Frank Scott, Esq.,
Vice-President and Treasurer,
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway,
Montreal.
Subsequently I received the following:
Montreal, March 4th, 1919. Hon. Sir Thomas White, K.C.M.G.,
Minister of Finance, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir Thomas,-I am instructed to inform the Government that in view of the fact that the increased rates applicable to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have not been sufficient to meet the increased operating expenses, it will not be possible for that Company to continue its operations when the present funds have been exhausted, which will be about the 10th inst.
May I ask you to he so good as to acknowledge receipt of this letter.
Yours very truly,
Frank Scott,
Vice-President.
I acknowledged that letter in these terms:
Ottawa, March 5, 1919.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 4th instant informing me of the intention of your company to discontinue operations about the 10th instant.
Yours truly,
W. T. White.
Frank Scott, Esq.,
Vice-President and Treasurer,
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway,
Montreal.
Under existing legislation it is not possible, except under proceedings for foreclosure or sale, to have a receiver appointed' for a system such as the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Government, therefore, was

confronted with what we regarded as imperative necessity in the national interest of providing for the uninterrupted operation of the system. It was found that the War Measures Act gave the Government a complete jurisdiction for the action which it took, viz:	by Order in Council to appoint the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals as receiver for the system. I have made a summary of the provisions of the Order in Council as follows:
Re___Grand Trunk Receivership.
Provisions of Order in Council.
<1) Order recites that the continued operation of the G.T.P. System is essential in the present position of Canada resulting from the war, especially in connection with the tr^ns" port of returning Canadian troops and or supplies, equipment and freight, and that the duty of continuing such operation is thrown upon the Government of Canada inasmuch as there are no effective provisions in the existing laws whereby such continued operation could be otherwise secured and that therefore immediate action is imperative.
<21 Order applies to Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the other companies embraced in its system.
<3) The Minister of Railways is appointed Receiver with all the powers and duties of a Receiver under the Exchequer Court Act.
(4) The Exchequer Court is authorized to make such orders respecting the Receiver and his powers and duties and the carrying out thereof as the Court may deem necessary or expedient in the public interest.
<5) Provides for taking possession by Receiver.	.
<6) Orders the several Companies embraced in the system and their officers to facilitate the carrying out of the powers and duties of the Receiver and the delivery to him of books and papers and personal property of the various companies.
<7) Provides that nothing in the Order contained shall render the Government or the Receiver liable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company or any Company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system or to any creditor or holder of any bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities of the said Companies or any of them for any claim by reason of the making of the order or anything done under the authority or under the authority of the Government Receiver or of the Exchequer Court, nor shall afford any defence to, nor prejudice any claim, action or proceeding of the Government of Canada which the Government might lawfully make or take had the Order not been made.
(8) All Officers of the System to continue to discharge their duties under the Reoeiver so that no interruption in operation may occur.
<9) Nothing in the Order shall prejudice the exercise by the Exchequer Court or by any Court of any Province of Canada of its present jurisdiction to appoint a Receiver or to order a sale of foreclosure of any railway orsection thereof or other property affected by the Order, provided that notice of any application for the purposes mentioned1 shall be given to the Minister of Railways and that he and Counsel for him shall be heard on the application and that the Court in granting.
refusing or postponing the application shall take into consideration the public interests involved and shall make such order as shall in the opinion of the Court protect the public interest.
(10) Provision is made whereby the Governor in Council may from time to time and upon the security of Receivers' certificates or otherwise, advance to the Receiver such sums as may be required to enable him to exercise his powers and perform his duties as Receiver.
While, under the War Measures Act, that Order in Council has the full effect of a statute, as Parliament is sitting, it is manifestly desirable that the Government should introduce legislation validating and confirming the Order in Council and sanctioning what the Government has done. Within a day or so, I shall introduce the necessary resolution to that end. There are two further letters which I desire to read. I am making, as I stated, a statement of the facts only. I received on Saturday a letter containing a cable from Mr. Smithers which refers to a statement made in one of the letters which I have read to the House. It is as follows:
Montreal, March 7, 1919. Hon. Sir Thomas White, K.C.M.G.,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,
I have been instructed by Mr. Smitners to forward the following cable message to you as from him:

"Mr. Howard G. Kelley has handed me cable message from Mr. Frank Scott containing extract from your letter to him, as follows:- ' That it is not intention of the Government to ask Parliament to provide further vote for Grand Trunk Pacific Railway while our negotiations with Grand Trunk remain in their present unsatisfactory condition. I beg to recall, when Ministers came over last summer, it was stated in Parliament negotiations would be resumed in London. I accordingly saw Ministers, with members of Board several times and at last was told that Ministers could make no advance in their original offer without consent of full Cabinet in Ottawa. In these circumstances progress in negotiations was impossible, but with a view to facilitating matters, just before the Prime Minister left for Canada, a committee of the Board and myself, saw him. with two of his colleagues, and made a fresh proposal involving very big reduction on our first offer. This offer was not accepted, but on the 5th November High Commissioner of Canada sent for me and said he had message from the Prime Minister asking me if we wished to continue negotiations, and if so, he thought I should go to Canada. I told High Commissioner of Canada, looking to the faot that the Government had given no sign of any intention of departing from their original offer, I thought it was useless going out, unless 1 had some further explanation, or assurance as to Government's intentions. To this we have had no reply, and I really fail to see how the company can be held responsible for the unsatisfactory condition of our negotiations. Mr. Howard G.

Kelley is returning in a few days and I think it would be advantageous if you could cable any reply you may wish to make to this communication before he leaves. S'mithers.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) Frank Scott, Vice-President and Treasurer."
To which I replied as follows:
"Replying to your cable received through Mr. Scott:	Government considers unsatisfactory
condition of negotiations due to Board of Directors of Grand Trunk Railway Company entirely failing to appreciate its responsibilities towards the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway undertaking and the bearing of its liabilities in respect thereto upon the question of the net earning power and value of the Grand Trunk Railway System. In November last the Prime Minister cabled to Sir George Perley to suggest to you that if your company desired further negotiations, the Government would he glad to see you in Canada as soon as convenient. He pointed out that it did not seem useful to continue discussion by correspondence. He also suggested that if you came you should be invested with ample powers to conclude an arrangement if one could be reached. Your attitude towards the reasonable suggestion contained in the Prime Minister's communication seemed clearly to indicate indifference towards the continuance of negotiations. Confirmatory of this i# the peremptory notification on Thursday last to the Government, without previous intimation, or discussion, that the Grand Trunk Pacific would, on March 10th, discontinue operations, entirely regardless of consequences to Canada through interruption of traffic over a ssytem so extensive and important.
(Sgd.) W. T. White,
Acting Prime Minister."
